knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Dual-Pairing Test for Cone Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic membership test for ambient interior of a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space. Then \[x\in\operatorname{int}K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle y,x\rangle>0\quad\text{for every }y\in K^*\setminus\{0\}.\] If \(K\) is not full-dimensional, \(K^*\) contains a nonzero line and the right-hand condition is impossible, consistently with \(\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is in the ambient interior of a closed convex cone exactly when it pairs strictly positively with every nonzero dual-cone vector.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq V\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Dual-Pairing Test for Cone Interior

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling and addition rules for interior points of a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a convex cone with nonempty interior. Then \[\lambda\operatorname{int}K=\operatorname{int}K\quad(\lambda>0),\qquad \operatorname{int}K+K\subseteq\operatorname{int}K.\] Thus the sum of an interior point and any cone point remains interior. In particular, \(\operatorname{int}K\) is convex and is closed under addition and positive scaling, although it need not contain the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interior of a convex cone is stable under positive scaling and under addition of any cone element.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq V\) is a convex cone with nonempty ambient interior.

children.title: Cone Boundary Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Boundary Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient boundary, including cones with empty ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a cone \(K\subseteq V\), its ambient boundary is
\[\partial K=\operatorname{cl}K\setminus\operatorname{int}K.\]
Equivalently, \(x\in\partial K\) precisely when every open ball centered at \(x\) meets both \(K\) and \(V\setminus K\). If \(K\) is closed, then \(\partial K=K\setminus\operatorname{int}K\). In particular, a closed cone with empty ambient interior satisfies \(\partial K=K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The boundary is closure minus interior; for a closed cone it is the cone minus its interior, and equals the whole cone when that interior is empty.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial K=\operatorname{cl}K\setminus\operatorname{int}K\), and if \(K\) is closed then \(\partial K=K\setminus\operatorname{int}K\).

source_refs.locator: 2 Convex Analysis on Symmetric Matrices p. 13

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting-Dual Characterization of Cone Boundary Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual supporting-hyperplane certificates for ambient and relative boundary membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space and let \(x\in K\). Then \[x\in\partial K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y\in K^*\setminus\{0\}\text{ such that }\langle y,x\rangle=0.\] Moreover, \[x\in\operatorname{relbd}K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y\in K^*\setminus K^\perp\text{ such that }\langle y,x\rangle=0.\] In the latter case, \(x\) lies in the proper exposed face \(K\cap y^\perp\). If \(K\) has empty ambient interior and \(x\in\operatorname{ri}K\), ambient-boundary certificates necessarily come from the annihilator \(K^\perp\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ambient boundary points have a nonzero zero-pairing dual certificate; relative-boundary points require a certificate that does not annihilate the whole cone.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq V\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\partial K\iff\exists y\in K^*\setminus\{0\}:\langle y,x\rangle=0\), while \(x\in\operatorname{relbd}K\iff\exists y\in K^*\setminus K^\perp:\langle y,x\rangle=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior taken relative to the cone's linear span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty convex cone \(K\subseteq V\), its relative interior is
\[\operatorname{ri}K=\left\{x\in K:\text{there exists }\varepsilon>0\text{ such that }B(x,\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{span}K\subseteq K\right\}.\]
Every nonempty convex cone in a finite-dimensional space has \(\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{ri}K=\operatorname{int}K\) when \(\operatorname{span}K=V\); otherwise \(\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\) although \(\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative interior uses neighborhoods inside the cone's span and is nonempty for every nonempty finite-dimensional convex cone.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
\(K\subseteq V\) is a nonempty convex cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Dual-Pairing Test for Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual characterization that removes annihilators of the cone's span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space. Then \[x\in\operatorname{ri}K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in K\ \text{ and }\ \langle y,x\rangle>0\quad\text{for every }y\in K^*\setminus K^\perp.\] Dual vectors in \(K^\perp\) are excluded because they vanish identically on \(K\). For a full-dimensional cone, \(K^\perp=\{0\}\), so this reduces to the ambient-interior strict-pairing test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior points pair strictly positively with every dual vector that does not annihilate the entire cone.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq V\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{ri}K\iff x\in K\) and \(\langle y,x\rangle>0\) for every \(y\in K^*\setminus K^\perp\).

notation.meaning: vectors orthogonal to every element of K

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Dual-Pairing Test for Relative Interior

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling and addition rules internal to a convex cone's span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a nonempty convex cone. Then \[\lambda\operatorname{ri}K=\operatorname{ri}K\quad(\lambda>0),\qquad \operatorname{ri}K+K\subseteq\operatorname{ri}K.\] Thus adding any cone element to a relative-interior point cannot move it to the relative boundary. In particular, \(\operatorname{ri}K\) is convex and closed under addition and positive scaling, although it need not contain the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative interior is stable under positive scaling and under addition of arbitrary points of the cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq V\) is a nonempty convex cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Interior Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of empty ambient interior for finite-dimensional convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a nonempty convex cone. Then
\[\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{span}K\neq V.\]
Thus an empty-interior cone is contained in a proper linear subspace of its declared ambient space. Nevertheless, its relative interior in \(\operatorname{span}K\) is nonempty. Consequently empty ambient interior records a failure of full dimensionality, not an absence of relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty finite-dimensional convex cone has empty ambient interior exactly when its linear span is a proper subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(K\subseteq V\) is a nonempty convex cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual geometric equivalent of failure of ambient full dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space. Then \[\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{lin}(K^*)\neq\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K^\perp\neq\{0\}.\] Equivalently, empty ambient interior is certified by a nonzero vector \(y\) satisfying \(\langle y,x\rangle=0\) for every \(x\in K\); both \(y\) and \(-y\) then lie in \(K^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex cone has empty ambient interior exactly when its dual contains a nonzero line, equivalently when a nonzero vector annihilates the cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Cone Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness characterized by the absence of nonzero two-sided directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex cone \(K\subseteq V\) is pointed when
\[K\cap(-K)=\{0\}.\]
Equivalently, \(K\) contains no nonzero linear subspace, or no nonzero vector \(x\) together with \(-x\). Hence pointedness is exactly the condition that the lineality space of \(K\) be trivial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is pointed exactly when it contains no nonzero line, equivalently when its intersection with its negative is only zero.

notation.meaning: the set of negatives of elements of K

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the dual-interior implication without closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex cone \[K=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\] is pointed but not closed, while \[K^*=\{(0,t):t\geq0\}\] has empty ambient interior. Thus pointedness alone does not imply \(\operatorname{int}K^*\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed pointed cone can have a dual cone with empty ambient interior.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual characterization of closed pointed cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, then \[K\text{ is pointed}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{int}K^*\neq\varnothing.\] Moreover, \[y\in\operatorname{int}K^*\Longleftrightarrow\langle y,x\rangle>0\quad\forall x\in K\setminus\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex cone is pointed exactly when its dual contains a functional strictly positive on every nonzero cone vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Strictly Positive Dual Functional Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized cross-section representation of nonzero closed pointed cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonzero closed convex cone \(K\) is pointed if and only if it admits a compact convex base. Specifically, for any \(y\in\operatorname{int}K^*\), \[B_y=\{x\in K:\langle y,x\rangle=1\}\] is nonempty and compact, \(K=\{tb:t\geq0,\ b\in B_y\}\), and each nonzero \(x\in K\) has the unique normalization \(x=\langle y,x\rangle b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero closed cone is pointed exactly when it has a compact base; strictly positive dual functionals provide canonical bases.
assumptions_latex: \(K\neq\{0\}\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ pointed}\Longleftrightarrow K\text{ admits a compact convex base}.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Dimensional Cone Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full dimensionality relative to the declared ambient vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A cone \(K\subseteq V\) is full-dimensional in \(V\) when
\[\operatorname{span}K=V.\]
If \(K\) is convex and \(V\) is finite-dimensional, this condition is equivalent to \(\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\), where the interior is taken in \(V\). Full dimensionality depends on the ambient space: every nonempty convex cone is full-dimensional when regarded as a subset of \(\operatorname{span}K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is full-dimensional when it spans its ambient space; for finite-dimensional convex cones this is equivalent to nonempty ambient interior.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(K\subseteq V\) is a convex cone for the interior equivalence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp separation of full dimensionality and pointedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In every nonzero finite-dimensional space \(V\), the cone \(V\) is full-dimensional but not pointed. In \(\mathbb R^2\), the ray \(\{t(1,0):t\geq0\}\) is pointed but not full-dimensional. Hence neither property implies the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The whole space and a planar ray show that full dimensionality and pointedness are independent.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual characterization of full dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\) in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, \[K\text{ is full-dimensional}\Longleftrightarrow K^*\text{ is pointed},\] because \(\operatorname{lin}K^*=(\operatorname{span}K)^\perp\). Closedness of \(K\) is unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone spans the ambient space exactly when its dual cone is pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.

children.title: Cone Lineality Spaces

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Lineality Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The maximal linear subspace contained in a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex cone \(K\subseteq V\), its lineality space is
\[\operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K).\]
This set is a linear subspace of \(V\), is contained in \(K\), and contains every linear subspace lying in \(K\); hence it is the unique maximal linear subspace contained in \(K\). The cone is pointed exactly when \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space is the intersection of a cone with its negative and is the largest linear subspace contained in the cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K)\), the maximal linear subspace contained in \(K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex cone, lineality is the orthogonal complement of the span of its dual cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Membership invariance along the maximal linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\) with \(L=\operatorname{lin}K\), \[K+L=K.\] Consequently \(x\in K\) if and only if \(x+\ell\in K\) for every \(\ell\in L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone membership is constant on affine cosets of the lineality space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inheritance of ambient lineality by cone faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a convex cone with \(L=\operatorname{lin}K\). Every nonempty face \(F\unlhd K\) contains \(L\), and \[\operatorname{lin}F=L.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face contains and has exactly the lineality space of the ambient cone.

children.title: Quotient-Cone Reduction
children.top_down_role: Structural organization obtained after separating lineality from the pointed component.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient-Cone Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Removal of lineality by passage to a quotient vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a convex cone, let \(L=K\cap(-K)\), and let \(\pi:V\to V/L\) be the quotient map. Then the quotient cone \(\overline K=\pi(K)\) is pointed and
\[K=\pi^{-1}(\overline K),\qquad x\in K\Longleftrightarrow\pi(x)\in\overline K.\]
Thus conic membership is unchanged after collapsing every lineality direction. If \(K\) is closed in finite-dimensional \(V\), then \(\overline K\) is closed in \(V/L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting by a cone's lineality space produces a pointed cone and preserves membership; closedness is also preserved in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline K=\pi(K)\) is pointed and \(K=\pi^{-1}(\overline K)\); closed \(K\) yields closed \(\overline K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{lin}K\) and \(\pi:V\to V/L\). The dual space \((V/L)^*\) identifies with the annihilator \(L^\perp\subseteq V^*\), and under this identification \[(\pi K)^*=K^*.\] Every functional nonnegative on \(K\) therefore annihilates \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of the quotient cone is canonically the original dual cone restricted to functionals annihilating lineality.

The maps \[F\mapsto\pi(F),\qquad \bar F\mapsto\pi^{-1}(\bar F)\] are mutually inverse inclusion-preserving bijections between the nonempty faces of \(K\) and \(\bar K\). They preserve properness and strict face chains.

Then \[C:=K\cap L^\perp\] is pointed, \[K=C+L,\] and the quotient map restricts to an isomorphism from \(C\) onto \(\pi(K)\). If \(K\) is closed, then \(C\) is closed.

children.title: Cone Faces

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Faces of finite-dimensional convex cones, including improper faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a convex cone. A subset \(F\subseteq K\) is a face of \(K\) when \(F\) is convex and, whenever \(x,y\in K\) and \(0<t<1\) satisfy \(tx+(1-t)y\in F\), one has \(x,y\in F\). Every nonempty face of a convex cone is itself a convex cone. The sets \(\varnothing\) and \(K\) are the improper faces; any other face is proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is a convex subset containing both endpoints whenever it contains an interior point of a segment in the cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is a face}\Longleftrightarrow [tx+(1-t)y\in F,\ x,y\in K,\ 0<t<1\Rightarrow x,y\in F]\), with \(F\) convex.

source_refs.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

source_witnesses.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent face criterion specialized to cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\) and convex subcone \(F\subseteq K\), \[F\unlhd K\Longleftrightarrow(x,y\in K,\ x+y\in F\Rightarrow x,y\in F).\] Equivalently, \(0\preceq_Kx\preceq_Kz\) and \(z\in F\) imply \(x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subcone is a face exactly when containing a sum forces it to contain both summands.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Summand Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic lattice operations for cone faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Arbitrary intersections of faces of a convex cone \(K\) are faces. If \(G\unlhd F\) and \(F\unlhd K\), then \(G\unlhd K\). Thus the faces form a complete inclusion lattice: meet is intersection, and join is the intersection of all faces containing the union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces are closed under intersections, faciality is transitive, and cone faces form a complete lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcap_iF_i\unlhd K,\qquad G\unlhd F\unlhd K\Rightarrow G\unlhd K.
knowledge_statements.title: Face-Lattice Closure and Transitivity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Face Determined by a Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition of a cone by relative interiors of its faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-dimensional convex cone \(K\) and \(x\in K\), there is a unique face \(F_x\unlhd K\) such that \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F_x\). It is \[F_x=\bigcap\{F:F\unlhd K,\ x\in F\}.\] Hence the relative interiors of nonempty faces form a disjoint partition of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every cone point lies in the relative interior of its unique minimal containing face.

notation.meaning: minimal face of K containing x

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Face Determined by a Point

children.title: Exposed Cone Faces

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone and \(F\) is a face of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is exposed if and only if \(F=K\cap y^\perp\) for some \(y\in K^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exposed faces under the nonnegative dual-cone convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone. A face \(F\) of \(K\) is an exposed face when there exists \(y\in K^*\) such that \[F=K\cap y^\perp=\{x\in K:\langle y,x\rangle=0\}.\] Thus an exposed face is precisely the set on which a linear functional nonnegative over \(K\) attains its minimum value \(0\). The choices \(y=0\) and, when available, \(y\in\operatorname{int}K^*\) expose \(K\) and \(\{0\}\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone face is exposed when it is the zero set on the cone of a linear functional that is nonnegative throughout the cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Cone Faces

source_witnesses.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verification conditions for an exposing vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\), a vector \(y\in K^*\) exposes \(F=K\cap y^\perp\). This face is proper exactly when \[y\notin K^\perp:=K^*\cap(-K^*).\] If \(K\) is closed and pointed, every \(y\in\operatorname{int}K^*\) exposes \(\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual membership validates an exposing vector, and failure to annihilate the whole cone makes the exposed face proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\in K^*\setminus K^\perp\Longleftrightarrow K\cap y^\perp\text{ is a proper exposed face}.
knowledge_statements.title: Proper-Exposure Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of exposed faces under finite meets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F_i=K\cap y_i^\perp\) with \(y_i\in K^*\), then \[\bigcap_{i=1}^mF_i=K\cap\left(\sum_{i=1}^my_i\right)^\perp.\] Thus finite intersections of exposed faces are exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite intersection of exposed faces is exposed by the sum of their exposing vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Intersections of Exposed Faces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Principal cone class whose every face is exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every face of a finite-dimensional polyhedral cone \(K\) is exposed: for each \(F\unlhd K\), there exists \(y\in K^*\) such that \[F=K\cap y^\perp.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face of a finite-dimensional polyhedral cone is exposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall F\unlhd K\ \exists y\in K^*:\ F=K\cap y^\perp.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Cones Are Facially Exposed

children.title: Minimal Feasibility Faces
children.top_down_role: Smallest cone faces containing a specified feasible image.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Feasibility Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal face containing a feasible slack set, without assuming that it is exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, and let \(S\subseteq K\) be a nonempty set of feasible conic slacks. Its minimal feasibility face is \[F_{\min}(S):=\bigcap\{F:F\unlhd K,\ S\subseteq F\}.\] This intersection is a face of \(K\), contains \(S\), and is contained in every face of \(K\) that contains \(S\). Thus it is the unique smallest face of \(K\) containing the feasible slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal feasibility face is the intersection of all faces of the cone containing the feasible slacks, and hence is the unique smallest such face.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone and \(S\subseteq K\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\min}(S)=\bigcap\{F:F\unlhd K,\ S\subseteq F\}\) is the unique smallest face of \(K\) containing \(S\).

notation.meaning: F is a face of K
minimal face of K containing S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal Feasibility Faces Need Not Be Exposed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of one-step supporting-hyperplane recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\unlhd K\) is nonexposed and \(s\in\operatorname{ri}F\), then for \(S=\{s\}\), \[F_{\min}(S)=F.\] Hence a minimal feasibility face of a general closed convex cone need not equal \(K\cap y^\perp\) for any \(y\in K^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal feasibility face can be nonexposed, so one ambient supporting hyperplane may not recover it.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone with a nonexposed face \(F\).
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Feasibility Faces Need Not Be Exposed

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility-preserving restriction to the minimal containing face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=(b-\mathcal AX)\cap K\neq\varnothing\) be a finite-dimensional affine conic slack set and let \(F_{\min}=F_{\min}(S)\). Then \[S=(b-\mathcal AX)\cap F_{\min},\qquad S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing.\] No proper face of \(F_{\min}\) contains all of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing the cone by the minimal feasibility face preserves the slack set exactly and restores relative strict feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(S=(b-\mathcal AX)\cap K\neq\varnothing\) is a finite-dimensional affine conic slack set.

notation.meaning: range of the system's linear map

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Minimal-Face Reformulation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition of the minimal face using a relative-interior slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a finite-dimensional convex cone and \(S\subseteq K\) be nonempty and convex. For every \(s\in\operatorname{ri}S\), the minimal face of \(K\) containing \(s\) equals \(F_{\min}(S)\). Consequently, for a face \(F\) containing \(S\), \[F=F_{\min}(S)\Longleftrightarrow S\cap\operatorname{ri}F\neq\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any relative-interior slack generates the minimal feasibility face and certifies its minimality.

notation.meaning: smallest face of K containing s

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Characterization

children.title: Nonexposed Face Regimes
children.top_down_role: Facial structures not recoverable from a single supporting hyperplane.

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone and \(F\unlhd K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is nonexposed exactly when no \(y\in K^*\) satisfies \(F=K\cap y^\perp\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\unlhd K\). The face \(F\) lies in the nonexposed regime when \[F\neq K\cap y^\perp\qquad\text{for every }y\in K^*.\] Equivalently, the family of dual vectors annihilating \(F\), \(F^\triangle:=K^*\cap F^\perp\), cannot expose \(F\). The smallest exposed face containing \(F\) is \[\widehat F:=K\cap(F^\triangle)^\perp,\] and nonexposedness is characterized by the strict containment \(F\subsetneq\widehat F\). Hence facial membership alone does not ensure representation by one supporting hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexposed face is a genuine face that no nonnegative supporting functional cuts out exactly; its exposed closure is strictly larger.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonexposed Face Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Cone with Nonexposed Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit witness that closed convex cone faces need not be exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|_2\leq1\}\cup\{(2,0)\}\bigr),\qquad K=\operatorname{cone}\{(z,1):z\in C\}.\] For \(q_\pm=(1/2,\pm\sqrt3/2)\), each ray \(R_\pm=\operatorname{cone}\{(q_\pm,1)\}\) is an extreme ray of the closed pointed cone \(K\), but is not exposed: the unique supporting line of \(C\) at \(q_\pm\) also contains \((2,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coning over the convex hull of the unit disk and an exterior point produces nonexposed extreme rays at the tangency points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_\pm\unlhd K\quad\text{but}\quad R_\pm\neq K\cap y^\perp\ \forall y\in K^*.

notation.meaning: tangency points from (2,0) to the unit disk

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension Boundary for Nonexposed Cone Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lowest ambient dimension permitting nonexposed cone faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every face of a closed convex cone in a real vector space of dimension at most two is exposed. Consequently, nonexposed faces of finite-dimensional closed convex cones require ambient dimension at least three, and the preceding three-dimensional example shows sharpness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dimension three is the first ambient dimension in which a closed convex cone can have a nonexposed face.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Boundary for Nonexposed Cone Faces

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\) is a closed convex cone and \(K^{**}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}K)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative dual convention in finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cone \(K\subseteq E\), its dual cone with respect to the fixed inner product is \[K^*:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.\] The set \(K^*\) is always a closed convex cone. Its bidual satisfies \[K^{**}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}K).\] Consequently, if \(K\) is already a closed convex cone, then \(K^{**}=K\). If \(K\) is proper, meaning closed, convex, pointed, and full-dimensional, then \(K^*\) is also proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual cone consists of vectors having nonnegative inner product with every cone vector; dualization produces a closed convex cone and recovers closed convex cones after two applications.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Cone Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal-complement relations connecting degeneracy of a closed convex cone with that of its dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone and define \(\operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K)\) and \(K^\perp:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle=0\ \forall x\in K\}\). Then \[\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=K^\perp=(\operatorname{span}K)^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{span}(K^*)=(\operatorname{lin}K)^\perp.\] Consequently, \(K\) is full-dimensional exactly when \(K^*\) is pointed, and \(K\) is pointed exactly when \(K^*\) is full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality of the dual is the orthogonal complement of the primal span, while the span of the dual is the orthogonal complement of primal lineality.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.

notation.meaning: vectors orthogonal to every element of K

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Lineality and Span Orthogonality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional calculus for duals of cone inclusions, sums, and intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K,L\subseteq E\) be convex cones in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Then \[K\subseteq L\Longrightarrow L^*\subseteq K^*,\qquad (K+L)^*=K^*\cap L^*.\] If \(K\) and \(L\) are closed, then \[(K\cap L)^*=\operatorname{cl}(K^*+L^*).\] The closure cannot generally be omitted because a sum of closed convex cones need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualization reverses inclusion, converts a cone sum to an intersection of duals, and converts an intersection to the closure of a sum of duals.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K,L\subseteq E\) are convex cones; they are closed for the intersection formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\subseteq L\Rightarrow L^*\subseteq K^*\), \((K+L)^*=K^*\cap L^*\), and \((K\cap L)^*=\operatorname{cl}(K^*+L^*)\) for closed \(K,L\).
knowledge_statements.title: Order Reversal and Dual-Cone Calculus

Let \(\mathbf K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) have nonempty interior. For the degree \(d\) defining \(C_d(\mathbf K)\),

\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^{s(d)}} C_d(\mathbf K)^*\ne\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If K has nonempty interior, then the dual cone of the degree-d polynomials nonnegative on K has nonempty interior in coefficient space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual cone of the degree-bounded K-nonnegative polynomial cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the dual cone using the coefficient-vector pairing on degree-bounded polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(C_d(\mathbf K)\subseteq\mathbb R[\mathbf x]_d\), identify each \(f\in\mathbb R[\mathbf x]_d\) with its coefficient vector \(\mathbf f\in\mathbb R^{s(d)}\). Then

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cone \(K\subseteq E\), define its polar cone by \[K^\circ:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.\] Under the dual-cone convention \(K^*:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\), the two constructions differ only by sign: \[K^\circ=-K^*.\] The bipolar identity is \[K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}K).\] In particular, every closed convex cone satisfies \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the nonpositive convention, the polar cone is the negative of the dual cone, and taking the polar twice recovers every closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Polar Cone Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moreau Decomposition for a Cone and Its Polar
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal projection decomposition under the nonpositive polar convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Every \(z\in E\) has the unique orthogonal decomposition \[z=P_Kz+P_{K^\circ}z,\qquad \langle P_Kz,P_{K^\circ}z\rangle=0,\] where \(P_Cz\) denotes metric projection onto \(C\). Equivalently, \(P_{K^\circ}z=z-P_Kz\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every vector decomposes uniquely into orthogonal projections onto a closed convex cone and its nonpositive polar.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.

notation.meaning: metric projection onto the closed convex set C

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Dual Cone Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-duality relative to a specified inner product, not merely linear isomorphism with the dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone. The cone \(K\) is self-dual with respect to the specified inner product when \[K=K^*=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.\] Standard Euclidean examples include \(\mathbb R_+^n\) and, under the trace inner product, \(\mathbb S_+^n\). Self-duality is relative to the chosen inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex cone is self-dual when it equals its dual under the specified inner product; the nonnegative orthant and positive-semidefinite cone are standard examples.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is self-dual exactly when \(K=K^*\) relative to the specified inner product.

notation.meaning: dual cone under the specified inner product

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a self-dual closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Then \[\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname{span}K=E.\] Hence \(K\) is pointed and full-dimensional and therefore proper. In particular, a nontrivial linear subspace or a lower-dimensional cone cannot be self-dual in the declared ambient positive-definite inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-dual closed convex cone is necessarily pointed and full-dimensional; lower-dimensional cones and nontrivial subspaces are excluded.

\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone satisfying \(K=K^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) and define \(\langle x,y\rangle_Q:=x^\mathsf TQy\). The dual of \(K\) under this inner product is \[K^{*_{Q}}:=\{y:x^\mathsf TQy\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}=Q^{-1}K^*,\] where \(K^*\) is the Euclidean dual. Therefore duality is not intrinsic to the cone alone: changing the inner product transforms its dual. In particular, \(K\) is self-dual under \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_Q\) exactly when \[K=Q^{-1}K^*,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad QK=K^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing the inner product by a positive-definite matrix transforms the dual cone by its inverse and can change whether the cone is self-dual.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Product Dependence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-cone blocks as exact conic encodings of affine equalities.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero cone in \(\mathbb R^m\) is \[\mathcal Z^m:=\{0\}^m.\] For a linear map \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and vector \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), the affine equality system has the exact conic representation \[Ax=b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Ax-b\in\mathcal Z^m.\] Under the nonnegative dual convention, every vector pairs nonnegatively with the sole element of \(\mathcal Z^m\), so \[(\mathcal Z^m)^*=\mathbb R^m.\] Accordingly, the multiplier associated with a zero-cone equality block is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership in a zero-cone block is exactly an affine equality, and the block's dual is the full space, giving unrestricted equality multipliers.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Cone Blocks

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and Projection of the Zero Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic geometry, Euclidean projection, and strict-feasibility boundary for a zero-cone block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal Z^m=\{0\}\subseteq\mathbb R^m\), the cone is closed, convex, pointed, and polyhedral, has dimension zero and only the face \(\mathcal Z^m\), and satisfies \(\operatorname{ri}\mathcal Z^m=\{0\}\). Its Euclidean projector and distance are \[\Pi_{\mathcal Z^m}(y)=0,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(y,\mathcal Z^m)=\|y\|_2.\] These require \(O(m)\) operations when the residual norm is evaluated. If \(m>0\), then \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^m}\mathcal Z^m=\varnothing\); hence a zero-cone equality block cannot satisfy ambient-interior strict feasibility, although its sole point lies in its relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero cone is a zero-dimensional pointed polyhedral cone; projection returns zero, and positive-dimensional equality blocks have no ambient interior.
assumptions_latex: Projection, distance, and ambient interior use \(\mathbb R^m\) with its Euclidean structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{\mathcal Z^m}(y)=0\), \(\operatorname{dist}(y,\mathcal Z^m)=\|y\|_2\), and for \(m>0\), \(\operatorname{int}\mathcal Z^m=\varnothing\) while \(\operatorname{ri}\mathcal Z^m=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projector onto the zero cone

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry and Projection of the Zero Cone

children.title: Free-Space Blocks
children.top_down_role: Unrestricted vector-space factors used by solver interfaces.

assumptions_latex: \(u\in\mathbb R^m\) is a conic block variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in\mathbb R^m\) imposes no restriction, and \((\mathbb R^m)^*=\{0\}^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full vector spaces viewed as cone blocks for unrestricted primal or dual components.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The free-space cone block of dimension \(m\) is the entire vector space \[\mathcal F^m:=\mathbb R^m.\] Thus the conic membership condition \(u\in\mathcal F^m\) imposes no restriction on \(u\). Under the Euclidean inner product and the nonnegative dual convention, \[(\mathcal F^m)^*=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:y^\mathsf Tu\geq0\text{ for every }u\in\mathbb R^m\}=\{0\}^m.\] Hence a free primal block corresponds to a zero dual block, while a zero primal block corresponds to an unrestricted dual block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A free-space block permits every vector. Its dual is the zero cone, so an unrestricted primal block forces the corresponding dual component to vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Free-Space Blocks

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary cone geometry of a full vector-space block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\ge0\), \(\mathcal F^m=\mathbb R^m\) is closed, convex, and polyhedral, with \[\operatorname{span}(\mathcal F^m)=\operatorname{lin}(\mathcal F^m)=\operatorname{int}(\mathcal F^m)=\mathbb R^m.\] Its boundary is empty. For \(m>0\), it is not pointed and hence is not a proper cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A free-space block is entirely lineality and interior; in positive dimension it is nonpointed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(\mathbb R^m)=\operatorname{int}(\mathbb R^m)=\mathbb R^m\), and \(\mathbb R^m\) is nonpointed for \(m>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Geometry of a Free-Space Cone

children.title: Signed Orthant Pair
children.top_down_role: Coordinatewise inequality blocks and their sign variants.

children.title: Nonnegative Orthants
children.top_down_role: Coordinatewise nonnegative cone blocks.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb R^n\) carries the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R_+^n=\{x:x_i\geq0\ \forall i\}\) is a closed, convex, polyhedral, self-dual cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean nonnegative orthant as an elementary polyhedral cone block.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonnegative orthant in \(\mathbb R^n\) is \[\mathbb R_+^n:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x_i\geq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n\}=\operatorname{cone}\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}.\] It is a closed convex polyhedral cone. For the Euclidean inner product, \[(\mathbb R_+^n)^*=\mathbb R_+^n,\] because \(y^\mathsf Tx\geq0\) for every \(x\geq0\) holds exactly when every coordinate of \(y\) is nonnegative. For \(n\geq1\), the orthant is pointed and full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative orthant contains vectors with coordinatewise nonnegative entries; it is polyhedral, proper in positive dimension, and self-dual under the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Orthants

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection, distance, and evaluation cost for the coordinatewise nonnegative cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\Pi_{\mathbb R_+^n}(x)=x_+,\qquad (x_+)_i=\max\{x_i,0\},\] and \[\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R_+^n)=\|x_-\|_2,\qquad (x_-)_i=\max\{-x_i,0\}.\] Projection and distance are computable in \(O(n)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean projection clips negative coordinates to zero, and the negative part gives the distance residual.
assumptions_latex: Projection and distance use the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection onto the Nonnegative Orthant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete facial structure of the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \[F_I:=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:x_j=0\text{ for }j\notin I\}=\operatorname{cone}\{e_i:i\in I\}\] is a face of \(\mathbb R_+^n\), and every face is uniquely of this form. For \(n\ge1\), the extreme rays are \(\mathbb R_+e_i\), the facets are \(\{x\ge0:x_i=0\}\), and \(\operatorname{int}\mathbb R_+^n=\{x:x_i>0\ \forall i\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces of the nonnegative orthant correspond exactly to subsets of coordinates permitted to be positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The face lattice of \(\mathbb R_+^n\) is isomorphic to the Boolean lattice of subsets of \([n]\).
knowledge_statements.title: Faces of the Nonnegative Orthant

children.title: Nonpositive Orthants
children.top_down_role: Coordinatewise nonpositive cone blocks.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb R^n\) carries the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R_-^n=-\mathbb R_+^n\) is closed, convex, and polyhedral, with \((\mathbb R_-^n)^*=\mathbb R_-^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean nonpositive orthant under the nonnegative dual-cone convention.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonpositive orthant in \(\mathbb R^n\) is \[\mathbb R_-^n:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x_i\leq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n\}=-\mathbb R_+^n.\] It is a closed convex polyhedral cone. Under the nonnegative dual convention and Euclidean inner product, \[(\mathbb R_-^n)^*=\mathbb R_-^n.\] Indeed, testing the dual inequality against each vector \(-e_i\) forces every dual coordinate to be nonpositive, and that condition is sufficient. For \(n\geq1\), this cone is pointed and full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonpositive orthant is the sign reversal of the nonnegative orthant and is likewise polyhedral, proper in positive dimension, and Euclidean self-dual.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonpositive Orthants

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection, distance, and evaluation cost for the coordinatewise nonpositive cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\bigl(\Pi_{\mathbb R_-^n}(x)\bigr)_i=\min\{x_i,0\},\qquad \operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R_-^n)=\|x_+\|_2.\] Projection and distance are computable in \(O(n)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection clips positive coordinates to zero, and the positive part gives the distance residual.
assumptions_latex: Projection and distance use the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection onto the Nonpositive Orthant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete facial structure of the nonpositive orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \[F_I^-:=\{x\in\mathbb R_-^n:x_j=0\text{ for }j\notin I\}=\operatorname{cone}\{-e_i:i\in I\}\] is a face of \(\mathbb R_-^n\), and every face is uniquely of this form. For \(n\ge1\), its extreme rays are \(\mathbb R_+(-e_i)\), its facets are \(\{x\le0:x_i=0\}\), and \(\operatorname{int}\mathbb R_-^n=\{x:x_i<0\ \forall i\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces of the nonpositive orthant correspond exactly to subsets of coordinates permitted to be negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The face lattice of \(\mathbb R_-^n\) is the Boolean lattice \(\{F_I^-:I\subseteq[n]\}\).

notation.meaning: nonpositive coordinate face indexed by I

knowledge_statements.title: Faces of the Nonpositive Orthant

children.title: Orthant Sign Reversal
children.top_down_role: Representation correspondence between the two coordinatewise sign domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthant Sign Reversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign reversal as an invertible linear cone representation and its dual transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a cone and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be invertible. Dualization under the Euclidean inner product obeys \[(AK)^*=A^{-\mathsf T}K^*.\] Taking \(A=-I\) gives \[(-K)^*=-K^*.\] Consequently, the coordinatewise nonpositive constraint is the sign-reversed nonnegative constraint: \[x\in\mathbb R_-^n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -x\in\mathbb R_+^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible linear transformation sends the dual cone by the inverse transpose. In particular, negation converts nonpositive orthant membership into nonnegative orthant membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((AK)^*=A^{-\mathsf T}K^*\); in particular, \((-K)^*=-K^*\) and \(x\in\mathbb R_-^n\iff -x\in\mathbb R_+^n\).

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.3 Polar and dual cones p. 12

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection and Distance under Sign Reversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation of Euclidean nearest-point operations under cone negation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty closed convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\Pi_{-K}(x)=-\Pi_K(-x),\qquad \operatorname{dist}(x,-K)=\operatorname{dist}(-x,K).\] Thus an oracle for projection onto \(K\) yields one for \(-K\) with \(O(n)\) additional coordinate operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating a cone conjugates its Euclidean projector by negation and preserves distance after negating the query point.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Projection and distance use the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection and Distance under Sign Reversal

children.title: Mixed-Sign Orthant Products
children.top_down_role: Product domains combining coordinate blocks with differing sign orientations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form Euclidean projection, distance, and evaluation cost for a fixed coordinate sign pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K_s=\{x:s_i x_i\ge0\ \forall i\}\), \[\bigl(\Pi_{K_s}(x)\bigr)_i=s_i\max\{s_i x_i,0\},\qquad \operatorname{dist}(x,K_s)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\max\{-s_i x_i,0\}^2.\] Both quantities are computable in \(O(n)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection clips each coordinate after orienting it by its prescribed sign; squared distance sums the squared sign violations.
assumptions_latex: Projection and distance use the Euclidean norm.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projector onto the mixed-sign orthant

knowledge_statements.title: Projection onto a Mixed-Sign Orthant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic geometry of the orthant selected by a fixed sign vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_s=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\) for \(s\in\{-1,1\}^n\), and let \(K_s=D_s\mathbb R_+^n\). For \(n\ge1\), \(K_s\) is a closed, full-dimensional, pointed polyhedral cone and, under the Euclidean pairing, \(K_s^*=K_s\). Its interior is \(\{x:s_i x_i>0\ \forall i\}\). Every face is uniquely of the form \[F_I=\operatorname{cone}\{s_i e_i:i\in I\}=\{x\in K_s:x_j=0\text{ for }j\notin I\},\qquad I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}.\] Its extreme rays are \(\mathbb R_+(s_i e_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-sign orthant is a proper Euclidean-self-dual polyhedral cone whose faces select the signed coordinate rays allowed to be nonzero.
assumptions_latex: Duality uses the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_s^*=K_s\), \(\operatorname{int}K_s=\{x:s_i x_i>0\}\), and \(\{F_I:I\subseteq[n]\}\) is its complete face lattice.

notation.meaning: face generated by signed coordinate rays indexed by I

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Orthant Geometry and Faces
Mixed-Sign Orthant Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise sign patterns and equivalent products of positive and negative orthants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sign vector \(s\in\{-1,1\}^n\), the mixed-sign orthant is \[K_s:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:s_i x_i\ge 0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n\}.\] If \(P:=\{i:s_i=1\}\) and \(N:=\{i:s_i=-1\}\), then coordinate permutation identifies \(K_s\) with \(\mathbb{R}_+^{|P|}\times\mathbb{R}_-^{|N|}\). Equivalently, \(K_s=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\mathbb{R}_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-sign orthant imposes a chosen nonnegative or nonpositive sign on each coordinate and is a signed image of the nonnegative orthant.

notation.meaning: orthant determined by the sign vector s

children.title: Polyhedral Representation Duality
children.top_down_role: Finite generator and half-space descriptions of polyhedral cone domains.

children.title: Polyhedral Generator Representations
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral cone domains organized through finite generating rays.

notation.meaning: matrix whose columns are the generating vectors
nonnegative hull of the listed vectors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite conic-hull descriptions of polyhedral cones in Euclidean space.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,p\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(v_1,\ldots,v_p\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Their finitely generated cone is \[\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_p):=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^p\lambda_jv_j:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^p\right\}.\] A generator representation of a polyhedral cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is an equality \(K=\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_p)\), equivalently \(K=V\mathbb{R}_+^p\), where \(V=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_p]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generator representation expresses a polyhedral cone as all nonnegative linear combinations of a finite, explicitly indexed family of vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Generator Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Span and Full Dimensionality from Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient span and interior criterion visible from a finite generator matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=V\mathbb R_+^p\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). Then \[\operatorname{span}K=\operatorname{range}V.\] Hence \(K\) is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb R^n\) if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}V=n\), equivalently if and only if \(K\) has nonempty ambient interior. Every finitely generated cone is convex and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The span of a finitely generated cone is the generator matrix's column space, so full dimensionality is exactly full row rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Span and Full Dimensionality from Generators

children.title: Polyhedral Inequality Representations
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral cone domains organized through homogeneous linear inequalities.

notation.meaning: cone defined by the homogeneous inequalities Ax greater than or equal to zero

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite homogeneous half-space descriptions of polyhedral cones.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\). The set \[K_A:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge0\}\] is a polyhedral cone, where the inequality is componentwise. An inequality representation of a polyhedral cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is an equality \(K=K_A\). If \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\) denotes row \(i\) of \(A\), this is equivalently \[K=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\ge0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality representation expresses a polyhedral cone as the intersection of a finite, explicitly indexed family of homogeneous closed half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Inequality Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality and Strict Feasibility of an Inequality Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel, pointedness, and full-dimensionality information from a homogeneous inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge0\}\). Then \[\operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K)=\ker A,\] so \(K\) is pointed if and only if \(\ker A=\{0\}\). After zero rows are discarded, \(K\) is full-dimensional if and only if there exists \(\bar x\) with \(A\bar x>0\); in that case \[\operatorname{int}K=\{x:Ax>0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality is the matrix kernel; pointedness means a trivial kernel, and strict feasibility characterizes full dimensionality after zero rows are removed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}K=\ker A\), and after deleting zero rows, \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\iff\exists\bar x:A\bar x>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality and Strict Feasibility of an Inequality Cone

children.title: Generator–Inequality Conversion
children.top_down_role: Structural conversion between ray-based and half-space-based cone descriptions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) has a finite generator representation if and only if it has a finite homogeneous inequality representation, with the displayed polar conversions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minkowski-Weyl equivalence and polar conversion for finite-dimensional polyhedral cones.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a cone. Then \(K\) is generated by finitely many vectors if and only if it is the intersection of finitely many homogeneous closed half-spaces. More precisely, if \(p\in\mathbb{N}\), \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\), and \(K=V\mathbb{R}_+^p\), then \[K^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:V^{\mathsf T}y\le0\}.\] Conversely, if \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge0\}\), and \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\) is row \(i\) of \(A\), then \[K^\circ=\operatorname{cone}(-a_1,\ldots,-a_m).\] Because every finitely generated or finitely inequality-defined cone is closed and convex, applying polarity twice recovers \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, finite generator and finite homogeneous inequality descriptions are equivalent; negative polarity converts generator columns into inequalities and inequality-row normals into generators.
knowledge_statements.title: Generator–Inequality Conversion

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact incremental conversion between finite ray and homogeneous half-space descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a pointed polyhedral cone represented by its extreme rays, an incremental double-description method adds one homogeneous inequality at a time. It retains rays on the nonnegative side and obtains candidate rays on the new boundary from appropriate adjacent extreme-ray pairs lying on opposite sides, followed by removal of nonextreme or duplicate candidates. Repeating the update yields the extreme rays of the final intersection. Applying the same construction to the polar cone converts a finite generator description to inequalities. Exact arithmetic gives finite termination, but intermediate and final descriptions may be exponentially large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The double-description method adds half-spaces incrementally, creates new boundary rays from adjacent crossing pairs, and removes nonextreme candidates.
assumptions_latex: The cone and data are finite-dimensional and polyhedral.
The maintained cone is pointed; lineality must otherwise be handled separately.
Arithmetic and sign tests are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite double-description updates produce an exact representation of the opposite type.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Double-Description Conversion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic output-size obstruction for generator–inequality conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(d\ge1\), the homogenized cone over the \(d\)-dimensional cross-polytope has \(2d\) extreme rays and \(2^d\) facets. Thus an irredundant ray-to-inequality conversion must sometimes output exponentially many inequalities. Polarity gives the reverse separation. Consequently, exact conversion cannot have running time polynomial solely in the smaller description and the dimension; its complexity must account for output size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ray and facet descriptions can differ exponentially in size, so exact conversion is necessarily output-sensitive.
assumptions_latex: Writing each output item has nonzero cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(2d\) extreme rays can require \(2^d\) facet inequalities, and polarity yields the reverse separation.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Output-Size Boundary

children.title: Redundant Polyhedral Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Representations containing unnecessary rays or dominated inequalities.

assumptions_latex: Generator and inequality families are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each applicable index \(j\), deletion preserves \(K\) exactly under the corresponding conic-hull membership condition.

notation.meaning: normal of the candidate redundant inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact redundancy tests for homogeneous inequalities and finite generators.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,p\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(v_1,\ldots,v_p\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(K=\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_p)\). For each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\), generator \(v_j\) is redundant if and only if \[v_j\in\operatorname{cone}(v_i:i\ne j).\] Separately, let \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\ge0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}\). For each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), inequality \(a_j^{\mathsf T}x\ge0\) is redundant if and only if \[a_j\in\operatorname{cone}(a_i:i\ne j).\] In each case, deleting the indicated item leaves \(K\) unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generator is redundant exactly when it belongs to the conic hull of the remaining generators; a homogeneous inequality is redundant exactly when its normal belongs to the conic hull of the remaining normals.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Polyhedral Descriptions

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immediate nonminimality caused by zero or repeated representation elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a finite generator description, a zero generator or a generator that is a positive multiple of another generator is redundant. In a homogeneous inequality description, a zero row is vacuous, and positive scalar multiples define the same half-space, so all but one are redundant. Negative scalar multiples are not duplicate inequalities: together they impose an equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero elements and positive duplicates are redundant, whereas opposite inequality normals jointly encode an equality.
assumptions_latex: The descriptions are finite and homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive rescaling preserves a ray or half-space, while opposite inequality normals are not redundant duplicates.
knowledge_statements.title: Duplicate and Positive-Scaling Redundancy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Irredundant Descriptions by Extreme Rays and Facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical minimal descriptions under pointedness and full dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a full-dimensional pointed polyhedral cone. A finite nonzero generator family is irredundant if and only if it contains exactly one positive multiple of a vector on each extreme ray of \(K\). A finite nonzero homogeneous inequality family is irredundant if and only if its inequalities define the distinct facets of \(K\). Thus irredundant descriptions of either type are unique up to permutation and positive rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional pointed polyhedral cone, irredundant generators are its extreme rays and irredundant inequalities are its facets.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is full-dimensional, pointed, and polyhedral.
All listed generators and inequality normals are nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{irredundant generators}\leftrightarrow\text{extreme rays}\) and \(\text{irredundant inequalities}\leftrightarrow\text{facets}\), up to positive scaling and permutation.
knowledge_statements.title: Irredundant Descriptions by Extreme Rays and Facets

knowledge_statements.title: Lorentz Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard second-order cone in each finite dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ge2\), the \(d\)-dimensional Lorentz cone is \[\mathcal{Q}^d:=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{d-1}:t\ge\|x\|_2\}.\] It is a closed, pointed, full-dimensional convex cone. Under the Euclidean inner product it is self-dual: \((\mathcal{Q}^d)^*=\mathcal{Q}^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lorentz cone consists of scalar-vector pairs whose scalar component dominates the vector's Euclidean norm; it is closed, pointed, full-dimensional, and self-dual.
assumptions_latex: The ambient inner product is Euclidean.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit linear isomorphism between standard and rotated second-order cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) by \[T(u,v,w)=(u+v,\ u-v,\ \sqrt2\,w).\] Then \(T\) is invertible, with \[T^{-1}(t,z_1,z')=\left(\frac{t+z_1}{2},\frac{t-z_1}{2},\frac{z'}{\sqrt2}\right),\] and \(T(\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm r}^d)=\mathcal{Q}^d\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete face classification for the standard Lorentz cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Real Symmetric Positive-Semidefinite Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the real PSD cone of side dimension \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an integer \(n\ge 1\), let \(\mathbb S^n=\{X\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}:X=X^{\mathsf T}\}\). The real symmetric positive-semidefinite cone is
\[
\mathbb S_+^n=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:u^{\mathsf T}Xu\ge 0\text{ for every }u\in\mathbb R^n\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\) precisely when every eigenvalue of \(X\) is nonnegative. This is a closed convex cone in the real inner-product space \(\mathbb S^n\), equipped with \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(XY)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The real PSD cone consists of symmetric matrices whose quadratic forms are nonnegative, equivalently whose eigenvalues are all nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb S_+^n=\{X=X^{\mathsf T}:u^{\mathsf T}Xu\ge0\ \forall u\in\mathbb R^n\}\) is a closed convex cone.

notation.meaning: real vector space of symmetric n-by-n matrices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes real PSD membership by principal determinant inequalities and gives the sharp failure of a leading-minors-only test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\in\mathbb S^n\),
\[
X\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \det X[I,I]\ge0\quad\text{for every }I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\},
\]
with the empty principal minor equal to one. Leading principal minors alone are insufficient for semidefiniteness: for example, \(\operatorname{diag}(0,-1)\) has nonnegative leading principal minors \(0,0\) but is not positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric matrix is PSD exactly when all principal minors are nonnegative; unlike the positive-definite criterion, leading principal minors alone do not suffice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\succeq0\iff\det X[I,I]\ge0\) for every principal index set \(I\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivatives of a log-determinant ratio at the origin
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local matrix-calculus identity under explicitly prescribed trace data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G(\alpha) be twice differentiable near 0, symmetric positive definite there, and let V(\alpha)=\ln(\det G(0)/\det G(\alpha)). Suppose real \tau_1,\ldots,\tau_n satisfy \operatorname{Tr}(G(0)^{-1}G'(0))=\sum_{i=1}^n(\tau_i-1) and \operatorname{Tr}(G(0)^{-1}G''(0)-G(0)^{-1}G'(0)G(0)^{-1}G'(0))=-\sum_{i=1}^n(\tau_i-1)^2. Then V'(0)=n-\sum_{i=1}^n\tau_i and V''(0)=\sum_{i=1}^n(\tau_i-1)^2. In particular, if (\|g\|_D^*)^2=\sum_i\tau_i, then V'(0)=n-(\|g\|_D^*)^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice-differentiable positive-definite matrix curve whose first two trace expressions have the stated coordinate forms, the log-determinant ratio has first derivative n minus the sum of the parameters and second derivative equal to the sum of their squared deviations from one.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the canonical primal SDP and its value conventions, and records its convexity and relationship to linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S_p\) be the real symmetric \(p\times p\) matrices, with \(A\succeq B\) meaning \(A-B\) is positive semidefinite and \(\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB)\). A canonical semidefinite program is \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{c^Tx:F(x):=F_0+\sum_{i=1}^nF_ix_i\succeq0\right\}.\] Its matrix constraint is a linear matrix inequality. Its value is \(-\infty\) when unbounded below and \(+\infty\) when infeasible; \(\min P\) denotes a finite value attained by some feasible \(x^*\). The feasible set is convex. When all coefficient matrices are diagonal, the LMI is a finite system of linear inequalities, and conversely any finite linear-inequality system can be represented by a diagonal LMI.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite program minimizes a linear objective subject to an affine symmetric matrix being positive semidefinite. This LMI defines a convex feasible set. The value is minus infinity for an unbounded problem and plus infinity for an infeasible problem, while “minimum” indicates attainment. Diagonal LMIs are exactly finite systems of linear inequalities, so linear programming is a special case of semidefinite programming.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{c^Tx:F_0+\sum_{i=1}^nF_ix_i\succeq0\right\}\text{ is a convex optimization problem, and diagonal LMIs represent linear inequalities.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation and reflection of positive semidefiniteness and positive definiteness under \(A\mapsto B^\top AB\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb S^n\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), and \(C=B^\top AB\in\mathbb S^m\). Then:
\[
A\succeq0\implies C\succeq0.
\]
If \(A\succ0\), then
\[
C\succ0\iff\operatorname{rank}B=m.
\]
If \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is invertible, then
\[
A\succ0\iff C\succ0,
\qquad
A\succeq0\iff C\succeq0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Congruence by any real matrix preserves positive semidefiniteness. When A is positive definite, the transformed matrix is positive definite exactly when B has full column rank. An invertible square congruence preserves and reflects both positive definiteness and positive semidefiniteness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\succeq0\Rightarrow C\succeq0;\quad A\succ0\Rightarrow(C\succ0\iff\operatorname{rank}B=m);\quad B\text{ square and invertible}\Rightarrow[(A\succ0\iff C\succ0)\land(A\succeq0\iff C\succeq0)]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Definiteness of a Real Symmetric Matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-form definitions and notation for positive and negative semidefiniteness and definiteness, including the invertibility boundary within the PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb S^n\),
\[
A\succeq0\iff x^\top Ax\geq0\quad\forall x\in\mathbb R^n,
\qquad
A\succ0\iff x^\top Ax>0\quad\forall x\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}.
\]
Define \(A\preceq0\iff-A\succeq0\) and \(A\prec0\iff-A\succ0\). If \(A\succeq0\), then
\[
A\succ0\iff A\text{ is invertible}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite when its quadratic form is nonnegative everywhere and positive definite when it is strictly positive on every nonzero vector. Negative semidefiniteness and definiteness are defined through negation. Within the PSD cone, positive definiteness is equivalent to invertibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equip \(\mathbb H^n\) with the real inner product \(\langle H,K\rangle=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(HK)=\operatorname{tr}(HK)\) for Hermitian \(H,K\). Then \[\left(\mathbb H_+^n\right)^*=\mathbb H_+^n.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral and Gram Characterizations of Hermitian Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent intrinsic membership and strict-membership conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(H=H^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\), \[H\succeq0\iff\lambda_{\min}(H)\ge0\iff H=C^*C\text{ for some complex }C.\] Moreover, \(H\in\operatorname{int}\mathbb H_+^n\) exactly when \(H\succ0\), equivalently all eigenvalues are positive.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transitive congruence action on the positive-definite interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonsingular \(G\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\), \(H\mapsto GHG^*\) is an automorphism of \(\mathbb H_+^n\). For any \(H_1,H_2\succ0\), some nonsingular \(G\) satisfies \(GH_1G^*=H_2\); hence \(\mathbb H_+^n\) is homogeneous.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric and Image Structure of Hermitian Realification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structured real image and trace-pairing scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-I\\I&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathcal R(A+\mathrm iB)=\begin{pmatrix}A&-B\\B&A\end{pmatrix}\). Then \[\mathcal R(\mathbb H^n)=\{M\in\mathbb S^{2n}:MJ=JM\},\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\mathcal R(H)\mathcal R(K))=2\operatorname{tr}(HK).\] Thus \(2^{-1/2}\mathcal R\) is an isometry. If a free real matrix variable is used in place of \(\mathcal R(H)\), the commuting equations are required to restrict it to the exact realification image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Realification occupies the symmetric matrices commuting with the complex structure and doubles trace inner products.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\) uses the displayed block convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R(\mathbb H^n)=\{M\in\mathbb S^{2n}:MJ=JM\}\) and \(\langle\mathcal R(H),\mathcal R(K)\rangle_F=2\langle H,K\rangle_{\mathrm{tr}}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces of the Hermitian PSD Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complex-subspace classification of Hermitian PSD faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a complex linear subspace \(L\subseteq\mathbb C^n\), define \[F_L^{\mathbb C}=\{H\in\mathbb H_+^n:\operatorname{range}(H)\subseteq L\}.\] Every face of \(\mathbb H_+^n\) is uniquely of this form. If \(U\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}\) has orthonormal columns spanning \(L\), then \[F_L^{\mathbb C}=\{USU^*:S\in\mathbb H_+^r\},\quad \operatorname{ri}F_L^{\mathbb C}=\{USU^*:S\in\mathbb H_{++}^r\},\quad \dim_{\mathbb R}F_L^{\mathbb C}=r^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Hermitian PSD face is supported on a unique complex subspace and is a smaller Hermitian PSD cone.
assumptions_latex: \(L\subseteq\mathbb C^n\) is a complex linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every face is uniquely \(F_L^{\mathbb C}\cong\mathbb H_+^r\), with real dimension \(r^2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Faces of the Hermitian PSD Cone
Complex Hermitian Positive-Semidefinite Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines Hermitian PSD matrices and their real symmetric solver embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(H=A+\mathrm iB\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\), Hermitian symmetry is equivalent to \(A^{\mathsf T}=A\) and \(B^{\mathsf T}=-B\). Define
\[
\mathbb H_+^n=\{H=H^*:z^*Hz\ge0\text{ for every }z\in\mathbb C^n\}.
\]
The realification
\[
\mathcal R(H)=\begin{pmatrix}A&-B\\B&A\end{pmatrix}
\]
is real symmetric and satisfies \(H\in\mathbb H_+^n\) if and only if \(\mathcal R(H)\in\mathbb S_+^{2n}\). Thus a complex Hermitian PSD constraint has an exact structured real PSD representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hermitian matrix is PSD exactly when its structured twice-sized realification is a real symmetric PSD matrix.

source_refs.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a subspace \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
F_L=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{range}(X)\subseteq L\}.
\]
Then \(F_L\) is a face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\), and every face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) has this form for a unique subspace \(L\). If \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) has orthonormal columns spanning \(L\), then
\[
F_L=\{USU^{\mathsf T}:S\in\mathbb S_+^r\}.
\]
Consequently, \(F_L\) is linearly isomorphic to \(\mathbb S_+^r\), where \(r=\dim L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face of the real PSD cone consists of matrices whose ranges lie in one fixed subspace, and is itself a smaller PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Faces

source_witnesses.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposing and Conjugate Faces of the PSD Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Every real PSD face is exposed, with an orthogonal conjugate face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(P_{L^\perp}\) be the orthogonal projector onto \(L^\perp\). Then \[F_L=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\langle P_{L^\perp},X\rangle=0\}.\] Hence every face is exposed, and under trace self-duality \[F_L^{\triangle}=\mathbb S_+^n\cap F_L^\perp=F_{L^\perp}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projector onto the orthogonal complement exposes each PSD face, whose conjugate face is supported on that complement.

notation.meaning: orthogonal projector onto the complement of L
conjugate face in the self-dual PSD cone

children.title: Positive-Semidefinite Rank Strata
