knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity of exact copositivity recognition for rational symmetric input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a symmetric matrix with rational entries encoded in binary, deciding membership in \(\operatorname{COP}_n\) is co-NP-complete when the dimension is part of the input. Thus the quadratic-form definition is an exact universal test but does not yield a polynomial-time recognition method in general, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact copositivity recognition for rational matrices is co-NP-complete when dimension varies.
assumptions_latex: The input is a rational symmetric matrix encoded in binary.
The matrix order is part of the input.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact interior test for the copositive cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb S^n\),
\[
A\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{COP}_n)
\iff x^{\mathsf T}Ax>0\quad\text{for every }0\ne x\in\mathbb R_+^n.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\min\{x^{\mathsf T}Ax:x\ge0,\ \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}x=1\}>0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A copositive matrix is interior exactly when its quadratic form is strictly positive on every nonzero nonnegative vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Copositivity and Interior Membership

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp dimension boundary for the elementary inner representation of the copositive cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb N^n=\{N\in\mathbb S^n:N_{ij}\ge0\}\). Then
\[
\operatorname{COP}_n=\mathbb S_+^n+\mathbb N^n\quad(n\le4),
\qquad
\mathbb S_+^n+\mathbb N^n\subsetneq\operatorname{COP}_n\quad(n\ge5).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Copositive matrices are exactly PSD-plus-entrywise-nonnegative through order four; from order five that cone is a strict inner approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Dimensional PSD-Plus-Nonnegative Characterization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence and solution recovery for SDP hierarchies approximating a copositive program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes attainment, monotone value convergence, and accumulation-point recovery under finite-value, linear-independence, and primal and dual interiority assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be the copositive program with finite optimal value \(\rho\), and suppose that \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) are linearly independent. Assume that for some \(d_0,d_1\) there exist \(X_0\in\mathcal S^n\) and \(\lambda_0\in\mathbb R^m\) such that
\[
\langle A_i,X_0\rangle=b_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad X_0\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal K_{d_0}^{2}),
\]
\[
C-\sum_{i=1}^m(\lambda_0)_iA_i\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal C_{d_1}^*).
\]
Then \(P\) and \(P^*\) both have optimal solutions. For the associated SDP-hierarchy values \(\rho_d\) and \(\psi_d\),
\[
\rho_d\downarrow\rho,\qquad \psi_d\uparrow\rho\qquad(d\to\infty).
\]
For every \(d\geq d_1\), problem (12.17) has an optimizer \(X_d^*\in\mathcal C_d\), and every accumulation point of \((X_d^*)_{d\geq d_1}\) is optimal for \(P\). For every \(d\geq d_0\), problem (12.16) has an optimizer \(\lambda_d^*\in\mathbb R^m\), and every accumulation point of \((\lambda_d^*)_{d\geq d_0}\) is optimal for \(P^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the copositive program has finite value, the constraint matrices are linearly independent, and the stated primal and dual approximation cones contain strictly feasible points at specified levels, then the original primal and dual programs attain their optima. The two SDP value sequences converge monotonically from above and below to the copositive-program value. Optimizers exist at the stated hierarchy levels, and every accumulation point of either optimizer sequence solves the corresponding original program.
assumptions_latex: \exists d_0,\ X_0\in\mathcal S^n:\ \langle A_i,X_0\rangle=b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ X_0\in\operatorname{int}(\mathcal K_{d_0}^{2})
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ and }P^*\text{ attain their optima};\quad \rho_d\downarrow\rho,\ \psi_d\uparrow\rho;\quad \operatorname{acc}(X_d^*)\subseteq\operatorname{Argmin}(P),\ \operatorname{acc}(\lambda_d^*)\subseteq\operatorname{Argmax}(P^*),\text{ with optimizer existence for }d\geq d_1\text{ and }d\geq d_0\text{ respectively}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines two tractable inner-approximation families and states their linear and semidefinite representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(\mathcal K_0:=\mathcal N^n+\mathcal S_+^n\subseteq\mathcal C\). For \(d\geq1\) and \(S\in\mathcal S^n\), define \(p_d^S(x):=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^d\sum_{i,j=1}^n x_i^2x_j^2S_{ij}\), \(\mathcal K_d^1:=\{S\in\mathcal S^n:p_d^S\text{ has nonnegative coefficients}\}\), and \(\mathcal K_d^2:=\{S\in\mathcal S^n:p_d^S\text{ is SOS}\}\). For each \(d\), membership in \(\mathcal K_d^1\) is described by linear inequalities in the entries of \(S\), while membership in \(\mathcal K_d^2\) is described by linear matrix inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two inner hierarchies are formed by requiring the associated homogenized polynomial either to have nonnegative coefficients or to be a sum of squares. The former is linearly representable and the latter semidefinite representable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal K_d^1=\{S\in\mathcal S^n:p_d^S\text{ has nonnegative coefficients}\},\qquad \mathcal K_d^2=\{S\in\mathcal S^n:p_d^S\text{ is SOS}\},\quad \mathcal K_d^1\text{ is LP-representable and }\mathcal K_d^2\text{ is LMI-representable}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Copositive programs and their conic duals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines copositive matrices and states the primal–dual conic formulation over the copositive and completely positive cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A matrix \(A\in\mathcal S^n\) is copositive if and only if \(x^TAx\geq 0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R_+^n\). Let \(\mathcal C\) be the cone of copositive matrices and let \(\mathcal C^*\) be its dual, the cone of completely positive matrices. A copositive program and its dual have the forms
\[
\rho=\inf_X\left\{\langle C,X\rangle:\langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ X\in\mathcal C\right\},
\]
\[
\rho^*=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m}\left\{b^T\lambda:C-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iA_i\in\mathcal C^*\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric matrix is copositive exactly when its quadratic form is nonnegative on the nonnegative orthant. A copositive program minimizes a linear functional over an affine slice of the copositive cone, while its conic dual requires the dual slack to lie in the completely positive cone.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal C^*\text{ is the completely positive cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho=\inf_X\{\langle C,X\rangle:\langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ X\in\mathcal C\},\qquad \rho^*=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m}\{b^T\lambda:C-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iA_i\in\mathcal C^*\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of coefficientwise and SOS inner hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States monotonicity and asymptotic exactness of the primal inner cones and their dual outer cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal K_0^i:=\mathcal K_0\) and let \(\mathcal K_d^i\), \(i\in\{1,2\}\), be the coefficientwise and SOS cones. For every \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(\mathcal K_d^i\subseteq\mathcal K_{d+1}^i\subseteq\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal C^*\subseteq(\mathcal K_{d+1}^i)^*\subseteq(\mathcal K_d^i)^*\). Moreover, \(\overline{\bigcup_{d=0}^{\infty}\mathcal K_d^i}=\mathcal C\) and \(\bigcap_{d=0}^{\infty}(\mathcal K_d^i)^*=\mathcal C^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both inner hierarchies increase inside the copositive cone and are dense in it. Their dual cones decrease and intersect exactly in the completely positive cone.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal K_d^i\text{ is the coefficientwise or SOS hierarchy}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal K_d^i\subseteq\mathcal K_{d+1}^i\subseteq\mathcal C,\quad \mathcal C^*\subseteq(\mathcal K_{d+1}^i)^*\subseteq(\mathcal K_d^i)^*,\quad \overline{\bigcup_{d=0}^{\infty}\mathcal K_d^i}=\mathcal C,\quad \bigcap_{d=0}^{\infty}(\mathcal K_d^i)^*=\mathcal C^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The completely positive cone of order \(n\) is
\[
\operatorname{CP}_n
=
\operatorname{cone}\{xx^{\mathsf T}:x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(A\in\operatorname{CP}_n\) if and only if there exist an integer \(r\ge1\) and an entrywise nonnegative matrix \(V\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n\times r}\) such that \(A=VV^{\mathsf T}\). Under the trace pairing, the completely positive and copositive cones are dual:
\[
\operatorname{CP}_n^*=\operatorname{COP}_n,
\qquad
\operatorname{COP}_n^*=\operatorname{CP}_n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is completely positive when it factors as a nonnegative matrix times its transpose; the completely positive cone is dual to the copositive cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Completely Positive Cones

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and Extreme Rays of the Completely Positive Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional geometry and bounded nonnegative rank-one generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cone \(\operatorname{CP}_n\subseteq\mathbb S^n\) is closed, convex, pointed, and full-dimensional. Its extreme rays are exactly
\[
\{\mathbb R_+xx^{\mathsf T}:0\ne x\in\mathbb R_+^n\}.
\]
Every \(A\in\operatorname{CP}_n\) has a decomposition
\[
A=\sum_{k=1}^r x_kx_k^{\mathsf T},\qquad x_k\in\mathbb R_+^n,
\]
with \(r\le n(n+1)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The completely positive cone is a proper full-dimensional cone whose extreme rays are the nonnegative rank-one matrices, and every member has a bounded such decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ExtRays}(\operatorname{CP}_n)=\{\mathbb R_+xx^{\mathsf T}:0\ne x\ge0\}\), and every member uses at most \(n(n+1)/2\) generators.

notation.meaning: Extreme rays of the completely positive cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb{N}^n=\{A\in\mathbb{S}^n:A_{ij}\ge0\text{ for all }i,j\}\). The doubly nonnegative cone is
\[
\operatorname{DNN}_n=\mathbb{S}_+^n\cap\mathbb{N}^n
=\{A\in\mathbb{S}^n:A\succeq0,\ A_{ij}\ge0\text{ for all }i,j\}.
\]
It is a closed convex cone with an explicit semidefinite-plus-linear-inequality description. Every completely positive matrix is doubly nonnegative, so
\[
\operatorname{CP}_n\subseteq\operatorname{DNN}_n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A doubly nonnegative matrix is simultaneously positive semidefinite and entrywise nonnegative. The resulting closed convex cone contains every completely positive matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Doubly Nonnegative Cones

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual of the Doubly Nonnegative Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trace-dual representation of the PSD-and-entrywise-nonnegative intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the trace pairing on \(\mathbb S^n\),
\[
\operatorname{DNN}_n^*=(\mathbb S_+^n\cap\mathbb N^n)^*=\mathbb S_+^n+\mathbb N^n.
\]
Consequently, \(Y\in\operatorname{DNN}_n^*\) exactly when \(Y=P+N\) for some \(P\succeq0\) and entrywise nonnegative symmetric \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of the doubly nonnegative cone is the sum of the PSD cone and the entrywise nonnegative symmetric cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global nonnegativity for real polynomials of bounded degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb{R}[x]_{\le 2d}\) be the vector space of real polynomials in \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) of degree at most \(2d\). The polynomial nonnegativity cone is
\[
P_{n,2d}:=\{p\in\mathbb{R}[x]_{\le 2d}:p(u)\ge 0\text{ for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.
\]
It is a closed convex cone: if \(p,q\in P_{n,2d}\) and \(\alpha,\beta\ge0\), then \(\alpha p+\beta q\in P_{n,2d}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cone consists of all real polynomials of degree at most 2d that are nonnegative at every point of real n-space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{n,2d}\) is a closed convex cone in \(\mathbb{R}[x]_{\le 2d}\).

notation.meaning: Real polynomials in n variables of degree at most 2d.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior and Properness of the Nonnegativity Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient-space geometry of the bounded-degree global nonnegativity cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p\in\mathbb R[x]_{\le 2d}\), let \(p^h\) be its degree-\(2d\) homogenization. Then
\[
p\in\operatorname{int}P_{n,2d}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p^h(z)>0\quad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb R^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}.
\]
Consequently, \(P_{n,2d}\) is full-dimensional and pointed and, together with its closedness and convexity, is a proper cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-degree nonnegative polynomial is an interior point exactly when its homogenization is positive away from the origin; the nonnegativity cone is proper.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior and Properness of the Nonnegativity Cone

children.title: Sum-of-Squares Cones
children.top_down_role: Polynomial cones admitting sum-of-squares certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Sum-of-Squares Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-degree sums of squares of real polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n,d\in\mathbb{N}\), the sum-of-squares cone is
\[
\Sigma_{n,2d}:=\left\{p\in\mathbb{R}[x]_{\le 2d}:p=\sum_{j=1}^{r}q_j^2\text{ for some }r\in\mathbb{N}\text{ and }q_j\in\mathbb{R}[x]_{\le d}\right\}.
\]
Every squared summand is pointwise nonnegative, so \(\Sigma_{n,2d}\subseteq P_{n,2d}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The SOS cone contains polynomials expressible as finite sums of squares of polynomials of degree at most d; every such polynomial is globally nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Sigma_{n,2d}\) is a convex cone and \(\Sigma_{n,2d}\subseteq P_{n,2d}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual SOS Cone as Positive Quadratic Functionals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic dual characterization of the bounded-degree SOS cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A linear functional \(L\in(\mathbb R[x]_{\le2d})^*\) belongs to the dual SOS cone exactly when
\[
L(q^2)\ge0\qquad\text{for every }q\in\mathbb R[x]_{\le d}.
\]
Equivalently, the bilinear form \((q,r)\mapsto L(qr)\) is positive semidefinite; in monomial coordinates its truncated moment matrix is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual SOS cone consists of linear functionals nonnegative on every degree-bounded square, equivalently functionals with a positive-semidefinite truncated moment matrix.

notation.meaning: Dual cone of the SOS cone under coefficient-functional pairing.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual SOS Cone as Positive Quadratic Functionals

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Proper Geometry of the SOS Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic coefficient-space geometry; the Gram representation remains in its sibling interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n,d\ge1\), the bounded-degree SOS cone \(\Sigma_{n,2d}\subset\mathbb R[x]_{\le2d}\) is closed, convex, pointed, and full-dimensional. Its interior consists precisely of polynomials admitting a positive-definite Gram matrix in the full monomial basis of degree at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bounded-degree SOS cone is proper, and its interior consists of the strictly SOS polynomials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Sigma_{n,2d}\text{ is closed, convex, pointed, and full-dimensional, and }\operatorname{int}\Sigma_{n,2d}\text{ is the strictly SOS locus}.

notation.meaning: Coefficient-space interior of the SOS cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Proper Geometry of the SOS Cone

children.title: Nonnegativity–SOS Relaxation Gap
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where sum-of-squares membership does not capture every nonnegative polynomial.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hilbert Equality Regimes for Nonnegative and SOS Polynomials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact bounded-degree regimes in which global nonnegativity and SOS membership coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n,d\ge 1\),
\[
P_{n,2d}=\Sigma_{n,2d}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n=1\;\text{or}\;d=1\;\text{or}\;(n,d)=(2,2).
\]
In every other regime, \(\Sigma_{n,2d}\subsetneq P_{n,2d}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative polynomials are always SOS only for univariate polynomials, quadratic polynomials, and bivariate quartics; in every other bounded-degree regime the inclusion is strict.

notation.meaning: Globally nonnegative polynomials in n variables of degree at most 2d.
SOS polynomials in n variables of degree at most 2d.

knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert Equality Regimes for Nonnegative and SOS Polynomials
Nonnegativity–SOS Relaxation Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete globally nonnegative polynomial that is not SOS.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Motzkin polynomial
\[
m(x,y):=x^4y^2+x^2y^4+1-3x^2y^2
\]
is globally nonnegative because the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality gives \(x^4y^2+x^2y^4+1\ge 3x^2y^2\). Nevertheless, \(m\) is not a sum of squares of real polynomials. Hence
\[
\Sigma_{2,6}\subsetneq P_{2,6},
\]
so replacing polynomial nonnegativity by an SOS constraint can be a strict relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Motzkin polynomial is nonnegative everywhere but is not a sum of polynomial squares, proving that the SOS cone can be strictly smaller than the nonnegativity cone.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative bivariate polynomials of degree at most six.
SOS bivariate polynomials of degree at most six.

children.title: Gram-Matrix Cone Interface
children.top_down_role: Semidefinite representation boundary for sum-of-squares polynomial cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Gram-Matrix Cone Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite representation of the bounded-degree SOS cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_d(x)\) be the column vector of all monomials in \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) of degree at most \(d\). A polynomial \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x]_{\le 2d}\) is a sum of squares if and only if there exists a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix \(Q\) such that
\[
p(x)=z_d(x)^{\mathsf T}Qz_d(x).
\]
Equating coefficients in this identity imposes affine constraints on \(Q\); thus membership in \(\Sigma_{n,2d}\) is the linear image of a positive-semidefinite feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial is SOS exactly when it has a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix in the monomial basis; coefficient matching turns this into semidefinite feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(z_d\) contains every monomial of degree at most \(d\).

notation.meaning: Vector of monomials of degree at most d.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Definite Gram Certificate for SOS Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-feasibility characterization for the full bounded-degree SOS cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With the full monomial vector \(z_d\), a polynomial \(p\in\mathbb R[x]_{\le2d}\) lies in the interior of \(\Sigma_{n,2d}\) if and only if it admits a positive-definite Gram matrix:
\[
p\in\operatorname{int}(\Sigma_{n,2d})
\iff \exists Q\succ0:\ p=z_d^{\mathsf T}Qz_d.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-degree polynomial is an interior SOS polynomial exactly when its Gram system has a positive-definite feasible matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(z_d\) contains all monomials of degree at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Definite Gram Certificate for SOS Interior

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gram Spectrahedron, Nonuniqueness, and SOS Length
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structure and size of the positive-semidefinite Gram systems representing a fixed polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(N=\binom{n+d}{d}\), let \(z_d\) be the full monomial vector, and define \(\mathcal A:\mathbb S^N\to\mathbb R[x]_{\le2d}\) by \(\mathcal A(Q)=z_d^{\mathsf T}Qz_d\). The Gram spectrahedron of \(p\) is
\[
\mathcal G(p)=\{Q\in\mathbb S_+^N:\mathcal A(Q)=p\}.
\]
If \(Q_0\) is one Gram matrix, all Gram matrices lie in \(Q_0+\ker\mathcal A\), so they need not be unique. A rank-\(r\) matrix in \(\mathcal G(p)\) yields an expression of \(p\) as \(r\) squares, and
\[
\ell_{\mathrm{SOS}}(p)=\min\{\operatorname{rank}Q:Q\in\mathcal G(p)\}.
\]
The interface uses an \(N\times N\) PSD variable and \(\binom{n+2d}{2d}\) coefficient equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasible Gram matrices form a spectrahedron; nonuniqueness is governed by the coefficient-map kernel, minimum Gram rank equals minimum SOS length, and the matrix and equation dimensions are explicit.
assumptions_latex: \(z_d\) is the full monomial vector of degree at most \(d\).

notation.meaning: Length of the full monomial vector.
Minimum number of squares in an SOS representation of p.

knowledge_statements.title: Gram Spectrahedron, Nonuniqueness, and SOS Length

children.title: Euclidean Metric Model Family
children.top_down_role: Euclidean norm epigraphs, distance constraints, and residual bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines Euclidean distance matrices intrinsically through realizability by a finite configuration and records the associated reconstruction property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\in\mathbf S^n\) have nonnegative entries and zero diagonal. Then \(D\) is a Euclidean distance matrix if and only if there exist an integer \(k\ge 1\) and vectors \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^k\) such that \(D_{ij}=\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert_2^2\) for all \(i,j\). Given \(D\) and a compatible vector \(z\) of squared lengths, configurations realizing these pairwise distances can be reconstructed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric matrix with nonnegative entries and zero diagonal is a Euclidean distance matrix exactly when its entries are the squared Euclidean distances among the points of some finite configuration. Given the matrix and a compatible vector of squared point lengths, realizing configurations can be reconstructed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is a Euclidean distance matrix}\iff \exists k\ge 1,\ \exists x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^k:\ D_{ij}=\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert_2^2\ \forall i,j.

children.title: Euclidean Norm Epigraph Models
children.top_down_role: Quadratic-cone representations of Euclidean norm epigraphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Norm Epigraph Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone representation of an affine Euclidean norm epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
t\ge\lVert Ax+b\rVert_2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(t,Ax+b)\in\mathcal{Q}_{m+1},
\]
where
\[
\mathcal{Q}_{m+1}:=\{(s,u)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^m:s\ge\lVert u\rVert_2\}.
\]
Thus the epigraph of an affine Euclidean norm is represented by one affine membership constraint in a second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph inequality t at least the Euclidean norm of Ax+b is exactly one affine second-order-cone membership constraint.

source_refs.locator: 9 Linear, quadratic, and geometric models p. 293

children.title: Distance Constraint Models
children.top_down_role: Quadratic-cone representations of distances from points or affine sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Constraint Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone model of Euclidean distance to an affine point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(g,c\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(r\in\mathbb{R}\). The distance constraint
\[
\lVert Fx+g-c\rVert_2\le r
\]
is equivalent to
\[
(r,Fx+g-c)\in\mathcal{Q}_{m+1}.
\]
Either condition implies \(r\ge 0\). Consequently, a Euclidean-ball constraint, or its affine preimage, is second-order-cone representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Requiring the affine point Fx+g to lie within Euclidean distance r of c is equivalent to one second-order-cone membership constraint, which also enforces a nonnegative radius.

children.title: Residual Bound Models
children.top_down_role: Quadratic-cone encodings of bounded vector residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Bound Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic formulation of a bounded affine Euclidean residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For data \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), a decision vector \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}\), the residual bound
\[
\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2\le\varepsilon
\]
is equivalent to
\[
(\varepsilon,Ax-b)\in\mathcal{Q}_{m+1}.
\]
The cone constraint enforces \(\varepsilon\ge0\). Minimizing \(\varepsilon\) as the residual objective minimizes \(\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2\), which has the same minimizers as the least-squares objective \(\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean bound on an affine residual is one second-order-cone constraint. Minimizing its epigraph variable minimizes the residual norm and has the same minimizers as ordinary least squares.

children.title: Zero-Radius Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Boundary cases where norm, distance, or residual bounds collapse to exact equalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Radius Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A zero Euclidean radius collapses a cone constraint to affine equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(u\in\mathbb{R}^m\),
\[
\lVert u\rVert_2\le0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u=0.
\]
Let \(F\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(g,c\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Then the zero-radius distance constraint \(\lVert Fx+g-c\rVert_2\le0\) is exactly the affine equality \(Fx+g=c\). In conic form, \((0,u)\in\mathcal{Q}_{m+1}\) holds only when \(u=0\). This point is the cone apex, so this cone block cannot satisfy strict conic feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At radius zero, a Euclidean distance constraint becomes an affine equality, and the corresponding cone block lies at the apex and cannot be strictly feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,u)\in\mathcal{Q}_{m+1}\iff u=0\), and this cone block cannot be strictly feasible.

notation.meaning: Vector constrained by the zero-radius bound.

children.title: Convex Quadratic Models
children.top_down_role: Convex quadratic inequalities and objectives represented through quadratic cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOC epigraph representation for positive-semidefinite quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb{S}_+^n\), \(q,x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(r,t\in\mathbb{R}\). Choose \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) satisfying \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\), and define \(f(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2q^{\mathsf T}x+r\). Then
\[
f(x)\le t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(t-2q^{\mathsf T}x-r,\tfrac12,Rx)\in\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm r}_{n+2},
\]
where
\[
\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm r}_{n+2}:=\{(a,b,u)\in\mathbb{R}^2\times\mathbb{R}^n:a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ 2ab\ge\lVert u\rVert_2^2\}.
\]
Thus convex quadratic inequalities and epigraph objectives admit rotated-second-order-cone formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factoring a positive-semidefinite quadratic form converts its epigraph inequality into a rotated second-order-cone constraint.

notation.meaning: Cone of symmetric positive-semidefinite n-by-n matrices.
A square factor satisfying Q equal to transpose(R) times R.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-over-Linear Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotated-cone epigraph of a quadratic-over-positive-linear expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(s>0\), and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
t\ge\frac{\lVert u\rVert_2^2}{s}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(t,\tfrac{s}{2},u)\in\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm r}_{m+2}.
\]
More generally, let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(d\in\mathbb{R}\). On the domain \(c^{\mathsf T}x+d>0\), replacing \(u\) by \(Ax+b\) and \(s\) by \(c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) gives a rotated-second-order-cone representation of the quadratic-over-linear epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a squared Euclidean norm divided by a positive scalar, including affine numerator and denominator expressions of compatible dimensions, is represented by a rotated second-order cone.
assumptions_latex: For the affine form, \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(d\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x+d>0\).

children.title: Quadratic-Perspective Models
children.top_down_role: Perspective formulations for convex quadratic functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative Curvature Excludes Convex Quadratic-Perspective Modeling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefiniteness boundary for convex quadratic-perspective cone models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\) has a vector \(v\) with \(v^{\mathsf T}Qv<0\), then \(x\mapsto x^{\mathsf T}Qx\) is not convex and its positive-scale perspective \((x,s)\mapsto x^{\mathsf T}Qx/s\) is not convex on \(s>0\). Consequently, its epigraph cannot equal a convex rotated-second-order-cone representation. The scalar choice \(Q=[-1]\) gives the example \(-x^2/s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic with a negative-curvature direction has a nonconvex positive-scale perspective, so the convex rotated-cone model requires a positive-semidefinite quadratic matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative Curvature Excludes Convex Quadratic-Perspective Modeling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Cone Structure of the Quadratic-Perspective Epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint convexity and positive homogeneity of the closed perspective of a positive-semidefinite quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\) and let \(\widetilde f\) be the closed perspective of \(x\mapsto x^{\mathsf T}Qx\). Then \(\widetilde f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Its epigraph is a closed convex cone, and for every \(\alpha>0\), \[\widetilde f(\alpha x,\alpha s)=\alpha\widetilde f(x,s).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective of a positive-semidefinite quadratic is a proper closed convex function and is positively homogeneous, so its epigraph is a closed convex cone.
assumptions_latex: \(\widetilde f\) is the closed perspective of \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f\) is a closed convex cone and \(\widetilde f(\alpha x,\alpha s)=\alpha\widetilde f(x,s)\) for \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Cone Structure of the Quadratic-Perspective Epigraph

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel Conjugate of a Closed Quadratic Perspective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual description of the closed perspective for a possibly singular positive-semidefinite quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), let \(Q^\dagger\) be its Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse, and let \(\widetilde f\) be the closed perspective of \(x\mapsto x^{\mathsf T}Qx\). Its Fenchel conjugate in variables \((y,\eta)\) is \[\widetilde f^*(y,\eta)=\begin{cases}0,&y\in\operatorname{range}(Q)\ \text{and}\ \eta+\tfrac14y^{\mathsf T}Q^\dagger y\le0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a closed PSD quadratic perspective is the indicator of a dual quadratic region, with an additional range condition when the matrix is singular.
assumptions_latex: \(\widetilde f\) is the closed perspective of \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx\).

notation.meaning: dual variable paired with the perspective scale
extended-real indicator of a set C

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel Conjugate of a Closed Quadratic Perspective

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Quadratic Perspective and Factorized Cone Epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the closed PSD quadratic perspective and gives its correctly scaled reduced-dimensional rotated-cone model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\) and choose \(R\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\) with \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\). The closed perspective of \(x\mapsto x^{\mathsf T}Qx\) is \[\widetilde f(x,s)=\begin{cases}\|Rx\|_2^2/s,&s>0,\\0,&s=0\text{ and }Rx=0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}\] Define \(\mathcal Q_{r+2}^{\mathrm r}:=\{(a,b,z):a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ 2ab\ge\|z\|_2^2\}\). Then \[t\ge\widetilde f(x,s)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(t,s/2,Rx)\in\mathcal Q_{r+2}^{\mathrm r}.\] Thus an \(r\)-row factor gives a rotated cone of dimension \(r+2\), including the closed zero-scale boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective of a PSD quadratic has an exact rotated-cone epigraph using the factor image; an r-row factor requires a cone of dimension r+2.

notation.meaning: rotated second-order cone under the displayed scaling
number of rows in the chosen quadratic factor

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Quadratic Perspective and Factorized Cone Epigraph
Quadratic-Perspective Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed perspective of a positive-semidefinite quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb{S}_+^n\) and choose \(R\) with \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\). The closed perspective of \(x\mapsto x^{\mathsf T}Qx\) is
\[
\widetilde f(x,s)=
\begin{cases}
x^{\mathsf T}Qx/s,&s>0,\\
0,&s=0\text{ and }Rx=0,\\
+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Its epigraph is
\[
\{(x,s,t):(t,s/2,Rx)\in\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm r}_{n+2}\}.
\]
This formulation includes the boundary regime \(s=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective of a positive-semidefinite quadratic is quadratic-over-scale for positive scale, with a rotated-cone epigraph that also captures zero scale.

notation.meaning: Factor of the positive-semidefinite matrix Q.

source_refs.locator: 9 Linear, quadratic, and geometric models p. 293

source_witnesses.locator: 9 Linear, quadratic, and geometric models p. 293

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated closed-perspective boundary formula is mathematically plausible and internally consistent, but the generic chapter-opening locator does not specifically support the zero-scale extension. An exact source locator for the closed perspective and its boundary regime is required.

children.title: Rotated-Cone Representation Bridge
children.top_down_role: Common rotated-cone structure linking the two quadratic model families.

knowledge_statements.title: Rotated-Cone Representation Bridge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between rotated and ordinary second-order cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm r}_{m+2}:=\{(a,b,u)\in\mathbb{R}^2\times\mathbb{R}^m:a\ge0,\ b\ge0,\ 2ab\ge\lVert u\rVert_2^2\}.
\]
Then
\[
(a,b,u)\in\mathcal{Q}^{\mathrm r}_{m+2}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(a+b,a-b,\sqrt2u)\in\mathcal{Q}_{m+2}.
\]
The displayed invertible linear transformation therefore converts every rotated-cone constraint, including quadratic-perspective epigraphs, into an ordinary second-order-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible linear change of coordinates maps the rotated second-order cone to the ordinary second-order cone, connecting quadratic perspectives to standard SOC models.

children.title: Zero-Scale Perspective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Closure-sensitive cases where the perspective scaling coordinate vanishes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Scale Perspective Epigraph Is Not Closed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure failure when the zero-scale face is omitted from the squared-norm perspective epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[E_+:=\{(x,s,z):s>0,\ z\geq\|x\|_2^2/s\}.\] For every integer \(k\geq1\), \((0,1/k,0)\in E_+\), while \((0,1/k,0)\to(0,0,0)\notin E_+\). Hence the positive-scale epigraph is not closed; its closed extension must add scale-zero points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting the quadratic-perspective epigraph to positive scales makes it nonclosed: feasible points can converge to an omitted zero-scale point.

notation.meaning: positive-scale epigraph of the squared-norm perspective

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Scale Perspective Epigraph Is Not Closed

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-scale closure of a positive-semidefinite quadratic perspective, including the nullspace boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\) and let \(p_Q\) be the closed perspective of \(x\mapsto x^TQx\). Then \[p_Q(x,t)=\begin{cases}x^TQx/t,&t>0,\\0,&t=0\text{ and }Q^{1/2}x=0,\\+\infty,&t=0\text{ and }Q^{1/2}x\ne0.\end{cases}\] Consequently, \[(x,0,z)\in\operatorname{epi}p_Q\iff Q^{1/2}x=0\text{ and }z\ge0.\] Thus zero scale forces \(x=0\) exactly when \(Q\succ0\); for singular \(Q\), every \(x\in\ker Q\) is permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At zero scale, a closed positive-semidefinite quadratic perspective permits precisely the nullspace of its quadratic form; only positive definiteness forces the numerator vector to vanish.
assumptions_latex: \(p_Q\) is the lower-semicontinuous closed perspective of \(x^TQx\).

notation.meaning: closed perspective of the positive-semidefinite quadratic form

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Quadratic Zero-Scale Face

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Scale Value of a Closed Perspective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General recession-function characterization of the zero-scale boundary of a closed perspective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex. Its closed perspective satisfies \[\widetilde f(x,t)=\begin{cases}t f(x/t),&t>0,\\ f^\infty(x),&t=0,\\ +\infty,&t<0.\end{cases}\] Hence \(\{(x,0,z):\widetilde f(x,0)\le z\}=\{(x,0,z):f^\infty(x)\le z\}\). For \(f(x)=x^TQx\) with \(Q\succeq0\), \(f^\infty(x)=0\) on \(\ker Q\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero-scale value of a closed convex perspective is the recession function; for a positive-semidefinite quadratic, its finite zero-scale directions are exactly the nullspace.
assumptions_latex: \(\widetilde f\) is the lower-semicontinuous closure of the positive-scale perspective.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Scale Value of a Closed Perspective
Zero-Scale Perspective Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed quadratic perspective at scale zero and its rotated-cone encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the closed perspective of the squared Euclidean norm, define \(q:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) by \[q(x,t)=\begin{cases}\|x\|_2^2/t,&t>0,\\0,&t=0\text{ and }x=0,\\+\infty,&t=0\text{ and }x\ne0.\end{cases}\] Its epigraph satisfies \[(x,t,z)\in\operatorname{epi}q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t\ge0,\ z\ge0,\ \|x\|_2^2\le tz.\] Consequently, at zero scale \(t=0\), cone feasibility forces \(x=0\), while every \(z\ge0\) is admissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed quadratic perspective is finite at zero scale only when the numerator vector vanishes; its epigraph is a rotated second-order cone.

notation.meaning: closed perspective of the squared Euclidean norm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed zero-scale perspective and rotated-cone representation are mathematically coherent and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Ellipsoidal Robust-Counterpart Models
children.top_down_role: Second-order cone interfaces arising from ellipsoidal uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoidal Robust-Counterpart Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOC counterpart of one affine inequality with ellipsoidal coefficient uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the uncertain coefficient be \(a(u)=a_0+Pu\), where \(u\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfies \(\|u\|_2\le\rho\). For any \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), the robust inequality has the exact counterpart \[a(u)^\top x\le b\quad\text{for every }\|u\|_2\le\rho\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a_0^\top x+\rho\|P^\top x\|_2\le b.\] Introducing \(s\ge0\), this is equivalently represented by \(\|P^\top x\|_2\le s\) and \(a_0^\top x+\rho s\le b\), which are second-order-cone and linear constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine inequality robust against Euclidean-ball coefficient uncertainty equals a nominal inequality plus a support-function norm term, yielding an SOC formulation.

notation.meaning: SOC epigraph variable for the uncertainty norm

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint Left- and Right-Hand-Side Ellipsoidal Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOC counterpart when one ellipsoid jointly perturbs an affine inequality's coefficient and right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \binom{a(u)}{b(u)}=\binom{a_0}{b_0}+Hu,\ \|u\|_2\le\rho\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bigl[a(u)^\top x\le b(u)\ \forall u\bigr]\iff a_0^\top x-b_0+\rho\left\|H^\top\binom{x}{-1}\right\|_2\le0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint ellipsoidal uncertainty in both sides of a scalar affine inequality produces one support-function norm evaluated at (x,−1).

children.top_down_role: Basic exponential-cone graph representations and perspective variants.

children.title: Exponential Epigraph Models
children.top_down_role: Exponential-cone representations of exponential-function epigraphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Epigraph Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential epigraph represented by one exponential-cone membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adopt the closed exponential cone \[K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\le w\}.\] For \(x,t\in\mathbb R\), the exponential epigraph admits the exact representation \[t\ge\exp(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (x,1,t)\in K_{\exp}.\] More generally, if \(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\) are affine scalar expressions, then \(b(x)\ge\exp(a(x))\) is represented by \((a(x),1,b(x))\in K_{\exp}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exponential epigraph constraint is exactly one exponential-cone constraint with its scale coordinate fixed to one.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponential-epigraph encoding is correct under the stated cone convention and fits the representation leaf, but it has no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Logarithm Hypograph Models
children.top_down_role: Exponential-cone representations of logarithm-function hypographs.

knowledge_statements.title: Logarithm Hypograph Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithm hypograph represented using the exponential cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,t\in\mathbb R\), membership in the logarithm hypograph is equivalent to an exponential-cone constraint: \[x>0\ \text{ and }\ t\le\log x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exp(t)\le x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (t,1,x)\in K_{\exp}.\] Because fixing the middle coordinate to one excludes the cone's zero-scale face, the conic constraint itself entails \(x>0\). Thus an affine constraint \(b(y)\le\log a(y)\) is encoded by \((b(y),1,a(y))\in K_{\exp}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A logarithm hypograph constraint becomes an exponential epigraph constraint after applying the exponential–logarithm inverse relation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logarithm-hypograph equivalence and domain implication are coherent, but no inspectable citation supports the representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized logarithm for a proper cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes logarithmic homogeneity, degree, additive normalization ambiguity, and the resulting cone-monotonicity and Euler identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let K\subseteq\mathbf R^q be a proper cone. A generalized logarithm of degree 	heta>0 for K is a closed concave function \psi with \operatorname{dom}\psi=\operatorname{int}K, twice continuously differentiable on \operatorname{int}K, such that 
abla^2\psi(y)\prec0 and \psi(sy)=\psi(y)+	heta\log s for every y\in\operatorname{int}K and s>0. Every such \psi satisfies 
abla\psi(y)\in\operatorname{int}K^*, hence is K-increasing, and y^T
abla\psi(y)=	heta. It is determined only up to an additive constant, and \exp\psi is homogeneous of degree 	heta.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized logarithm on a proper cone is a closed, strictly concave, twice continuously differentiable function on the cone interior that changes by theta times log s when its argument is scaled by s. Its gradient lies in the interior of the dual cone, it is increasing in the cone order, and its gradient satisfies the Euler identity y dot grad psi(y)=theta. Adding a constant produces another generalized logarithm of the same degree.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbf R^q\text{ is a proper cone}

source_evidence.locator: Interior-point methods / 11.6. Problems with generalized inequalities / Definition 11.6-extra-2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual generalized logarithm and generalized Young inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the dual logarithm by convex conjugacy and records its cone, degree, inequality, and equality characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $K$ be a proper cone and let $\psi$ be a generalized logarithm for $K$ of degree $\theta$. Define, for $v\in\operatorname{int}K^*$, $\bar\psi(v)=-(-\psi)^*(-v)=\inf_{u\in\operatorname{int}K}\{v^Tu-\psi(u)\}$. Then $\bar\psi$ is concave and is a generalized logarithm for $K^*$ with degree $\theta$. Moreover, for every $u\in\operatorname{int}K$ and $v\in\operatorname{int}K^*$, $\bar\psi(v)+\psi(u)\le u^Tv$, with equality if and only if $\nabla\psi(u)=v$, equivalently $\nabla\bar\psi(v)=u$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper cone K, conjugating the negative of a degree-theta generalized logarithm psi defines a concave dual generalized logarithm on the interior of the dual cone, with the same degree. Every interior primal-dual pair satisfies the corresponding generalized Young inequality, and equality holds exactly when the two points are paired by the gradients of the primal and dual logarithms.
assumptions_latex: \psi:\operatorname{int}K\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is a generalized logarithm of degree }\theta
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar\psi(v):=-(-\psi)^*(-v)=\inf_{z\in\operatorname{int}K}\{v^Tz-\psi(z)\}\text{ is a degree-}\theta\text{ generalized logarithm for }K^*,\quad \bar\psi(v)+\psi(u)\le u^Tv,\quad [\bar\psi(v)+\psi(u)=u^Tv]\iff[\nabla\psi(u)=v]\iff[\nabla\bar\psi(v)=u].

children.title: Exponential–Logarithm Inverse Relation
children.top_down_role: Representation correspondence induced by inverse graph orientations.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential–Logarithm Inverse Relation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-preserving inverse correspondence on the positive real domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The natural exponential \(\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)\) is strictly increasing and bijective, with inverse \(\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\). Hence, for every \(s\in\mathbb R\) and \(x>0\), \[\log(\exp s)=s,\qquad \exp(\log x)=x,\qquad s\le\log x\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exp s\le x.\] The last equivalence converts logarithm hypographs into exponential epigraphs without reversing the inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponential and natural logarithm are increasing inverses, so a logarithm hypograph inequality is equivalent to an exponential epigraph inequality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The increasing inverse relation is stated precisely and the property kind fits the leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative locator.

children.title: Exponential Perspective Variants
children.top_down_role: Homogenized exponential graph models with explicit scaling coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and Positive Homogeneity of the Closed Exponential Perspective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural properties distinguishing the perspective model from the scale-one epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) be the closed exponential perspective from the deferred seed. It is convex and positively homogeneous: for every \(\lambda>0\), \[p(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\lambda p(x,y).\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{epi}p=K_{\exp}\) is a closed convex cone, and its slice \(y=1\) is the ordinary exponential epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed exponential perspective is convex and degree-one homogeneous, so its epigraph is a cone whose unit-scale slice is the exponential epigraph.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity and Positive Homogeneity of the Closed Exponential Perspective
Exponential Perspective Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed perspective epigraph of the exponential function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the closed exponential perspective \(p:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R_+\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) by \[p(x,y)=\begin{cases}y\exp(x/y),&y>0,\\0,&y=0\text{ and }x\le0,\\+\infty,&y=0\text{ and }x>0.\end{cases}\] Then its epigraph is exactly \[\operatorname{epi}p=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:(x,y,z)\in K_{\exp}\}.\] Thus \(z\ge y\exp(x/y)\) for \(y>0\), together with its lower-semicontinuous zero-scale closure, is represented by one exponential-cone membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential cone is the epigraph of the closed perspective of the exponential, including its zero-scale boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated lower-semicontinuous perspective, including its zero-scale boundary, agrees with the closed exponential cone, but it lacks inspectable evidence.

children.title: Exponential Aggregation Model Family
children.top_down_role: Multi-term exponential aggregation and normalization models.

children.title: Log-Sum-Exp Models
children.top_down_role: Exponential-cone representations of logarithmic exponential aggregation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel dual representation of finite log-sum-exp on the probability simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta_n:=\{p\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_i p_i=1\}\), with \(0\log0:=0\). For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{x_i}\right)=\max_{p\in\Delta_n}\left\{\langle p,x\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\log p_i\right\}.\] Equivalently, its Fenchel conjugate is \(f^*(p)=\sum_i p_i\log p_i\) on \(\Delta_n\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise. The maximizer is unique and has coordinates proportional to \(e^{x_i}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log-sum-exp is the convex conjugate of negative entropy on the simplex, and its unique variational maximizer is the normalized exponential vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\max_{p\in\Delta_n}\{\langle p,x\rangle-\sum_i p_i\log p_i\}\) and \(f^*(p)=\sum_i p_i\log p_i+\delta_{\Delta_n}(p)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Entropy Variational Representation of Log-Sum-Exp

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity, Smoothness, and Maximum Bounds of Log-Sum-Exp
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core analytic properties of finite log-sum-exp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{x_i}\right)\), \(f\) is finite, convex, and infinitely differentiable on \(\mathbb R^n\). For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\max_i x_i\leq f(x)\leq\max_i x_i+\log n.\] The constants are sharp: the upper bound is attained when all coordinates are equal, while the lower-bound gap approaches zero when one coordinate dominates the others.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log-sum-exp is a smooth convex approximation of the maximum lying between the maximum and the maximum plus log n, with sharp constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\) is convex and \(\max_i x_i\leq f(x)\leq\max_i x_i+\log n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity, Smoothness, and Maximum Bounds of Log-Sum-Exp

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order analytic structure of finite log-sum-exp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\log(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{x_i})\), define \(p_i=e^{x_i}/\sum_j e^{x_j}\). Then \[\nabla f(x)=p,\qquad \nabla^2f(x)=\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^T.\] For \(n\geq2\), the Hessian is positive semidefinite with nullspace \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\). Consequently, \(f\) is not strictly convex on \(\mathbb R^n\), while its restriction to an affine subspace is strictly convex whenever that subspace's direction space intersects \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\) only at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradient of log-sum-exp is the normalized exponential vector, and its Hessian is the corresponding categorical covariance matrix; the common-shift direction is its only flat direction.

notation.meaning: Normalized exponential vector associated with x

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient and Hessian of Log-Sum-Exp

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal global Euclidean Lipschitz constant of the finite log-sum-exp gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\log(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{x_i})\). For all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_2\leq 	frac12\|x-y\|_2,\qquad 0\preceq
abla^2 f(x)\preceq	frac12 I.\] For \(n\ge2\), \(1/2\) is the least global Lipschitz constant: it is attained for \(n=2\) when the two normalized weights are equal, and for \(n>2\) it is approached by concentrating equal mass on two coordinates. For \(n=1\), the optimal constant is \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-sum-exp gradient is globally one-half-Lipschitz in Euclidean norm; this constant is optimal for at least two coordinates, while the one-dimensional gradient is constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_2\le\frac12\|x-y\|_2\), with optimal constant \(1/2\) for \(n\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Euclidean Smoothness of Log-Sum-Exp

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order and perturbation properties of finite log-sum-exp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\log(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{x_i})\), coordinatewise order \(x\le y\) implies \(f(x)\le f(y)\). Moreover, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\), \[|f(x)-f(y)|\le\|x-y\|_\infty.\] The Lipschitz constant \(1\) is sharp, since \(f(x+c\mathbf1)-f(x)=c\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log-sum-exp is coordinatewise increasing and globally one-Lipschitz in the infinity norm, with a sharp constant.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity and Infinity-Norm Lipschitz Continuity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite log-sum-exp epigraph, feasibility equivalence, and lift footprint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_{\exp}:=\operatorname{cl}\{(a,b,c):b>0,\ b e^{a/b}\le c\}\). For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\), \[t\ge\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{x_i}\right)\] if and only if there exist \(u\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \[\sum_{i=1}^n u_i\le1,\qquad (x_i-t,1,u_i)\in K_{\exp}\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).\] The lift uses \(n\) scalar auxiliaries, \(n\) three-dimensional exponential-cone blocks, and one aggregate linear inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-sum-exp epigraph is exactly represented by one exponential-cone block and one auxiliary per summand, plus a single sum bound.

notation.meaning: closed exponential cone under the displayed coordinate convention

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Exponential-Cone Epigraph Lift
Log-Sum-Exp Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential-cone epigraph formulation of finite log-sum-exp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\), \[t\ge\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\exp x_i\right)\] holds if and only if there exist \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\ge0\) such that \[\sum_{i=1}^n u_i\le1,\qquad (x_i-t,1,u_i)\in K_{\exp}\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).\] Indeed, each cone constraint imposes \(u_i\ge\exp(x_i-t)\), and the sum constraint is equivalent to \(\sum_i\exp x_i\le\exp t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-sum-exp epigraph uses one exponential-cone constraint per summand and one linear normalization inequality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite log-sum-exp epigraph formulation is mathematically consistent and appropriately classified as a representation, but no source locator is provided.

children.title: Soft-Max Models
children.top_down_role: Normalized exponential models producing simplex-valued weights.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact range and nonuniqueness of logits for soft-max.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge2\), \[\operatorname{range}(\operatorname{softmax})=\operatorname{ri}\Delta_n=\{p\in\mathbb R_{++}^n:\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}p=1\}.\] For every such \(p\), \[\operatorname{softmax}(x)=p\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=\log p+c\mathbf1\ \text{ for some }c\in\mathbb R.\] Hence no finite score vector produces a simplex-boundary probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Soft-max maps onto the simplex interior, and logits for one positive probability vector differ exactly by a common constant.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Simplex Range and Fibers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential structure of the finite-score soft-max map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=\operatorname{softmax}(x)\) for \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(n\ge2\). Then \[D\operatorname{softmax}(x)=\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^{\mathsf T}\succeq0.\] It has rank \(n-1\) and kernel \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The soft-max Jacobian is a categorical covariance matrix whose only null direction is a common score shift.
knowledge_statements.title: Soft-Max Jacobian and Translation Kernel
Soft-Max Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized exponential map and its relation to log-sum-exp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb R^n\), the soft-max vector is \[\operatorname{softmax}(x)_i=\frac{\exp x_i}{\sum_{j=1}^n\exp x_j}=\exp\!\bigl(x_i-\operatorname{LSE}(x)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\] Every component is strictly positive, \(\sum_i\operatorname{softmax}(x)_i=1\), and \[\nabla\operatorname{LSE}(x)=\operatorname{softmax}(x).\] Thus soft-max maps finite score vectors into the relative interior of the probability simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Soft-max normalizes exponentiated scores into positive probabilities and equals the gradient of log-sum-exp.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The soft-max definition, simplex properties, and log-sum-exp gradient identity are correct and locally appropriate, but the record has no cited source.

children.title: Exponential Normalization Structure
children.top_down_role: Normalization relationship connecting exponential aggregates to soft-max outputs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-base-weight variant of finite exponential normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_i>0\) and \(x_i\in\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). The equations \[p_i=a_i e^{x_i-t},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\] have the unique solution \[t=\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i e^{x_i}\right),\qquad p_i=\frac{a_i e^{x_i}}{\sum_j a_j e^{x_j}}.\] Equivalently, positive base weights may be absorbed into shifted scores \(x_i+\log a_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive base weights determine a unique weighted log-partition constant and normalized exponential vector.

notation.meaning: positive base weight of term i

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Exponential Normalization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted normalization relation connecting a finite score vector, its log-partition constant, and normalized weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), the equations \[p_i=e^{x_i-t}\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\] have the unique solution \[t=\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{x_i}\right),\qquad p_i=\frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}}.\] Equivalently, \[\sum_i e^{x_i-t}=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t=\log\!\left(\sum_i e^{x_i}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Requiring shifted exponentials to sum to one uniquely determines the log-partition constant and normalized exponential vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Exponential Normalization Identity
Exponential Normalization Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Log-partition normalization of exponentiated finite scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), a scalar \(t\) and vector \(p\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfy exact exponential normalization precisely when \[p_i=\exp(x_i-t)\quad(i=1,\ldots,n),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1.\] These equations determine uniquely \[t=\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\exp x_i\right),\qquad p_i=\frac{\exp x_i}{\sum_j\exp x_j}.\] In convex epigraph models, the relaxed inequalities \((x_i-t,1,p_i)\in K_{\exp}\) and \(\sum_i p_i\le1\) encode \(t\ge\operatorname{LSE}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalizing exponentials uniquely determines the log-partition value and the associated soft-max probability vector.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalization identities and relaxed exponential-cone epigraph encoding are coherent, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Shift-Invariant Encoding Regimes
children.top_down_role: Equivalent representations induced by common shifts of exponential arguments.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical common-shift choice avoiding positive exponential overflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(m=\max_i x_i\). Then \[\operatorname{LSE}(x)=m+\log\!\left(\sum_i e^{x_i-m}\right),\qquad \operatorname{softmax}(x)_i=\frac{e^{x_i-m}}{\sum_j e^{x_j-m}}.\] In exact arithmetic, \(0<e^{x_i-m}\le1\) and \(1\le\sum_i e^{x_i-m}\le n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting the largest score gives equivalent log-sum-exp and soft-max formulas whose exponentials do not exceed one.

notation.meaning: maximum component of the score vector

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Shift Stable Evaluation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of shift-based scaling for widely separated exponential arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(c\in\mathbb R\), \[\max_i(x_i+c)-\min_i(x_i+c)=\max_i x_i-\min_i x_i.\] Thus a common shift cannot reduce dynamic range; sufficiently negative shifted arguments can still underflow in finite precision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common shift preserves all score differences, so it cannot cure a large score spread or eliminate underflow.
knowledge_statements.title: Common Shifts Preserve Score Spread
Shift-Invariant Encoding Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-shift equivariance of log-sum-exp and invariance of soft-max.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(c\in\mathbb R\), and let \(\mathbf1\) denote the all-ones vector. Then \[\operatorname{LSE}(x+c\mathbf1)=c+\operatorname{LSE}(x),\qquad \operatorname{softmax}(x+c\mathbf1)=\operatorname{softmax}(x).\] Consequently, the exponential-cone epigraph encoding is unchanged under the simultaneous replacement \(x_i\leftarrow x_i+c\) and \(t\leftarrow t+c\), because every cone argument \(x_i-t\) remains fixed. A common shift may therefore be chosen for numerical scaling without changing normalized probabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding one constant to every score shifts log-sum-exp equally, leaves soft-max unchanged, and preserves the conic encoding differences.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shift equivariance, soft-max invariance, and preservation of cone arguments are correct, but the property lacks an inspectable citation.

children.title: Entropic Model Family
children.top_down_role: Entropy, relative-entropy, and divergence representations.

children.title: Entropy Models
children.top_down_role: Cone representations of scalar or separable entropy terms.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum Entropy on the Probability Simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp range and maximizers of finite discrete Shannon entropy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in\mathbb R_+^n\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\), the Shannon entropy \(H(p)=-\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\log p_i\) satisfies \[0\le H(p)\le\log n.\] The upper bound is attained exactly at \(p_i=1/n\) for all \(i\), and the lower bound is attained exactly at the vertices of the probability simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Probability-vector entropy ranges from zero at point masses to log n at the uniform distribution.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Entropy on the Probability Simplex
Entropy Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential-cone hypograph model for finite discrete entropy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in\mathbb R_+^n\), define Shannon entropy by \(H(p)=-\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\log p_i\), using \(0\log0=0\). Its hypograph has the representation \[h\le H(p)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists\eta\in\mathbb R^n:\ h\le\sum_{i=1}^n\eta_i,\quad (\eta_i,p_i,1)\in K_{\exp}\ \ (i=1,\ldots,n).\] Each cone membership is equivalent to \(\eta_i\le-p_i\log p_i\), including the closed boundary value at \(p_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hypograph of discrete entropy is represented by separable exponential-cone constraints and one linear aggregation inequality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The entropy hypograph formulation has the correct exponential-cone orientation and closed boundary convention, but it is unsupported by a cited locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conic hull of the entropy epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-coordinate epigraph cone for the scalar relative-entropy perspective; the strict domain conditions are part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cone Q consists of triples whose first two coordinates are strictly positive and whose third coordinate is at least x_1 times log x_1 minus log x_2.
