children.title: Root-Determinant Models
children.top_down_role: Cone interfaces for root-determinant objectives or hypographs.

knowledge_statements.title: Root-Determinant Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypograph cone of the concave root-determinant function on the PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb{S}_+^n\), define \(\operatorname{detroot}_n(X)=(\det X)^{1/n}\), including the boundary value zero when \(X\) is singular. Its hypograph cone is \[\mathcal D_n=\{(X,t)\in\mathbb{S}_+^n\times\mathbb{R}:t\le(\det X)^{1/n}\}.\] Because \(\operatorname{detroot}_n\) is concave and positively homogeneous of degree one, \(\mathcal D_n\) is a closed convex cone. Thus maximizing a root determinant over affine matrix inequalities is a convex conic model whenever membership in \(\mathcal D_n\) is available directly or through an exact lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The root determinant is concave and degree-one homogeneous on PSD matrices, so its hypograph is a closed convex cone suitable for conic modeling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\le(\det X)^{1/n}\iff(X,t)\in\mathcal D_n\), where \(\mathcal D_n\) is a closed convex cone.

children.title: Log-Determinant Models
children.top_down_role: Cone interfaces for logarithmic determinant expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Log-Determinant Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Log-determinant hypograph represented through a root-determinant variable and exponential cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\). Since \(\log\det X=n\log((\det X)^{1/n})\), its hypograph admits the exact representation \[t\le\log\det X\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists s>0:\ s\le(\det X)^{1/n},\quad t\le n\log s.\] Under the exponential-cone convention \(\mathcal K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w):v>0,\ v e^{u/v}\le w\}\), the second inequality is equivalent to \((t/n,1,s)\in\mathcal K_{\exp}\). Hence a log-determinant model combines a root-determinant hypograph constraint with one exponential-cone constraint and retains the strict domain \(X\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A log-determinant hypograph factors exactly into a root-determinant constraint and one exponential-cone logarithm constraint, with a positive-definite matrix domain.
assumptions_latex: The stated closed exponential-cone convention is used.

children.title: Matrix-Mean Models
children.top_down_role: Cone-representable interfaces for matrix-mean constructions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of the Unlifted Hypograph LMI
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar counterexample to identifying the full Löwner hypograph with one block PSD constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In dimension one, take A=B=1 and T=-2. Then A\#B=1, so T\le A\#B, but \begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\-2&1\end{pmatrix} has eigenvalues 3 and -1 and is not positive semidefinite. Therefore T\preceq A\#B is not equivalent to \begin{pmatrix}A&T\\T&B\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently negative scalar lies below the geometric mean but fails the proposed block PSD constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of the Unlifted Hypograph LMI

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lifted Hypograph of the Midpoint Matrix Geometric Mean
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted PSD representation correcting the rejected unlifted equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For A,B\in\mathbb S_{++}^n and T\in\mathbb S^n, \quad T\preceq A\#B\Longleftrightarrow\exists Z\in\mathbb S^n:\ T\preceq Z,\ \begin{pmatrix}A&Z\\Z&B\end{pmatrix}\succeq0. Thus the full Löwner hypograph is a spectrahedral shadow rather than the block LMI obtained by substituting T directly for Z.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The midpoint matrix-geometric-mean hypograph needs an auxiliary maximal block variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Hypograph of the Midpoint Matrix Geometric Mean

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximal-element characterization underlying the midpoint matrix-geometric-mean lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For A,B\in\mathbb S_{++}^n, A\#B is the greatest element in Löwner order of \left\{Z\in\mathbb S^n:\begin{pmatrix}A&Z\\Z&B\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\right\}. Every feasible Z satisfies Z\preceq A\#B, and Z=A\#B is feasible. This maximal statement does not make the same block LMI valid for every T\preceq A\#B.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The geometric mean is the greatest feasible off-diagonal block, not a characterization of every matrix below it by the same LMI.
knowledge_statements.title: Ando Maximal Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithmic-size rational-weight construction, with the full Löwner hypograph obtained by a final dominance LMI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For reduced \theta=p/q\in[0,1], a rational-weight recursion can construct a nonnegative auxiliary Z\preceq A\#_\theta B using at most 2\lfloor\log_2q\rfloor+1 midpoint-type PSD blocks of order 2n. Adding T\preceq Z gives the full Löwner hypograph. For q=2^k, a binary-geodesic recursion needs at most k midpoint stages; a balanced tree of 2^k copies of A and B is not valid because the matrix geometric mean is not associative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational weights admit logarithmic-depth recursive lifts; the proposed exponential balanced-leaf construction is invalid for noncommuting matrices.

notation.meaning: number of midpoint-type PSD blocks of order 2n

knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Weight Recursive Lift Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and endpoint conventions for the weighted operator geometric mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted matrix geometric mean interpolates from A to B and specializes at one half to the midpoint mean.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Two-Matrix Geometric Mean

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite exact SDP representation for genuinely irrational weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \theta\in(0,1)\setminus\mathbb Q, the scalar slice t\le a^{1-\theta}b^\theta is not semialgebraic. Since every finite spectrahedral shadow is semialgebraic, the full hypograph T\preceq A\#_\theta B cannot have a finite exact semidefinite representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational weights have finite SDP lifts, whereas a genuinely irrational weight cannot have one in the standard finite-dimensional exact sense.
knowledge_statements.title: Irrational-Weight Semidefinite-Representability Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous extension of weighted matrix means and the exact midpoint lift to singular inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For A,B\in\mathbb S_+^n,\quad A\#_\theta B:=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}(A+\varepsilon I)\#_\theta(B+\varepsilon I).\quad For\ \theta=1/2,\quad T\preceq A\#B\Longleftrightarrow\exists Z:\ T\preceq Z,\ \begin{pmatrix}A&Z\\Z&B\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted means extend continuously to singular PSD inputs, and the lifted midpoint hypograph remains exact there.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Boundary Extension

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite semidefinite lifts for rationally weighted two-matrix geometric means.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \theta\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1],\quad \{(A,B,T):A,B\in\mathbb S_{++}^n,\ T\preceq A\#_\theta B\}\quad\text{is a spectrahedral shadow obtained using finitely many symmetric auxiliaries.}
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every rationally weighted two-matrix geometric-mean hypograph has a finite semidefinite lift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\preceq A\#_\theta B\ \text{has a finite PSD lift}
knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Weight Matrix-Mean Hypographs
Matrix-Mean Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite hypograph of the two-matrix geometric mean at weight one half.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A,B\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\), define their geometric mean by \(A\#B=A^{1/2}(A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})^{1/2}A^{1/2}\). For a symmetric matrix \(T\), Ando's maximal characterization gives \[T\preceq A\#B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\begin{pmatrix}A&T\\T&B\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\] Therefore the hypograph of the midpoint matrix geometric mean has a single affine positive-semidefinite representation. Positive-semidefinite boundary arguments are obtained by closure, equivalently by replacing \(A,B\) with \(A+\varepsilon I,B+\varepsilon I\) and taking \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The midpoint matrix geometric mean has an exact block-PSD hypograph representation; singular inputs are handled by closure from positive-definite matrices.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Ando's result is a maximal characterization, not the asserted equivalence for every symmetric matrix T. Even in the scalar case, T less than or equal to the geometric mean permits arbitrarily negative T, whereas block positive semidefiniteness also imposes a lower bound. The claimed single-LMI hypograph representation is therefore false under the stated domain.

children.title: Spectral Domain Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Positive-definiteness and eigenvalue boundaries affecting these matrix models.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Domain Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary characterization for closed interval spectral domains of real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R\) be a closed interval with nonempty interior, let \(\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dom}\phi=D\), and define \(\Phi(X)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(\lambda_i(X))\) for \(X\in\mathbb S^n\). Then \(\operatorname{dom}\Phi=\mathcal D_n\), its interior consists of the matrices whose eigenvalues all belong to \(\operatorname{int}D\), and its boundary consists of the matrices whose eigenvalues all belong to \(D\) with at least one eigenvalue in \(\partial D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the scalar function is finite exactly on a closed interval D, a symmetric matrix lies on the boundary of the induced spectral domain exactly when all its eigenvalues lie in D and at least one lies on the boundary of D.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb R\) is a closed interval with nonempty interior.
\(\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, with \(\operatorname{dom}\phi=D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\mathcal D_n=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:\lambda_i(X)\in D\ \forall i,\ \lambda_j(X)\in\partial D\ \text{for some }j\}\).

notation.meaning: Spectral matrix domain induced by the scalar effective domain.
Eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix, counted with multiplicity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral Distance to a Finite-Interval Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-norm margin from an interior matrix to the boundary of a bounded closed spectral interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=[a,b]\) with \(a<b\), and let \(\mathcal D_n=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:aI\preceq X\preceq bI\}\). If \(aI\prec X\prec bI\), then \(\operatorname{dist}_{\|\cdot\|_2}(X,\partial\mathcal D_n)=\min\{\lambda_{\min}(X)-a,\,b-\lambda_{\max}(X)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded interval spectral domain, the operator-norm distance of an interior matrix to the boundary is its smaller extreme-eigenvalue margin.

notation.meaning: Matrices whose eigenvalues lie in the interval D.

knowledge_statements.title: PSD Matrix Completion Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real symmetric PSD completion as semidefinite feasibility and as a projected PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) specify the entries of a partial symmetric matrix \(a\). The matrix \(a\) is PSD-completable exactly when the affine semidefinite slice \(\{X\in\mathbb S_+^{|V|}:X_{ij}=a_{ij}\ \text{for all }\{i,j\}\in E\}\) is nonempty. Equivalently, the set of all PSD-completable partial matrices on \(E\) is the coordinate projection \(\pi_E(\mathbb S_+^{|V|})\). Linear objectives and constraints on the projected entries therefore give semidefinite-representable models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial symmetric matrix is PSD-completable exactly when a positive semidefinite matrix matches all specified entries; collectively, completable partial matrices form the projection of the PSD cone onto those entries.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph containing every loop.

notation.meaning: Cone of real symmetric positive semidefinite matrices.
Partial symmetric matrix indexed by the specified graph entries.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a chordal sparsity graph, every positive semidefinite matrix having zeros outside \(E\) is a sum of positive semidefinite matrices embedded on maximal cliques. Explicitly, \(X\in\mathbb S_+^{|V|}\cap\mathbb S^{|V|}(E,0)\) if and only if there exist \(Y_k\succeq0\) such that \(X=\sum_{k=1}^mP_{C_k}^{\mathsf T}Y_kP_{C_k}\). Thus one sparse PSD constraint has an extended formulation using clique-sized PSD blocks and linear assembly equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under chordal sparsity, a sparse positive semidefinite matrix is exactly a sum of embedded positive semidefinite clique matrices.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse PSD Models

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonchordal Failure of Maximal-Clique PSD Summation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-theoretic boundary of maximal-clique summation for zero-filled sparse PSD matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) contain every loop, let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) be its maximal cliques, and set \(K_E=\mathbb S_+^{|V|}\cap\mathbb S^{|V|}(E,0)\). If \(G\) is chordal, then \(K_E=\{\sum_{k=1}^mP_{C_k}^{\mathsf T}Y_kP_{C_k}:Y_k\succeq0\}\). For every graph the displayed clique-sum cone is contained in \(K_E\), but for a nonchordal graph equality need not hold; some matrices in \(K_E\) may have no decomposition over the original maximal cliques.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximal-clique PSD summation is exact for chordal sparsity; for nonchordal sparsity it remains sufficient but need not represent every sparse PSD matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph containing every loop.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A block-diagonal symmetric matrix \(X=\operatorname{diag}(X_1,\ldots,X_m)\) is positive semidefinite if and only if each diagonal block \(X_k\) is positive semidefinite. Therefore a PSD constraint with fixed block-diagonal structure is represented exactly by independent constraints \(X_k\in\mathbb S_+^{n_k}\). Linear equations may couple entries of different blocks without changing the underlying cone, which remains the product \(\prod_{k=1}^m\mathbb S_+^{n_k}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-diagonal matrix is PSD exactly when every diagonal block is PSD, yielding a product of smaller semidefinite cones.

children.title: Perspective Activation Models
children.top_down_role: Perspective-based activation of homogeneous and cone-representable structures.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact zero-scale value of the closed perspective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper closed convex function \(f\), its closed perspective satisfies \(\widetilde f(x,z)=zf(x/z)\) for \(z>0\) and \(\widetilde f(x,0)=f^{\infty}(x)\), where \(f^{\infty}\) is the recession function. Consequently, zero activation forces \(x=0\) only if \(f^{\infty}(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x\ne0\), or if additional constraints impose \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At zero scale the closed perspective equals the recession function, so zero activation need not force the original variables to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Perspective Zero-Branch Recession Formula

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogenizing-cone and closed-convex-hull interpretation of perspective activation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\) for a proper closed convex function \(f\), and let \(E_1=\{(x,1,t):(x,t)\in E\}\). Then \(\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(E_1)\). Its slice \(0\le z\le1\) is therefore the closed convex hull of \(E_1\) and the zero-scale recession slice \(\{(d,0,\tau):(d,\tau)\in\operatorname{rec}E\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective epigraph is the closed homogenizing cone of the original epigraph.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the epigraph E.
Unit-scale embedding of the original epigraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Epigraph Homogenization

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\operatorname{epi}f\) is representable using a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,z,t):z>0,\ zf(x/z)\le t\}\) is cone representable and gives the closed perspective activation set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex perspective formulation for binary or continuous activation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z>0\), the perspective of \(f\) is \(\widetilde f(x,z)=zf(x/z)\). Its closed epigraph is \(\operatorname{cl}\{(x,z,t):z>0,\ zf(x/z)\le t\}\). If an epigraph formulation of \(f\) is positively homogenized by scaling its affine constants with \(z\), the resulting conic system represents this closed perspective. With \(z\in\{0,1\}\) and suitable constraints forcing the intended inactive recession behavior, it yields an exact activation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perspective activation homogenizes a convex epigraph with an activation variable and closes the zero branch, often giving a strong conic formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Perspective Activation Models

children.title: Big-M Cone-Domain Models
children.top_down_role: Bound-dependent conditional cone models and their validity boundary.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least deactivation magnitude for a cone direction and inactive base domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) be a closed convex cone, let \(d\in K\), and define \(\tau_d(y)=\inf\{t\ge0:y+td\in K\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). For a residual map \(g:X\to\mathbb R^q\), the least nonnegative constant satisfying \(g(x)+Md\in K\) for every \(x\in X\) is \(M^*=\sup_{x\in X}\tau_d(g(x))\). A finite directional deactivation constant exists exactly when \(M^*<+\infty\), and every valid constant satisfies \(M\ge M^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the deactivation direction lies in the cone, the smallest valid big-M is the worst-case displacement needed to move an inactive residual into the cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M^*=\sup_{x\in X}\inf\{t\ge0:g(x)+td\in K\}\), and a finite valid \(M\) exists if and only if \(M^*<+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Least nonnegative displacement along d needed to enter K.
Least uniformly valid directional deactivation constant.

knowledge_statements.title: Least Directional Big-M Constant

assumptions_latex: \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(x\in X\), and \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
\(g\) is affine and \(d\) is a fixed deactivation direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)+M(1-z)d\in K\) validly models \(z=1\Rightarrow g(x)\in K\) only if \(g(x)+Md\in K\) for every \(x\in X\) allowed when \(z=0\).

notation.meaning: Direction used to move residuals into the cone.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity condition for a finite big-M deactivation of cone membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The big-M inclusion \(g(x)+M(1-z)d\in K\) reproduces the active constraint when \(z=1\). It is a valid representation of the indicator implication only if every inactive point \(x\in X\) satisfies \(g(x)+Md\in K\). Exactness additionally requires that the inclusion introduce no restriction beyond \(x\in X\) on the inactive branch. Thus a finite valid \(M\) must be derived from explicit bounds on the attainable residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic big-M model is valid only when the chosen finite constant makes every allowed inactive residual cone-feasible without restricting the inactive branch.
knowledge_statements.title: Big-M Cone-Domain Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inactive-branch condition correctly captures the validity boundary of this directional conic big-M construction, and condition is the appropriate kind, but the record supplies no inspectable source.

children.title: Primal Feasibility Components
children.top_down_role: Primal-side domain and affine-consistency components of conic optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Feasibility Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form finite-dimensional conic minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(F\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and consider \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\). A point \(x\in E\) is primal feasible exactly when both components hold: the affine equation \(Ax=b\) and the cone-membership condition \(x\in K\). Equivalently, with \(r_p(x)=Ax-b\) and \(v_K(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\), primal feasibility is characterized by \(r_p(x)=0\) and \(v_K(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal feasibility requires simultaneous satisfaction of the affine constraints and membership in the primal cone; equivalently, both the equality residual and cone-distance violation vanish.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is primal feasible}\iff Ax=b\text{ and }x\in K\iff r_p(x)=0\text{ and }v_K(x)=0.\)

children.title: Dual Feasibility Components
children.top_down_role: Dual-side cone and stationarity components of conic optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Feasibility Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual feasibility for the standard conic primal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the conic primal problem \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), define \(K^*=\{s\in E:\langle s,z\rangle\ge 0\ \forall z\in K\}\). A pair \((y,s)\in F\times E\) is dual feasible exactly when the stationarity equation \(A^*y+s=c\) and cone condition \(s\in K^*\) both hold. Equivalently, defining \(r_d(y,s)=A^*y+s-c\) and \(v_{K^*}(s)=\operatorname{dist}(s,K^*)\), dual feasibility means \(r_d(y,s)=0\) and \(v_{K^*}(s)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual feasibility consists of the adjoint stationarity equation and membership of the slack in the dual cone, equivalently vanishing stationarity and cone-distance residuals.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((y,s)\text{ is dual feasible}\iff A^*y+s=c\text{ and }s\in K^*.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Paired Feasibility Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of primal and dual feasible points under one sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x\in K\), \(Ax=b\), \(s\in K^*\), and \(A^*y+s=c\). The primal and dual components are compatible because they use the same operator, data, adjoint, and dual-cone convention. Their objectives satisfy \[\langle c,x\rangle-\langle b,y\rangle=\langle A^*y+s,x\rangle-\langle y,Ax\rangle=\langle s,x\rangle\ge 0.\] Thus every simultaneously feasible tuple \((x,y,s)\) obeys weak duality, and objective equality is compatible precisely when \(\langle x,s\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-dual feasible tuple is compatible when both systems share the same data and sign convention; then its objective gap equals the nonnegative cone pairing.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and \(K^*\) is its dual.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Residual Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual certificate for exact or approximate primal-dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a candidate tuple \((x,y,s)\), define \(r_p=Ax-b\), \(r_d=A^*y+s-c\), \(v_p=\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\), and \(v_d=\operatorname{dist}(s,K^*)\). The vector residuals measure violation of the affine primal and stationarity equations, while \(v_p\) and \(v_d\) measure violations of cone membership. Exact primal-dual feasibility is certified by \(\|r_p\|=\|r_d\|=v_p=v_d=0\). Given absolute tolerances \(\tau_p,\tau_d\ge0\), the corresponding approximate certificate requires \(\max\{\|r_p\|,v_p\}\le\tau_p\) and \(\max\{\|r_d\|,v_d\}\le\tau_d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine residuals measure equation violations, while distances to the primal and dual cones measure membership violations. Their joint vanishing certifies exact feasibility.

The norms and distances are induced by fixed inner products.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Tolerances Do Not Imply Distance to Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on what nonzero primal-dual feasibility residuals certify without conditioning assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Bounds on \(\|Ax-b\|\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\), \(\|A^*y+s-c\|\), and \(\operatorname{dist}(s,K^*)\) certify only that the declared residual tests pass in the stated coordinates, norms, and scales. Without an error bound or metric-regularity condition for the relevant conic systems, such bounds need not control the distance from \(x\) or \((y,s)\) to an exactly feasible point. They also do not by themselves certify objective accuracy or optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small feasibility residuals are coordinate- and scale-dependent acceptance measures; without a suitable error bound they need not imply proximity to an exact feasible point, objective accuracy, or optimality.
assumptions_latex: Residuals and cone distances are computed using declared coordinates, norms, and data scaling.
No error-bound or metric-regularity hypothesis is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{small residuals}\not\Longrightarrow\text{small distance to the feasible set or objective error}\) without additional conditioning assumptions.

children.title: Duality-Gap Components

knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Gap Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap decomposition for an exactly feasible conic primal-dual tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal objective \(p(x)=\langle c,x\rangle\) and dual objective \(d(y)=\langle b,y\rangle\), define the duality gap by \(g(x,y)=p(x)-d(y)\). If \(Ax=b\) and \(A^*y+s=c\), then \[g(x,y)=\langle x,s\rangle+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle-\langle x,A^*y+s-c\rangle=\langle x,s\rangle.\] When additionally \(x\in K\) and \(s\in K^*\), the cone-pairing component is nonnegative. Hence the gap comprises objective disagreement, equivalently the complementarity pairing under exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal objective minus the dual objective decomposes into complementarity plus feasibility residual terms; for exact feasible tuples it equals the nonnegative cone pairing.
assumptions_latex: \(A^*y+s=c\) uses the stated dual sign convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x,y)=\langle x,s\rangle\ge0\) for every primal-dual feasible tuple.

children.title: Objective-Consistency Components

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Consistency Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimality certificate assembled from feasibility and objective agreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tuple \((x,y,s)\) is an objective-consistent primal-dual certificate when \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), \(A^*y+s=c\), \(s\in K^*\), and \(\langle c,x\rangle=\langle b,y\rangle\). The feasibility equations imply that objective equality is equivalent to \(\langle x,s\rangle=0\). Weak duality then yields, for every primal feasible \(z\) and dual feasible \((w,t)\), \[\langle b,w\rangle\le\langle b,y\rangle=\langle c,x\rangle\le\langle c,z\rangle.\] Consequently, \(x\) and \((y,s)\) are optimal and their common objective value is the primal and dual optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility plus equality of primal and dual objectives is an objective-consistency certificate: both points are optimal and the common value is the optimum.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual use mutually consistent data and sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle c,x\rangle=\langle b,y\rangle\Longrightarrow x\text{ and }(y,s)\text{ are optimal}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Objective Agreement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute-gap certificate for an exactly feasible primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\varepsilon\ge0\). If \(x\) is primal feasible and \((y,s)\) is dual feasible, then weak duality gives \(g=\langle c,x\rangle-\langle b,y\rangle=\langle x,s\rangle\ge0\). The inequality \(g\le\varepsilon\) certifies approximate objective agreement. Writing \(p^*\) and \(d^*\) for the primal and dual optimal values with the convention \(d^*\le p^*\), one has \[0\le\langle c,x\rangle-p^*\le\,g\le\varepsilon,\qquad 0\le d^*-\langle b,y\rangle\le g\le\varepsilon.\] Thus each feasible objective lies within absolute error \(\varepsilon\) of its corresponding optimum whenever those values are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible pair with nonnegative gap at most epsilon certifies that each objective value is within epsilon of its respective finite optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \((y,s)\) are primal and dual feasible.
The primal and dual optimal values are finite.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Conflict Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic boundary imposed by weak duality on reported objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the convention that the primal is a minimization problem and the dual is a maximization problem, every exactly feasible pair must satisfy \(g=\langle c,x\rangle-\langle b,y\rangle\ge0\). Therefore a reported value \(g<0\) cannot coexist with exact primal feasibility, exact dual feasibility, consistent problem data, and the stated sign convention. At least one of these components is erroneous. A value \(g>0\) is not itself a conflict: it is compatible with feasibility and indicates absent objective agreement. A zero gap certifies objective consistency, while an approximately negative gap must be judged against documented residual and rounding tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative primal-minus-dual gap conflicts with exact compatible feasibility. A positive gap is allowed but indicates missing objective agreement; near-zero signs require tolerance-aware interpretation.
assumptions_latex: The primal objective is minimized and the dual objective is maximized.
Primal and dual data use the same operator and sign convention.
Exact feasibility claims are interpreted without numerical tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g<0\Longrightarrow\) at least one claimed feasibility, data-consistency, or sign-convention condition fails.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-specific forms of the universal complementarity pairing, using the standard self-dual Lorentz-cone convention.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in K\) and \(s\in K^*\), complementarity is the universal condition \(\langle x,s\rangle=0\). For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), it is equivalent to \(x_i s_i=0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For the Lorentz cone \(L_m=\{(u_0,\bar u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{m-1}:u_0\ge\|\bar u\|_2\}\), two nonzero complementary elements \(x=(x_0,\bar x)\) and \(s=(s_0,\bar s)\) lie on the boundary and satisfy \(\bar s=-\alpha\bar x\) for some \(\alpha>0\). For \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\), complementarity is equivalent to \(XS=0\), hence \(\operatorname{range}(X)\perp\operatorname{range}(S)\). For a general nonsymmetric cone, complementarity remains the dual-pairing condition and implies \(s\in K^*\cap x^\perp\), without requiring a cone-specific algebraic product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementarity is always zero primal-dual pairing. It becomes coordinatewise zero products for an orthant, opposing spatial boundary directions for the standard Lorentz cone, and matrix-product orthogonality for the positive-semidefinite cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Complementarity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial definition, with standard orthant and semidefinite specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in K\) and \(s\in K^*\) satisfy \(\langle x,s\rangle=0\), and let \(F=\operatorname{face}_K(x)\) be the minimal face of \(K\) containing \(x\). Define its conjugate face by \(F^\triangle=K^*\cap F^\perp\). The pair is strictly complementary when \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\) and \(s\in\operatorname{ri}F^\triangle\). For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), this says \(x_i+s_i>0\) for every \(i\). For \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\), it says \(X+S\succ0\), equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}X+\operatorname{rank}S=n\) under complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complementary pair is strict when each member lies in the relative interior of the corresponding conjugate face; this yields positive support coverage or full rank coverage.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.

notation.meaning: minimal face of the cone containing x

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Partition Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal partition induced by complementary semidefinite optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a semidefinite primal-dual optimal pair \((X,S)\) with \(X,S\in\mathbb S_+^n\) and \(XS=0\), define \(B=\operatorname{range}(X)\), \(N=\operatorname{range}(S)\), and \(T=(B+N)^\perp\). Then \(B\perp N\) and \(\mathbb R^n=B\oplus T\oplus N\). Choosing \(X\) and \(S\) in the relative interiors of their respective optimal faces makes \((B,T,N)\) the maximal optimal partition: \(B\) and \(N\) record directions supported by primal and dual optima, while \(T\) records directions supported by neither. Strict complementarity holds exactly when \(T=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary semidefinite optima split the ambient space into primal-supported, unsupported, and dual-supported orthogonal subspaces. Strict complementarity is precisely the absence of an unsupported subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(X,S\in\mathbb S_+^n\) form an optimal complementary pair.
\(X\) and \(S\) are chosen in the relative interiors of their optimal faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R^n=B\oplus T\oplus N\), and strict complementarity holds iff \(T=\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invariance and Maximality of the SDP Optimal Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Choice-independent characterization of the maximal optimal partition by the primal and dual optimal sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X^*\) and \(\mathcal S^*\) be the nonempty convex sets of primal optimal matrices and dual optimal slacks for an SDP whose primal and dual attain the same finite value. Define \(B_*:=\sum_{X\in\mathcal X^*}\operatorname{range}(X)\) and \(N_*:=\sum_{S\in\mathcal S^*}\operatorname{range}(S)\). If \(\bar X\in\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal X^*)\) and \(\bar S\in\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal S^*)\), then \(\operatorname{range}(\bar X)=B_*\) and \(\operatorname{range}(\bar S)=N_*\). Moreover \(B_*\perp N_*\), so with \(T_*=(B_*+N_*)^\perp\), the decomposition \(\mathbb R^n=B_*\oplus T_*\oplus N_*\) is independent of the relative-interior choices and is the maximal optimal partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior primal and dual optima realize the maximum supported subspaces of their optimal sets, making the resulting primal, transition, and dual partition choice-independent.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X^*\) and \(\mathcal S^*\) are nonempty convex sets of positive-semidefinite primal optima and dual optimal slacks.
The primal and dual attain the same finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{range}(\bar X)=B_*,\quad \operatorname{range}(\bar S)=N_*,\quad \mathbb R^n=B_*\oplus T_*\oplus N_*\), independently of the relative-interior choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Complementarity Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric characterization of failure in semidefinite optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume a semidefinite primal-dual pair has attained optimal solutions and zero duality gap. Strict complementarity fails when every complementary optimal pair \((X,S)\) satisfies \(X+S\not\succ0\). Equivalently, \[\max\{\operatorname{rank}X+\operatorname{rank}S:(X,S)\text{ is a complementary optimal pair}\}<n.\] In the optimal-partition representation, this is equivalent to a nonzero common unsupported subspace \(T=(\operatorname{range}X+\operatorname{range}S)^\perp\) for maximally complementary optima. Thus attainment and objective agreement alone do not imply strict complementarity; the obstruction is incomplete coverage of the ambient space by the primal and dual optimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict complementarity fails when no optimal complementary matrices jointly cover the ambient space, equivalently every such pair has rank sum below the matrix dimension.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual semidefinite optima are attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment and Zero Gap without Strict Complementarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit three-by-three SDP whose unique complementary optimal matrices leave a common unsupported direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_{ij}\) denote the symmetric matrix units and set \(A_1=E_{11}\), \(A_2=E_{22}-E_{13}-E_{31}\), and \(C=E_{33}\). Consider \[\min\{\langle C,X\rangle:\langle A_1,X\rangle=1,\ \langle A_2,X\rangle=0,\ X\succeq0\}.\] Its dual is \[\max\{y_1:A_1y_1+A_2y_2+S=C,\ S\succeq0\}.\] The unique primal optimum is \(X^*=E_{11}\), the unique dual optimum is \((y_1^*,y_2^*,S^*)=(0,0,E_{33})\), and both optimal values are zero. Thus \(\operatorname{rank}X^*+\operatorname{rank}S^*=2<3\), so no strictly complementary optimal pair exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concrete three-by-three SDP has attained equal optimal values but unique primal and dual slacks of total rank two, leaving one unsupported direction.

\(E_{13}+E_{31}\) supplies the symmetric off-diagonal coefficient in \(A_2\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Complementarity Does Not Imply Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-programming counterexample delimiting sensitivity conclusions available from strict complementarity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{0:x_1+x_2=1,\ x\in\mathbb R_+^2\}\), the dual is \(\max\{y:y+s_1=0,\ y+s_2=0,\ s\in\mathbb R_+^2\}\). For every \(0<t<1\), \(x=(t,1-t)\), \(y=0\), and \(s=0\) form a strictly complementary optimal triple, since \(x_i+s_i>0\) for both coordinates. Nevertheless, the primal optimal set is the entire segment \(\{(t,1-t):0\le t\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict complementarity can hold at every relative-interior point of a nontrivial optimal face, so it does not imply uniqueness or a single-valued solution map.
assumptions_latex: The standard nonnegative-orthant primal-dual convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_i+s_i>0\ (i=1,2),\qquad \operatorname{argmin}P=\{(t,1-t):0\le t\le1\}\text{ is not a singleton}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stable Optimal Basis under Strict Complementarity and Nondegeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-programming sensitivity specialization separating strict complementarity from the basis regularity required for a stable solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank. Suppose a basis \(B\) satisfies \(A_B\) nonsingular, \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b>0\), \(x_N=0\), and \(s_N=c_N-A_N^TA_B^{-T}c_B>0\). Then the same basis remains primal feasible, dual feasible, and uniquely optimal for all sufficiently small perturbations of \((A,b,c)\). Its basic primal-dual solution depends smoothly on the perturbed data; with \(A\) fixed, it is affine in \(b\) and \(c\) throughout that basis region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular strictly complementary LP basis persists under small data perturbations and gives a locally unique smooth solution; strict complementarity without basis nondegeneracy does not suffice.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\varepsilon>0\text{ such that basis }B\text{ remains uniquely optimal whenever }\|(\Delta A,\Delta b,\Delta c)\|<\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Stable Optimal Basis under Strict Complementarity and Nondegeneracy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral-Gap Test for Stable Semidefinite Support Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite stability consequence within the class of complementary positive-semidefinite perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,S\in\mathbb S_+^n\) satisfy \(XS=0\) and \(X+S\succ0\). Put \(U=\operatorname{range}X\) and \[\gamma:=\min\{\lambda_{\min}(X|_U),\lambda_{\min}(S|_{U^\perp})\}>0.\] If \(\widehat X,\widehat S\succeq0\) are complementary and \[\|\widehat X-X\|_2<\gamma/2,\qquad\|\widehat S-S\|_2<\gamma/2,\] then \(\operatorname{rank}\widehat X=\operatorname{rank}X\), \(\operatorname{rank}\widehat S=\operatorname{rank}S\), and \(\widehat X+\widehat S\succ0\). This does not assert uniqueness or differentiability of the optimizer mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly complementary PSD pair retains its rank partition under sufficiently small complementary PSD perturbations controlled by its positive spectral margin.
assumptions_latex: The perturbed pair remains positive semidefinite and complementary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robinson Strong Regularity Gives a Lipschitz Solution Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-general sensitivity conclusion at the generalized-equation level; strong regularity is not inferred from strict complementarity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the primal-dual KKT system near \((\bar z,\bar p)\) be represented by \[0\in\Phi(z,p)+N_C(z),\] where \(C\) is closed and convex and \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable. If this generalized equation is strongly regular at \((\bar z,\bar p)\), then there are neighborhoods \(P\) of \(\bar p\) and \(Z\) of \(\bar z\) and a unique Lipschitz mapping \(z:P\to Z\) such that \(z(\bar p)=\bar z\) and \[0\in\Phi(z(p),p)+N_C(z(p))\qquad(p\in P).\] Strict complementarity alone does not imply strong regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable near \((\bar z,\bar p)\).
The generalized equation is strongly regular at \((\bar z,\bar p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\) a locally unique Lipschitz solution mapping \(p\mapsto z(p)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differentiability from a Nonsingular Face-Reduced KKT System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit-function sensitivity after complementary faces have been locally identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose fixed complementary faces are locally identified near data \(\bar p\), and the resulting face-reduced KKT conditions are \(H(z,p)=0\), where \(H\) is continuously differentiable near \((\bar z,\bar p)\). If \(H(\bar z,\bar p)=0\) and \(D_zH(\bar z,\bar p)\) is nonsingular, then a unique continuously differentiable local solution mapping \(z(p)\) exists and \[Dz(\bar p)=-D_zH(\bar z,\bar p)^{-1}D_pH(\bar z,\bar p).\] Strict complementarity alone implies neither local face identification under arbitrary data perturbations nor the required nonsingularity.

An optimal pair \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) satisfies strict complementarity: \(x^*\in\operatorname{ri}F\) and \(s^*\in\operatorname{ri}F^\triangle\) for the minimal primal face \(F\).

Consequently, sufficiently small perturbations that preserve the same optimal faces preserve complementarity locally. Strict complementarity alone does not imply uniqueness, differentiability, or Lipschitz continuity of the optimal solution mapping; such conclusions additionally require appropriate primal-dual nondegeneracy and, when curvature is present, second-order sufficient conditions.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: strict complementarity identifies relative-interior complementary faces, but stronger sensitivity claims require nondegeneracy hypotheses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates face stability supplied by strict complementarity from stronger solution-map regularity requiring nondegeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the conic pair \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and \(\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\). Let \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) be optimal, and suppose \(x^*\in\operatorname{ri}F\) and \(s^*\in\operatorname{ri}F^\triangle\), where \(F\) is the minimal face of \(K\) containing \(x^*\) and \(F^\triangle=K^*\cap F^\perp\). Then complementarity is locally stable under perturbations for which these faces remain optimal. This condition alone does not guarantee uniqueness or a locally Lipschitz or differentiable solution map; primal-dual nondegeneracy and suitable second-order sufficiency are additionally required for those sensitivity conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict complementarity stabilizes the complementary optimal faces, but uniqueness and Lipschitz or differentiable solution dependence require additional nondegeneracy and second-order assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Sensitivity Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary concerning uniqueness and solution-map regularity is plausible, but the asserted local stability under face-preserving perturbations is not formulated precisely enough to assess and has no supporting source.

children.title: Slater Regularity Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Slater Regularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional primal and dual Slater alternatives, including opposite-side attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(A:E\to Y\) be linear with adjoint \(A^*:Y\to E\), let \(b\in Y\), \(c\in E\), and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Define \(p^*=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and \(d^*=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\). If some \(\bar x\in\operatorname{int}K\) satisfies \(A\bar x=b\) and \(p^*>-\infty\), then \(p^*=d^*\) and the dual supremum is attained. If some \((\bar y,\bar s)\in Y\times E\) satisfies \(A^*\bar y+\bar s=c\) with \(\bar s\in\operatorname{int}K^*\), and \(d^*<+\infty\), then \(p^*=d^*\) and the primal infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional conic primal-dual pair, strict primal feasibility and a finite primal value give equal values and dual attainment; strict dual feasibility and a finite dual value give equal values and primal attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(A:E\to Y\) is linear, and \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
The relevant side is strictly feasible and has a finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal Slater regularity yields \(p^*=d^*\) and dual attainment; dual Slater regularity yields \(p^*=d^*\) and primal attainment.

notation.meaning: Primal cone and its dual cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior Slater Theorem in the Effective Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong duality for a conic problem after explicitly declaring the cone's effective linear ambient space and corresponding reduced dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, \(L=\operatorname{span}K\), \(A_L=A|_L\), \(c_L=P_Lc\), and \(K_L^*=\{z\in L:\langle z,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\). Consider \[p_L^*=\inf\{\langle c_L,x\rangle:A_Lx=b,\ x\in K\}\] and its reduced-space dual \[d_L^*=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:A_L^*y+s=c_L,\ s\in K_L^*\}.\] If some \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}K\) satisfies \(A_L\bar x=b\) and \(p_L^*>-\infty\), then \(p_L^*=d_L^*\) and the reduced dual attains its supremum. The analogous statement applies to any dual-slack conic problem after its slack cone, effective span, adjoint, and reduced dual are declared in the same way.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior feasibility is Slater feasibility in the cone's span. For the explicitly defined reduced primal-dual pair it yields zero gap and opposite-side attainment; the same construction applies separately to a dual-slack cone.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and the constraint space are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone and the primal value is finite below.
The primal-dual pair is formed in \(L=\operatorname{span}K\) using the projected objective, restricted constraint map, its reduced adjoint, and the dual cone taken in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\in\operatorname{ri}K,\ A_L\bar x=b\Longrightarrow p_L^*=d_L^*\ \text{and the reduced dual optimum is attained}.

notation.meaning: Effective linear ambient space of the cone.
Orthogonal projection onto the effective space.
Dual cone of K taken inside L.
Adjoint of the restricted map with codomain L.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{span}K\), and regard \(K\) as a full-dimensional cone in \(L\). If there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}K\) with \(A\bar x=b\), then the primal problem restricted to \(L\) satisfies Slater regularity. Hence, when its primal value is finite, its reduced-space dual has the same value and attains it. The symmetric statement holds when the dual affine constraint admits a slack in the relative interior of the dual cone defined in its effective linear span.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior feasibility is ordinary strict feasibility in the cone's effective span and therefore supplies strong duality and opposite-side attainment there.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-Route Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence obtained by changing the ambient space to the cone's linear span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty convex cone, and set \(L=\operatorname{span}K\). Then \(K\) has nonempty interior in \(L\) and \[\operatorname{ri}K=\operatorname{int}_L K.\] Hence, for any finite-dimensional Euclidean space \(Y\), linear map \(A:E\to Y\), and vector \(b\in Y\), the condition \(\{x\in E:Ax=b\}\cap\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing\) is exactly the ordinary Slater condition for the same feasibility system restricted to \(L\). The same identity applies to a dual slack cone after replacing its ambient space by its own linear span.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior feasibility in the original space is exactly strict feasibility after restricting the cone to its linear span; the same geometric identity applies to a specified dual slack cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty convex cone, \(L=\operatorname{span}K\), and \(A:E\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identity \(\operatorname{ri}K=\operatorname{int}_L K\) makes relative-interior regularity equivalent to ordinary Slater regularity on \(L\).

notation.meaning: Effective linear ambient space of the cone
Interior in the topology of the effective space
Relative interior in the original ambient space

children.title: Regularity Applicability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Lower-dimensional or degenerate settings requiring qualified regularity interpretation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary conic pair showing that failure of both ambient Slater conditions need not cause a gap or nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb R_+^2\), \(A(x_1,x_2)=x_1\), \(b=0\), and \(c=0\). The primal value is \(0\), attained by every \((0,t)\) with \(t\ge0\), but no primal feasible point lies in \(\operatorname{int}K\). Dual feasibility requires \(s=(-y,0)\in K^*\), so the dual value \(0\) is attained while every feasible slack lies on \(\partial K^*\). Hence both ambient Slater conditions fail although both optima are attained and equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-dimensional orthant problem has equal attained primal and dual values even though neither side has an ambient Slater point.
assumptions_latex: The canonical pair is \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and \(\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Failure of both ambient Slater conditions does not imply a duality gap or nonattainment.}
knowledge_statements.title: Slater Regularity Is Not Necessary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient and Relative Slater Applicability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric boundary for applying ambient or relative-interior Slater conditions to a nonempty conic affine system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\), where \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. If \(\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\), ambient Slater feasibility is impossible. If \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\), the minimal face \(F_{\min}\unlhd K\) containing \(S\) is proper and \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing\). Thus neither ambient nor relative-interior Slater conclusions for \(K\) may be invoked; Slater reasoning applies only to a precisely defined problem restricted to \(\operatorname{span}F_{\min}\) with cone \(F_{\min}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ambient Slater is impossible for an empty-interior cone, and failure of relative-interior feasibility confines a nonempty feasible system to a proper minimal face. Strong-duality conclusions then require a precisely defined reduced problem on that face.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

notation.meaning: Smallest face of the cone containing the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient and Relative Slater Applicability Boundaries

assumptions_latex: The cone \(K\) is closed and convex in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
The affine feasible set is nonempty but may meet only a proper face of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ambient Slater regularity is unavailable when \(\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\), and relative-interior regularity fails when feasibility is confined to \(K\setminus\operatorname{ri}K\); facial reduction is then required before applying Slater-type conclusions.

notation.meaning: Minimal face of the cone containing the feasible set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Slater applicability is limited by empty ambient interior or feasibility confined to a proper face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when ambient or relative-interior Slater tests fail and a smaller feasible face must be exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{x:Ax=b\}\cap K\). If \(\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\) in the chosen ambient space, classical ambient Slater feasibility is impossible even when \(S\neq\varnothing\). If \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\), then neither ambient nor relative-interior Slater regularity holds for \(K\). In that case \(S\) lies in a proper face, and Slater-type reasoning becomes applicable only after replacing \(K\) by the minimal face \(F_{\min}\) containing \(S\), provided \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing\). Without such reduction, strong duality or attainment cannot be inferred from these regularity routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slater tests fail for empty ambient interior or feasibility restricted to a proper face; facial reduction is then needed before invoking regularity consequences.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularity Applicability Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is mathematically plausible, but the claim that the minimal-face replacement restores the applicable Slater route requires a precise facial-reduction source and hypotheses.

children.title: Strong-Duality Regime
children.top_down_role: Regular conic systems classified by coincident primal and dual values.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Duality Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value equality separated from primal and dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(A:E\to Y\) be linear with adjoint \(A^*:Y\to E\), let \(b\in Y\), \(c\in E\), and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Define \[p^*=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\},\qquad d^*=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}.\] Weak duality gives \(d^*\le p^*\). This pair is in the strong-duality regime precisely when \(p^*,d^*\in\mathbb R\) and \(p^*=d^*\). This condition asserts equality of values and does not by itself assert attainment on either side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional conic pair is in the strong-duality regime when its finite primal and dual values are equal; this equality alone does not assert attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(A:E\to Y\) is linear, and \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
The displayed primal and dual values are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong duality is the equality \(p^*=d^*\); attainment is a separate property.

children.title: Primal Attainment
children.top_down_role: Strong-duality settings with an attained primal optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal attainment defined independently of dual feasibility, duality gap, and uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(A:E\to Y\) be linear, let \(b\in Y\), \(c\in E\), and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Set \(P=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\), and suppose \(p^*=\inf_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle\in\mathbb R\). The primal optimum is attained if and only if there exists \(x^*\in P\) satisfying \(\langle c,x^*\rangle=p^*\), equivalently if and only if \[P^*=\{x\in P:\langle c,x\rangle=p^*\}\neq\varnothing.\] Attainment does not imply that \(P^*\) is bounded or a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite primal value is attained exactly when a feasible primal point achieves the infimum; the optimizer need not be unique or bounded as a set.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(A:E\to Y\) is linear, and \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
The primal feasible set \(P\) is nonempty and \(p^*\in\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compactness criteria sufficient for primal attainment, independent of strong duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a closed primal feasible set and let \(p^*=\inf_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle\in\mathbb R\). If some nonempty lower-level set \(L_\alpha=\{x\in P:\langle c,x\rangle\le\alpha\}\), with \(\alpha>p^*\), is bounded, then \(P^*\) is nonempty and compact. More generally, the existence of any bounded primal minimizing sequence implies \(P^*\neq\varnothing\), although it does not imply that the entire optimal set is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded primal lower-level set gives a compact optimal set; a bounded minimizing sequence is sufficient for attainment but not for boundedness of all optimizers.
assumptions_latex: The primal feasible set is closed in a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_\alpha\text{ bounded}\Rightarrow P^*\text{ nonempty and compact};\quad\text{a bounded minimizing sequence}\Rightarrow P^*\neq\varnothing
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Boundedness and Bounded-Sequence Criteria

children.title: Dual Attainment
children.top_down_role: Strong-duality settings with an attained dual optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual attainment distinguished from strong duality, primal attainment, and uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(A:E\to Y\) be linear with adjoint \(A^*:Y\to E\), let \(b\in Y\), \(c\in E\), and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Set \(D=\{(y,s)\in Y\times E:A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\), and suppose \(d^*=\sup_{(y,s)\in D}\langle b,y\rangle\in\mathbb R\). The dual optimum is attained if and only if there exists \((y^*,s^*)\in D\) satisfying \(\langle b,y^*\rangle=d^*\), equivalently if and only if \[D^*=\{(y,s)\in D:\langle b,y\rangle=d^*\}\neq\varnothing.\] Attainment does not imply that \(D^*\) is bounded or a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite dual value is attained exactly when a feasible multiplier-slack pair achieves the supremum; the optimal pair need not be unique or bounded as a set.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(A:E\to Y\) is linear, and \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
The dual feasible set \(D\) is nonempty and \(d^*\in\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a closed dual feasible set and let \(d^*=\sup_{(y,s)\in D}\langle b,y\rangle\in\mathbb R\). If some nonempty upper-level set \(L_\alpha=\{(y,s)\in D:\langle b,y\rangle\ge\alpha\}\), with \(\alpha<d^*\), is bounded, then \(D^*\) is nonempty and compact. More generally, the existence of any bounded dual maximizing sequence implies \(D^*\neq\varnothing\), although it does not imply that the entire optimal set is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded dual upper-level set gives a compact optimal set; a bounded maximizing sequence is sufficient for attainment but not for boundedness of all optimizers.
assumptions_latex: The dual feasible set is closed in a finite-dimensional space.

children.title: One-Sided Attainment Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Value-coincident regimes where attainment differs across the paired problems.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semidefinite Realization of Both One-Sided Orientations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two explicit two-by-two SDP pairs show that either side alone may attain under zero gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(B=(E_{12}+E_{21})/2\), the pair \[\inf\{\langle E_{11},X\rangle:\langle B,X\rangle=1,\ X\succeq0\},\qquad \sup\{y:E_{11}-yB\succeq0\}\] has common value \(0\), an unattained primal infimum, and an attained dual supremum at \(y=0\). Conversely, the pair \[\inf\{\langle E_{12}+E_{21},X\rangle:X_{11}=1,\ X_{22}=0,\ X\succeq0\},\qquad \sup\{-u:\begin{pmatrix}u&1\\1&v\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\}\] has common value \(0\), an attained primal minimum at \(X=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\), and an unattained dual supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two elementary two-by-two SDPs realize zero gap with only the dual attaining and zero gap with only the primal attaining.
assumptions_latex: Optimization is over real symmetric two-by-two matrices with the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Realization of Both One-Sided Orientations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact asymmetric-attainment subregime within finite strong duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(p^*=d^*\in\mathbb R\). One-sided attainment holds exactly when one, but not both, of the optimal solution sets is nonempty: \[(P^*\neq\varnothing,\ D^*=\varnothing)\quad\text{or}\quad(P^*=\varnothing,\ D^*\neq\varnothing).\] Equality of the optimal values alone does not exclude either orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under equal finite values, one-sided attainment means that exactly one of the primal and dual optimal solution sets is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual optimal values are finite and equal.

notation.meaning: Primal and dual optimal solution sets

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Attainment Regime

assumptions_latex: The primal and dual feasible sets are nonempty and their optimal values are finite.
The relevant feasible set need not be compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality \(p^*=d^*\) permits exactly four attainment patterns; therefore strong duality alone cannot determine whether either side attains its value.

notation.meaning: Primal and dual optimal solution sets

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality of infimum and supremum is logically independent of membership of optimizers in the feasible sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies attainment independently on the two sides of a finite strong-duality pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(p^*=d^*\in\mathbb R\). Primal attainment is the predicate \(P^*
eq\varnothing\), while dual attainment is the independent predicate \(D^*
eq\varnothing\). Thus the strong-duality regime decomposes into the four logical cases \[(P^*
eq\varnothing,D^*
eq\varnothing),\quad(P^*
eq\varnothing,D^*=\varnothing),\quad(P^*=\varnothing,D^*
eq\varnothing),\quad(P^*=\varnothing,D^*=\varnothing).\] Value equality alone excludes none of these patterns. A theorem asserting one-sided attainment therefore requires an additional hypothesis, such as Slater regularity on the opposite side or an appropriate compactness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with equal finite values, primal and dual attainment are independent; opposite-side Slater regularity or compactness is needed to force an optimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Attainment Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The four predicates are logically enumerable, but the stronger assertion that conic strong duality excludes none of the four patterns is a realizability claim requiring sourced conic examples or a precise theorem.

children.title: Finite Duality-Gap Regime
children.top_down_role: Irregular conic systems with distinct finite primal and dual values.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Duality-Gap Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible conic pairs having distinct but finite primal and dual values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(A:E\to Y\) be linear with adjoint \(A^*:Y\to E\), let \(b\in Y\), \(c\in E\), and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Define \(p^*=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and \(d^*=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\). By weak duality, \(d^*\le p^*\). The pair belongs to the finite duality-gap regime when \[p^*,d^*\in\mathbb R\qquad\text{and}\qquad g:=p^*-d^*>0.\] This definition does not specify whether either finite value is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite duality gap occurs when both conic optimal values are real and the dual supremum is strictly smaller than the primal infimum; attainment is a separate issue.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(A:E\to Y\) is linear, and \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
The primal and dual optimal values \(p^*\) and \(d^*\) are real.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite duality gap is \(g=p^*-d^*>0\), consistently with \(d^*\le p^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Finite Gap Excludes Either Slater Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary regularity failure for a canonical finite-dimensional conic pair with a positive finite gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the canonical conic pair with \(p^*,d^*\in\mathbb R\), if \(p^*-d^*>0\), then no primal feasible point lies in \(\operatorname{int}K\) and no dual feasible slack lies in \(\operatorname{int}K^*\). Either Slater condition would instead imply \(p^*=d^*\). The converse is false: failure of both Slater conditions need not produce a positive gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive finite gap requires failure of both primal and dual Slater conditions, but their joint failure is not sufficient for a gap.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual form the canonical finite-dimensional conic pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*-d^*>0\Longrightarrow\mathcal F_p\cap\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\ \text{and no dual feasible slack belongs to }\operatorname{int}K^*.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Finite Gap Excludes Either Slater Route

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementarity representation of the finite duality gap over independently feasible primal and dual points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \((y,s)\), \[\langle c,x\rangle-\langle b,y\rangle=\langle x,s\rangle\ge0.\] If both optimal values are finite, then \[p^*-d^*=\inf\{\langle x,s\rangle:x\text{ is primal feasible},\ (y,s)\text{ is dual feasible}\}.\] In the positive-gap regime every feasible tuple therefore has \(\langle x,s\rangle\ge g>0\), and equality is achieved by a feasible tuple exactly when both optimal values are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite duality gap is the infimum of primal-dual complementarity over feasible tuples, and that infimum is achieved exactly under two-sided attainment.
assumptions_latex: The primal constraint is \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\), and the dual constraint is \(A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\).
Both feasible sets are nonempty and \(p^*,d^*\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g=p^*-d^*=\inf\langle x,s\rangle>0\quad\text{in the finite positive-gap regime}.
knowledge_statements.title: Gap as Infimal Complementarity

children.title: Nonattainment Regime
children.top_down_role: Finite-value systems whose limiting optima are absent from a feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite limiting values absent from one or both feasible sets, independently of the duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(A:E\to Y\) be linear with adjoint \(A^*:Y\to E\), let \(b\in Y\), \(c\in E\), and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Define \(P=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\) and \(D=\{(y,s)\in Y\times E:A^*y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\). The primal side is nonattaining when \(p^*:=\inf_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle\in\mathbb R\) but \(P^*:=\{x\in P:\langle c,x\rangle=p^*\}=\varnothing\). Equivalently, feasible points can approach \(p^*\), but none achieves it. The dual side is nonattaining when \(d^*:=\sup_{(y,s)\in D}\langle b,y\rangle\in\mathbb R\) but \(D^*:=\{(y,s)\in D:\langle b,y\rangle=d^*\}=\varnothing\). Nonattainment is independent of whether the duality gap is zero or positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonattainment occurs when a primal infimum or dual supremum is finite but no feasible point realizes it; this is distinct from the size of the duality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(A:E\to Y\) is linear, and \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
At least one of the feasible sets \(P\) and \(D\) is nonempty with a finite corresponding optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A side is nonattaining exactly when its optimal value is finite and its optimal solution set is empty.

notation.meaning: Primal and dual optimal solution sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential signature of finite nonattainment for closed finite-dimensional conic feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(D\) be the closed feasible sets of a finite-dimensional conic pair. If \(p^*\in\mathbb R\) is not attained, then every minimizing sequence \((x_k)\subset P\) with \(\langle c,x_k\rangle\to p^*\) satisfies \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\). If \(d^*\in\mathbb R\) is not attained, then every maximizing sequence \(((y_k,s_k))\subset D\) with \(\langle b,y_k\rangle\to d^*\) satisfies \(\|(y_k,s_k)\|\to\infty\). Equivalently, a bounded optimizing sequence forces attainment on the corresponding side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every sequence approaching a finite unattained optimum escapes to infinity; a bounded optimizing sequence would yield an optimizer.
assumptions_latex: The spaces are finite-dimensional and the relevant feasible set is closed.
The relevant feasible set is nonempty and its optimal value is finite.

notation.meaning: Finite primal and dual optimal values

knowledge_statements.title: Escape of Optimizing Sequences
