children.title: Cone Projection Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Projection capability families across supported cone domains.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability property of the Euclidean projection service.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty closed convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\|\Pi_Kx-\Pi_Ky\|_2^2\leq\langle\Pi_Kx-\Pi_Ky,x-y\rangle.\] Consequently, \(\|\Pi_Kx-\Pi_Ky\|_2\leq\|x-y\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean cone projection is firmly nonexpansive and therefore cannot amplify input distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Firm Nonexpansiveness of Cone Projection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal decomposition induced by projections onto a closed convex cone and its negative polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone and \(K^\circ:=\{y:\langle y,z\rangle\leq0\ \forall z\in K\}\). Then every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \[x=\Pi_K(x)+\Pi_{K^\circ}(x),\qquad\langle\Pi_K(x),\Pi_{K^\circ}(x)\rangle=0.\] Consequently, \(\Pi_K(x)=x-\Pi_{K^\circ}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every vector decomposes into orthogonal projections onto a closed convex cone and its negative polar.
knowledge_statements.title: Moreau Cone Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp roles of closedness and convexity in the generic single-valued projection interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_1=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\). This is a nonclosed convex cone, and for \(x=(1,0)\), \(d_{K_1}(x)=0\) is not attained, so \(\Pi_{K_1}(x)\) does not exist. Let \(K_2=(\mathbb R_+\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R_+)\). This is a closed nonconvex cone, and \((1,1)\) has the two nearest points \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\), so projection is not single-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without closedness a nearest cone point may not exist, and without convexity it may not be unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projection onto \(K_1\) fails to exist at \((1,0)\), while projection onto \(K_2\) is nonunique at \((1,1)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Failure Without Closed Convexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Homogeneity and Retraction of Cone Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic properties specific to Euclidean projection onto a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\alpha\geq0\), \[\Pi_K(\alpha x)=\alpha\Pi_K(x),\qquad \Pi_K(\Pi_K(x))=\Pi_K(x).\] Moreover, \(\Pi_K(x)=x\) if and only if \(x\in K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a closed convex cone is positively homogeneous, idempotent, and fixes exactly the cone's points.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Homogeneity and Retraction of Cone Projection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential representation supplied by the Euclidean projection service.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex cone and define \(q_K(x):=\tfrac12d_K(x)^2\). Then \[q_K(x)=\tfrac12\|x-\Pi_K(x)\|_2^2,\qquad \nabla q_K(x)=x-\Pi_K(x).\] Moreover, \(q_K\) is continuously differentiable and \(\nabla q_K\) is 1-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half the squared distance to a closed convex cone is continuously differentiable; its gradient is the projection residual and is 1-Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

notation.meaning: Half the squared distance to K

knowledge_statements.title: Squared Distance from a Cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean Cone Projection and Output Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the generic projection service and exactly validates a proposed output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\Pi_K(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in K}\frac12\|z-x\|_2^2\] exists uniquely. A vector \(p\) equals \(\Pi_K(x)\) exactly when \[p\in K,\qquad \langle x-p,z-p\rangle\le0\quad\forall z\in K.\] Because \(K\) is a cone, this is equivalently \[p\in K,\qquad x-p\in K^\circ,\qquad \langle p,x-p\rangle=0,\] where \(K^\circ:=\{y:\langle y,z\rangle\le0\ \forall z\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection is the unique nearest cone point, and membership, polar residual membership, and orthogonality exactly certify its output.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p=\Pi_K(x)\iff p\in K,\ x-p\in K^\circ,\ \langle p,x-p\rangle=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Cone Projection and Output Certificate
Cone Projection Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection capability for a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the Euclidean projection interface maps each \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) to
\[
\Pi_K(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in K}\frac12\|z-x\|_2^2.
\]
The minimizer exists and is unique. Its output \(p=\Pi_K(x)\) is characterized by \(p\in K\) and \(\langle x-p,z-p\rangle\le0\) for every \(z\in K\); equivalently, \(x-p\in K^\circ\) and \(\langle p,x-p\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection returns the unique cone point nearest to the input and satisfies the standard variational and polar-cone optimality conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_K(x)\) exists uniquely and satisfies \(x-\Pi_K(x)\in K^\circ\) with \(\langle\Pi_K(x),x-\Pi_K(x)\rangle=0\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the generic projection theorem and its polar optimality characterization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection theorem and polar optimality characterization are correct and fit the projection-interface topic, but no source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Barrier Evaluation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Cone-local access to barrier values and associated derivative information.

knowledge_statements.title: Barrier Evaluation Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order oracle for an interior-point barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\operatorname{int}K\to\mathbb{R}\) be a three-times continuously differentiable convex barrier for a full-dimensional closed convex cone \(K\). A second-order barrier interface is the partial map
\[
\mathcal{B}_F(x)=\bigl(F(x),\nabla F(x),\nabla^2F(x)\bigr),\qquad x\in\operatorname{int}K.
\]
It returns a scalar, a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and a self-adjoint positive-semidefinite linear operator. For \(x\notin\operatorname{int}K\), the interface reports a domain failure rather than finite derivative data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inside the cone, the barrier oracle returns its value, gradient, and Hessian; outside the interior, evaluation fails.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a three-times continuously differentiable convex barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\).

children.title: Primal–Dual Scaling Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Cone-local scaling capabilities used by primal–dual solver machinery.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise composition of scaling services supplied by cone factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\). Suppose each factor service returns an invertible scaling map \(W_i\) satisfying \(W_iK_i=K_i\) and \(W_is_i=x_i\) for its admitted pair \((x_i,s_i)\). Then \[W=\operatorname{diag}(W_1,\ldots,W_m)\] is invertible and satisfies \(WK=K\) and \(Ws=x\), where \(x=(x_i)_i\) and \(s=(s_i)_i\). Any additional adjoint, self-adjointness, or inverse-orientation contract required of the factor services is inherited blockwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product-cone scaling service is assembled blockwise from compatible scaling services on its factors.
assumptions_latex: Each \(W_i\) is invertible, maps \(K_i\) onto itself, satisfies \(W_is_i=x_i\), and meets the same declared scaling-interface contract.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W=\operatorname{diag}(W_1,\ldots,W_m)\) satisfies \(WK=K\) and \(Ws=x\), with factorwise interface properties inherited blockwise.

notation.meaning: scaling map returned for cone factor i

review_flags: This conditional composition result does not select or define the underlying Nesterov–Todd scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Cone Scaling Decomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transport Equation Does Not Determine a Scaling Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness under an underspecified cone-automorphism interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb R_+^2\) and \(x=s=(1,1)\). Both \[W_1=I,\qquad W_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\] are invertible cone automorphisms satisfying \(W_iK=K\) and \(W_is=x\), but \(W_1\ne W_2\). Thus transport and cone-automorphism requirements alone do not determine a unique scaling operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even on the nonnegative orthant, two different cone automorphisms can transport the same dual point to the same primal point.
assumptions_latex: The interface requires only invertibility, \(WK=K\), and \(Ws=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{W:WK=K,\ Ws=x\}\text{ need not be a singleton}.
review_flags: A structural contract such as a specified quadratic representation is necessary for uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Transport Equation Does Not Determine a Scaling Operator
Primal–Dual Scaling Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nesterov–Todd scaling on a symmetric cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a symmetric cone in a Euclidean Jordan algebra and identify \(K^*=K\). For \(x,s\in\operatorname{int}K\), the Nesterov–Todd scaling interface returns the unique \(w\in\operatorname{int}K\) satisfying
\[
Q_w(s)=x,
\]
where \(Q_w\) is the quadratic representation. The operator \(Q_w\) is self-adjoint, positive definite, invertible, and maps \(K\) onto itself; hence it transports the dual interior point \(s\) to the primal interior point \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For interior primal–dual points on a symmetric cone, Nesterov–Todd scaling returns the unique cone automorphism generated by a scaling point.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a symmetric cone in a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra.

children.title: Scaling-Point Regimes
children.top_down_role: Interior regimes affecting the availability and conditioning of scaling data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Approach Can Destroy Scaling Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite scaling regime approaching a singular primal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb{S}_+^2\), let \[X_t=\operatorname{diag}(t,1),\qquad S=I,\qquad 0<t\le1.\] The positive-definite congruence factor \(W_t=X_t^{1/2}=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt t,1)\) satisfies \(W_tSW_t=X_t\). Its spectral condition number is \[\kappa_2(W_t)=t^{-1/2}\to\infty\quad\text{as }t\downarrow0.\] Thus strict interiority at each fixed \(t>0\) does not provide uniform scaling conditioning near the cone boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interior semidefinite scaling can become arbitrarily ill-conditioned as a primal or dual point approaches the cone boundary.
assumptions_latex: Scaling is represented by the positive-definite congruence factor satisfying \(W_tSW_t=X_t\).

notation.meaning: primal positive-definite matrix approaching the PSD boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Approach Can Destroy Scaling Conditioning

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singular Endpoint Excludes Invertible PSD Congruence Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact semidefinite boundary failure under a congruence-factor convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=I_2\) and \(X=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\). No invertible matrix \(W\) satisfies \[WSW^{\mathsf T}=X.\] Thus an invertible congruence-scaling service under this convention cannot admit this boundary primal point paired with the interior dual point \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible PSD congruence cannot map the identity to a singular boundary matrix.
review_flags: The boundary conclusion is specific to the stated congruence-factor convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Endpoint Excludes Invertible PSD Congruence Scaling
Scaling-Point Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible domain for symmetric-cone scaling points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a symmetric cone and let \(Q_w\) denote its quadratic representation. The strict primal–dual scaling regime is
\[
\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sc}}:=\operatorname{int}K\times\operatorname{int}K.
\]
For every \((x,s)\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sc}}\), there is a unique \(w\in\operatorname{int}K\) with \(Q_w(s)=x\). If either argument leaves \(\operatorname{int}K\), this strict scaling-point interface is outside its domain and need not return an invertible cone automorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unique invertible symmetric-cone scaling is guaranteed when both primal and dual points are strictly interior.

children.title: Barrier-Domain Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Boundary or exterior inputs for which barrier services are unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Barrier-Domain Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite barrier evaluation at or beyond the cone boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a closed convex cone. If \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\), let \(F:\operatorname{int}K\to\mathbb{R}\) be a twice continuously differentiable convex barrier satisfying
\[
x_j\in\operatorname{int}K,\quad x_j\to\bar{x}\in\partial K
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F(x_j)\to+\infty.
\]
The associated finite barrier oracle \(\bigl(F(x),\nabla F(x),\nabla^2F(x)\bigr)\) has domain \(\operatorname{int}K\); it is not required to return finite derivative data on \(\partial K\) or outside \(K\). If \(\operatorname{int}K=\varnothing\), this interior-domain oracle has an empty domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the cone has nonempty interior, a barrier oracle is defined only there and its value diverges along interior sequences approaching the boundary. If the cone has empty interior, the oracle domain is empty.
assumptions_latex: When \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\), \(F\) is a twice continuously differentiable convex barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every sequence \(x_j\in\operatorname{int}K\) with \(x_j\to\bar{x}\in\partial K\), one has \(F(x_j)\to+\infty\), and the finite barrier oracle has domain \(\operatorname{int}K\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Span reduction for a cone whose ambient interior is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty convex cone with \(L=\operatorname{span}K\). Although \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}^n}K\) may be empty, \(\operatorname{ri}K=\operatorname{int}_L K\) is nonempty. A barrier on \(\operatorname{int}_L K\) can be evaluated after the interface represents arguments in \(L\) and interprets derivatives as vectors and operators on \(L\). Merely replacing ambient interior by relative interior does not produce an invertible ambient-space Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-dimensional cone can support a barrier on its span, but the interface must reduce coordinates; relative interior alone does not make an ambient Hessian invertible.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty finite-dimensional convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}K=\operatorname{int}_L K\ne\varnothing\), and an intrinsic barrier oracle acts on \(L\), not generally on all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic-Interior Recovery for Lower-Dimensional Cones

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Cone Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative-inner-product convention for the dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its dual cone is
\[
K^*:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}.
\]
A dual-cone interface represents or tests membership in this set. The set \(K^*\) is always a closed convex cone. If \(K\) is closed and convex, the bipolar identity under this convention is \(K^{**}=K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual cone consists of vectors having nonnegative inner product with every vector in the original cone.
assumptions_latex: \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) is the ambient Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\), and closed convex \(K\) satisfies \(K^{**}=K\).

notation.meaning: dual cone under the nonnegative convention

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Cone Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonpositive-inner-product convention for the polar cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its negative polar cone is
\[
K^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\le0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}.
\]
A polar-cone interface represents or tests membership in this set. The set \(K^\circ\) is always a closed convex cone. If \(K\) is closed and convex, then \((K^\circ)^\circ=K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative polar cone consists of vectors having nonpositive inner product with every vector in the original cone.
assumptions_latex: \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) is the ambient Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le0\ \forall x\in K\}\), and closed convex \(K\) satisfies \((K^\circ)^\circ=K\).

children.title: Sign-Convention Mapping
children.top_down_role: Orientation conventions connecting dual-cone and polar-cone data.

knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Convention Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation between nonnegative dual and nonpositive polar conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
K^*:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\},
\qquad
K^\circ:=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le0\ \forall x\in K\}.
\]
Then the conventions are related exactly by
\[
K^\circ=-K^*,\qquad K^*=-K^\circ.
\]
Accordingly, a certificate \(y\in K^*\) maps to the polar certificate \(-y\in K^\circ\), and a polar inequality \(\langle z,x\rangle\le0\) maps to the dual inequality \(\langle -z,x\rangle\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual and negative-polar conventions differ only by negation, so certificates translate by changing sign.
assumptions_latex: Dual and polar cones use the displayed nonnegative and nonpositive conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Certificate Rejection Is Not Status Refutation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of an independent certificate-interpretation interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(v)\) be the exact model-level predicate assigned to the declared certificate role of a submitted vector \(v\). If the interpretation interface accepts only after verifying \(P(v)\), acceptance establishes the conclusion implied by \(P(v)\). If the interface rejects because \(P(v)\) fails or cannot be verified, the only valid conclusion is that this submitted vector was not validated. Rejection does not imply that no other valid certificate exists or that the claimed problem status is false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Passing a sound exact certificate predicate proves its claimed status, but rejecting one submitted vector does not disprove that status.
assumptions_latex: Each supported certificate role has a sound exact predicate \(P\).
Acceptance occurs only after \(P(v)\) is verified.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Variable Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine left-inverse recovery for primal variables represented in a finite-dimensional canonical cone program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) be embedded as \(z=Tx+t\in\mathbb R^p\), where \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) is linear and \(t\in\mathbb R^p\). Given \(\widehat z\in\mathbb R^p\), recover \(\widehat x=R\widehat z+r\), where \(R:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^n\) is linear and \(r\in\mathbb R^n\). This recovery is exact for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) represented by \(z=Tx+t\) if and only if \(RT=I_n\) and \(Rt+r=0\). For an approximate solver output, original-model feasibility must be evaluated at \(\widehat x\) rather than inferred solely from canonical feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover the model variable using an affine left inverse of the canonical embedding. It is exact on the entire model-variable space exactly when RT is the identity and Rt+r is zero; approximate recovered values must be checked in the original model.
assumptions_latex: The model-variable and canonical spaces are \(\mathbb R^n\) and \(\mathbb R^p\), respectively.
Canonicalization uses \(z=Tx+t\), with linear \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) and \(t\in\mathbb R^p\).
Recovery uses \(x=Rz+r\), with linear \(R:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^n\) and \(r\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact recovery for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is equivalent to \(RT=I_n\) and \(Rt+r=0\).

children.title: Auxiliary Variable Elimination
children.top_down_role: Treatment of canonicalization variables absent from the source model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness of auxiliary values after source-variable recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For recovered \(\widehat x\), let \(r=q-M_x\widehat x\). An auxiliary recovery satisfying \(M_ww=r\) exists exactly when \(r\in\operatorname{range}M_w\). If \(w_0\) is one solution, every solution is in \(w_0+\ker M_w\), and the auxiliary value is unique exactly when \(\ker M_w=\{0\}\). Nonuniqueness is harmless for a reported source quantity only when that quantity is invariant on this affine solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary recovery requires range consistency; all recoveries differ by kernel elements, with uniqueness exactly under injectivity.
assumptions_latex: \(M_x\) and \(M_w\) are compatible finite-dimensional linear maps.
\(\widehat x\) is a recovered source-model value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{w:M_ww=q-M_x\widehat x\}\) is empty or equals \(w_0+\ker M_w\), and is a singleton exactly when \(\ker M_w=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Residual assigned to the auxiliary block

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Recovery Solution Set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical recovery choice when a bridge auxiliary block is consistent but not injective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=q-M_x\widehat x\). If \(r\in\operatorname{range}M_w\), then \[w^\dagger:=M_w^\dagger r\] is the unique solution of \(M_ww=r\) having minimum Euclidean norm. Every solution has the form \(w^\dagger+v\) with \(v\in\ker M_w\), and \(\langle w^\dagger,v\rangle=0\). If \(r\notin\operatorname{range}M_w\), no exact auxiliary recovery exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a consistent nonunique auxiliary system, the pseudoinverse returns its unique minimum-norm recovery; inconsistency precludes exact recovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(r\in\operatorname{range}M_w\), then \(M_w^\dagger r\) is the unique minimum-norm solution of \(M_ww=r\).

notation.meaning: Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse of the auxiliary block

knowledge_statements.title: Recovery Consistency Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Post-recovery validation in the original finite-dimensional model and across a finite family of bridge equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let recovered values \((\widehat x,\widehat s,\widehat w)\) correspond to the model equation \(A x+s=b\) with \(s\in K\). Fix \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), a finite index set \(J\), bridge residual maps \(G_j\), and tolerances \(\varepsilon_j\ge 0\) for every \(j\in J\). Recovery passes the consistency check when \(\|A\widehat x+\widehat s-b\|\le\varepsilon\), \(\operatorname{dist}(\widehat s,K)\le\varepsilon\), and \(\|G_j(\widehat x,\widehat s,\widehat w)\|\le\varepsilon_j\) for every \(j\in J\). Passing establishes consistency only at the stated tolerances; it does not establish exact feasibility or optimality unless the relevant tolerances are zero and all required optimality predicates are separately checked.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovery is consistent at the declared tolerances only when the original affine residual, distance to the cone, and every specified bridge residual satisfy their respective bounds.

The adjoint identity alone establishes only equality of the bridge pairing; it does not establish dual feasibility or optimality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, nonuniqueness, and sign failures associated with linear residual transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the directed bridge \(\widehat r=T r\), every fixed solver multiplier \(\widehat y\) induces the unique source coefficient \(T^*\widehat y\), but a prescribed source multiplier has a solver-space representative only when it lies in \(\operatorname{range}(T^*)\); that representative is nonunique exactly when \(\ker(T^*)\neq\{0\}\). In particular, residual reversal has \(T=-I\) and requires \(y=-\widehat y\). Retaining the same multiplier sign after reversal changes the Lagrangian pairing unless the multiplier-residual pairing vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adjoint range controls representability, the adjoint kernel controls solver-multiplier nonuniqueness, and reversing a residual requires reversing its multiplier sign.
assumptions_latex: The residual bridge is \(\widehat r=T r\) between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Recovery Range and Sign Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjoint recovery through an explicitly directed linear residual bridge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(F\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let a source residual \(r(x)\in E\) be mapped to the solver residual \(\widehat r(x)=T r(x)\in F\), and let \(\widehat y\in F\) multiply \(\widehat r\). The induced source multiplier is \(y=T^*\widehat y\), since \(\langle\widehat y,Tr(x)\rangle_F=\langle T^*\widehat y,r(x)\rangle_E\). For a chain \(T_m\cdots T_1\), recovery applies adjoints in reverse order: \(y=T_1^*\cdots T_m^*\widehat y\). Any residual reversal or dual-versus-polar convention change is represented by its own declared linear map and is therefore included in the same adjoint composition.
