The conic-geometry citation does not establish the reverse bridge maps, offset omission, or layer-specific sign conversions.

children.title: Status-Accuracy Qualification Crosswalk
children.top_down_role: Mapping solver-specific termination codes to modeling-interface status families.

children.title: Solver Termination Status Families
children.top_down_role: Solver termination codes grouped by modeling-interface outcome category.

assumptions_latex: A solver run terminates with a finite code \(\tau\).
The interface supplies a documented interpretation map \(F\) from native codes to semantic families.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The semantic termination family is \(F(\tau)\), not a claim about numerical accuracy.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: termination families conventionally separate logical outcomes from numerical qualifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic partition of native termination codes, independent of accuracy qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solver termination status family is the value \(F(\tau)\) assigned to a native code \(\tau\) by a documented map whose codomain is \(\{\mathrm{optimal},\mathrm{primal\ infeasible},\mathrm{dual\ infeasible},\mathrm{limit},\mathrm{numerical\ failure},\mathrm{interrupted},\mathrm{unknown}\}\). The family records the solver's logical termination interpretation. It does not by itself assert exactness, a residual bound, or the availability of a primal point, dual point, or certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A documented map groups native solver codes into logical outcome families without silently asserting numerical accuracy or solution availability.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver Termination Status Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition structurally fits the leaf, but the proposed family codomain is an interface-specific taxonomy with no authoritative solver-status specification or cited crosswalk.

children.title: Accuracy Qualification Levels
children.top_down_role: Accuracy labels attached to reported solution or certificate outcomes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit on interpreting a residual qualification as distance to an exact reported object.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H(u)=0\) collect the exact predicates required of a reported object and suppose \(\|H(\widehat u)\|\le\varepsilon\). This residual bound alone need not bound \(\operatorname{dist}(\widehat u,H^{-1}(0))\). If an error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(u,H^{-1}(0))\le\kappa\|H(u)\|\) holds on the relevant neighborhood, then \(\operatorname{dist}(\widehat u,H^{-1}(0))\le\kappa\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual qualification becomes a forward-error guarantee only when an applicable conditioning or error-bound estimate is available.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a specified residual map with \(H^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A residual bound alone gives no general forward-error bound; under the stated error bound, \(\operatorname{dist}(\widehat u,H^{-1}(0))\le\kappa\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Residual map for the reported object

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-to-Forward-Accuracy Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Qualification Is Scale Dependent Without Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of declared residual normalization for portable accuracy levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(u)=0\) be an exact scalar predicate and let \(c>0\). The equations \(h(u)=0\) and \(ch(u)=0\) have the same exact solution set, but in general \[|h(\widehat u)|\leq\varepsilon\quad\not\Longleftrightarrow\quad|ch(\widehat u)|\leq\varepsilon.\] Hence a residual-based accuracy level is invariant under equivalent rescalings only when the interface prescribes compatible residual normalization or rescales the corresponding threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent rescalings preserve exact solutions but can change a raw residual qualification, so portable accuracy levels require declared normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Raw residual thresholding is not representation invariant without compatible normalization or threshold scaling.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Qualification Is Scale Dependent Without Normalization

assumptions_latex: A solution or certificate has normalized residual vector \(r\in\mathbb R_+^q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The strongest attained level is the smallest \(j\) with \(\|r\|_\infty\le\varepsilon_j\); no level is attained if none exists.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: residual thresholds provide a checkable accuracy hierarchy
threshold values and residual normalization require an interface specification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based accuracy levels independent of the solver's logical termination family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix normalized residual components \(r_1,\ldots,r_q\) covering every predicate required for the reported object and ordered tolerances \(0\le\varepsilon_1<\cdots<\varepsilon_m\). Accuracy level \(j\) is attained when \(\|r\|_\infty\le\varepsilon_j\). The reported qualification is the strongest attained level, namely the smallest such \(j\). If no threshold is met or a required residual is unavailable, the result is unqualified rather than assigned an accuracy level by termination code alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign the strongest accuracy level whose threshold bounds every required normalized residual; missing or excessive residuals leave the result unqualified.
knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy Qualification Levels

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold rule is coherent only after an interface defines every normalized residual, threshold, and the convention that smaller indices denote stronger levels. No source supplies those definitions.

children.title: Status–Accuracy Crosswalk
children.top_down_role: Supported pairings between interface status families and accuracy levels.

assumptions_latex: A native code \(\tau\) has semantic family \(F(\tau)\).
An independently computed qualification \(Q(r)\) is available from original-model residuals \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The crosswalk returns \((F(\tau),Q(r))\) only when the required result object exists and both components are compatible.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: logical status and numerical accuracy are orthogonal interface outputs
concrete crosswalk table requires an authoritative solver-interface specification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility rule joining logical status with independently measured accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The status-accuracy crosswalk maps a native termination code and recovered result to the pair \((F(\tau),Q(r))\). A solution-bearing family may receive an accuracy qualification only when the required primal or dual object exists. An infeasibility or unboundedness family may receive one only when a corresponding back-mapped certificate exists and its defining residuals were evaluated. Limit, interruption, or numerical-failure families remain distinct even when an incumbent satisfies some tolerance; the incumbent may be reported separately with \(Q(r)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combine logical status with independently checked accuracy only when the appropriate solution or certificate exists; keep limit and failure outcomes distinct.
knowledge_statements.title: Status–Accuracy Crosswalk

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orthogonality of logical status and measured accuracy is reasonable, but the concrete compatibility rules need an authoritative interface specification. The statement also mentions an unboundedness family that is absent from the preceding proposed codomain.

children.title: Ambiguous or Unsupported Termination Codes
children.top_down_role: Solver codes lacking a unique or supported interface-level classification.

assumptions_latex: The native code \(\tau\) is absent from the documented map or admits multiple incompatible interpretations.
No independently verified original-model certificate resolves the ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface must return \(\mathrm{unknown}\) or \(\mathrm{unsupported}\) and must not infer optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unsupported codes cannot soundly imply a semantic optimization status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservative behavior outside the documented termination-code mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\tau\notin\operatorname{dom}F\), or if available metadata permits two incompatible values of \(F(\tau)\), the termination code is unsupported or ambiguous. In the absence of a separately verified original-model certificate, no semantic claim of optimality, primal infeasibility, dual infeasibility, or unboundedness follows. The interface returns \(\mathrm{unknown}\) or \(\mathrm{unsupported}\), preserves the native code for diagnosis, and may expose recovered iterates only as unqualified candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unknown or multiply interpretable native codes cannot imply an optimization outcome; preserve the code and expose any iterate only as an unqualified candidate.
knowledge_statements.title: Ambiguous or Unsupported Termination Codes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conservative failure boundary fits the leaf, but the mandated unknown-or-unsupported behavior and exposure of iterates are interface policy claims without a source. Unsupported is also not included in the preceding proposed codomain of F.

children.title: Cone-Interface Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Canonicalization and result-recovery failures specific to cone-domain interfaces.

children.title: Domain-Closure Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Incorrect handling of open-domain expressions and closed cone representations.

children.title: Open-Domain Expression Semantics
children.top_down_role: Source expressions whose valid inputs exclude domain boundary points.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The effective domain remains exactly \(D\); replacing it by \(\overline D\) changes the expression unless boundary values are separately specified.

notation.meaning: effective domain of an extended-real-valued function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-value semantics for expressions whose finite domain is open.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extended-real interpretation of \(f\) is the function \(\bar f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) defined by \[\bar f(x)=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}\] Thus \(\operatorname{dom}\bar f=D\), not \(\overline D\). A cone-interface formulation is semantically exact only if its decoded feasible set excludes every point of \(\overline D\setminus D\), or if the expression has been explicitly extended to those boundary points with the intended values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open-domain expression is infinite outside its stated domain. A conic encoding that admits closure boundary points changes its semantics unless boundary values are explicitly defined.
knowledge_statements.title: Open-Domain Expression Semantics

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes an open-domain expression from the function obtained by closing its epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex, and suppose \(g(x):=\liminf_{z\to x}f(z)\) is proper. Then \(g\) is the lower-semicontinuous hull of \(f\) and \[\operatorname{epi}g=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}.\] The function \(g\) may be finite at points of \(\overline{\operatorname{dom}f}\setminus\operatorname{dom}f\); consequently it is a closed extension and need not have the original open-domain semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing the epigraph of a proper convex expression yields its proper lower-semicontinuous hull, which may assign finite boundary values and is therefore a new extension.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuous Closed Extension

children.title: Closed-Cone Representation Limits
children.top_down_role: Limits arising when a solver cone includes the closure of a source domain.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible set \(F^{-1}(K)\) is closed, so a nonclosed domain cannot have this exact representation without lifting, projection, or additional semantics.

notation.meaning: inverse image of the cone under the constraint map

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit for direct continuous preimages of closed solver cones.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(K\) is closed and \(F\) is continuous, the direct conic feasible set \[S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:F(x)\in K\}=F^{-1}(K)\] is closed. Consequently, if \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonclosed, then no direct formulation \(D=\{x:F(x)\in K\}\) of this form exists. A lifted closed-cone set may have a nonclosed projection, but then exactness depends on the projection and attainment semantics and does not follow merely from closedness of the lifted cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous preimage of a closed cone is closed. Therefore a direct closed-cone constraint cannot exactly describe a nonclosed domain, although lifted projections require separate analysis.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Cone Representation Limits

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

children.title: Boundary-Point Misclassification
children.top_down_role: Incorrect feasibility or status outcomes associated with domain boundaries.

assumptions_latex: An interface replaces strict positivity by membership in \(\mathbb{R}_+\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The boundary point \(x=0\) is falsely classified as feasible although the original expression is undefined there.

notation.meaning: natural logarithm on the positive ray

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical strict-domain error at a closure boundary point.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the expression \(f(x)=-\log x\), whose effective domain is \(D=(0,\infty)\). If a cone interface encodes its domain only by \(x\in\mathbb{R}_+\), the decoded feasible set is \([0,\infty)=\overline D\). Hence \(x=0\) satisfies the conic membership test but does not belong to \(\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(f(0)\) is not a finite real value. The interface has therefore produced a false feasible classification at the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding strict positivity as nonnegativity admits zero. For a logarithmic expression, zero then passes the cone test even though the expression is outside its domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Point Misclassification

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

children.title: Closure-Induced Model Drift
children.top_down_role: Changes in source-model meaning caused by replacing an open domain with its closure.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Induced Model Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model drift caused solely by replacing a domain with its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(0,\infty)\) and minimize \(f(x)=x\) over \(D\). Then \(\inf_{x\in D}f(x)=0\), but no \(x\in D\) attains this value. Replacing \(D\) by \(\overline D=[0,\infty)\) gives \(\min_{x\in\overline D}f(x)=0\), attained at \(x=0\). Thus closure can preserve the infimum while changing feasibility at the boundary, existence of an optimizer, and any solver status or certificate that asserts attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing x over x>0 has infimum zero but no optimizer. Closing the domain adds x=0 and creates an attained optimum, changing status and certificates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal value stays \(0\), but attainment changes from absent to present; thus closure changes the optimization model.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value Preservation Does Not Imply Attainment Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General optimization-model drift caused by closing the feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(f:\overline D\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous. Then \[\inf_{x\in D}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\overline D}f(x).\] If the minimum over \(\overline D\) is attained, the original problem attains that value if and only if \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\overline D}f(x)\cap D\neq\varnothing\). Thus equality of optimal values does not imply equality of optimizer sets or attainment status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous objective has the same infimum on a nonempty domain and its closure, but closure may create boundary optimizers and change attainment status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_D f=\inf_{\overline D}f,\qquad D\text{ attains this value}\iff\operatorname*{argmin}_{\overline D}f\cap D\ne\varnothing.

notation.meaning: topological closure of the original domain

knowledge_statements.title: Value Preservation Does Not Imply Attainment Preservation

children.title: Cone-Convention Translation Failures
children.top_down_role: Semantic corruption caused by incompatible cone conventions.

children.title: Coordinate Ordering Conventions
children.top_down_role: Cone-coordinate layouts whose differing orderings affect data interpretation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact translation of a slack-form cone block and all row-aligned data between coordinate orderings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be a permutation matrix. For \(Ax+s=b\) with \(s\in K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), define \(A'=PA\), \(b'=Pb\), \(s'=Ps\), and \(K'=PK\). Then \(Ax+s=b,\ s\in K\) is equivalent to \(A'x+s'=b',\ s'\in K'\). If the receiver leaves the cone unchanged, validity for every slack holds exactly when \(PK=K\). A row-indexed dual vector must be stored as \(y'=Py\), for which \(\langle y',s'\rangle=\langle y,s\rangle\) and \((A')^{\mathsf T}y'=A^{\mathsf T}y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate permutation must be applied to the cone, affine rows, right-hand side, slack, and row-indexed dual vector. An unchanged cone is valid only when it is permutation invariant.

notation.meaning: permutation matrix translating the row-coordinate ordering
dual vector indexed by affine rows

review_flags: Corrects the malformed formulas in the deferred seed.
knowledge_statements.title: Consistent Coordinate Permutation

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is the cone expected by the solver.
\(P\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) is a permutation matrix describing the interface ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A coordinate reordering is valid exactly when the transmitted cone is \(PK\), or when \(PK=K\) if the solver cone is left unchanged.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition for exchanging cone coordinates between interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the model produces \(z\infK\) and transmits \(w=Pz\). Exact cone membership is preserved when the receiving solver tests \(w\in PK\), because \[z\in K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Pzin PK.\] If the receiver instead tests \(w\in K\), the ordering convention is valid for every model vector exactly when \(PK=K\). Otherwise there exists \(z\in K\) with \(Pz\notin K\), so an otherwise feasible cone block can be rejected or an infeasible block accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A permutation must also be applied to the cone. Leaving the solver cone unchanged is valid only when that cone is invariant under the coordinate permutation.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Ordering Conventions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordering condition is mathematically plausible and appropriately classified as a condition, but no source is supplied. The statement also contains malformed expressions such as \(z\infK\) and \(Pzin PK\), which must be repaired after sourcing.

children.title: Sign Convention Reversals
children.top_down_role: Semantic corruption caused by incompatible primal, slack, or multiplier signs.

assumptions_latex: Dual cones use the pairing \(\langle y,s\rangle\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reversing residual sign requires replacing \(K\) by \(-K\) and transforms a compatible dual vector by \(y'=-y\).

notation.meaning: dual cone under the nonnegative-pairing convention

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent residual forms under simultaneous cone and multiplier transformation.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 A primal-dual interior-point method p. 44
source_refs.source_title: Advances in Linear Matrix Inequality Methods in Control

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The residual convention \[s=b-Ax\in K\] is equivalent to \[s'=Ax-b=-s\in -K.\] Under \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,s\rangle\ge 0\text{ for every }s\in K\}\), one has \((-K)^*=-K^*\). Therefore the corresponding dual multiplier is \(y'=-y\), which preserves the pairing \(\langle y',s'\rangle=\langle y,s\rangle\). Reversing only the residual, cone, or multiplier sign is not this equivalence and can reverse feasibility or dual inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing b-Ax to Ax-b requires negating the cone and dual multiplier as well. Negating only part of this representation changes feasibility or dual signs.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign Convention Reversals

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 A primal-dual interior-point method p. 44
source_witnesses.source_title: Advances in Linear Matrix Inequality Methods in Control

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for leaving a cone unchanged while reversing every possible residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), the equivalence \(s\in K\Longleftrightarrow -s\in K\) for every \(s\in\mathbb{R}^m\) holds exactly when \(K=-K\), equivalently when \(K\) is a linear subspace. Thus reversing a residual while leaving its cone unchanged preserves every cone-membership constraint only in this sign-invariant regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual can be negated without changing its cone only when the cone is sign invariant, which for a convex cone means it is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall s,\ s\in K\iff -s\in K)\iff K=-K\iff K\text{ is a linear subspace}.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Invariant Cone Exception

children.title: Primal–Dual Cone Identification
children.top_down_role: Convention choices governing identification of primal cones with their dual counterparts.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Cone Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between valid self-dual identification and general dual-cone handling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual cone is \[K^*=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m:\langle y,s\rangle\ge 0\text{ for every }s\in K\}.\] Using \(K\) for both primal slacks and dual multipliers is valid exactly when \(K=K^*\) under the interface's chosen coordinates and inner product. More generally, after an invertible coordinate change \(z=Ts\), the primal cone becomes \(TK\), whereas its dual becomes \(T^{-\mathsf T}K^*\). Applying \(T\) to both blocks therefore need not preserve primal-dual identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver may reuse one cone for primal and dual blocks only under self-duality in the same pairing. Coordinate changes transform primal and dual cones differently.
assumptions_latex: The dual cone is defined using a specified Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal and dual cone blocks may be identified only when self-duality has been established in the same coordinates and inner product.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

children.title: Convention Translation Failures
children.top_down_role: Cases where interface conventions cannot be translated without changing model meaning.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic semantic boundary common to coordinate, sign, and primal-dual convention translations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the set of source representations accepted under one convention, let \(T\) be the bijective translation applied to transmitted representations, and let \(S'\) be the set accepted by the receiving convention. Translation preserves feasibility for every represented object exactly when \(T(S)=S'\). If \(T(S)\ne S'\), then some transmitted object is classified differently, so the unpaired convention translation changes model meaning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convention translation preserves feasibility exactly when it maps the source acceptance set onto the receiver's acceptance set; otherwise some object is misclassified.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a bijection between the two representation spaces}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\forall z,\ z\in S\iff Tz\in S'\bigr)\iff T(S)=S'.

notation.meaning: acceptance set under the source convention
acceptance set under the receiving convention

knowledge_statements.title: Unpaired Convention Transformation Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a cone not invariant under a proposed permutation \(P\).
The receiver tests the transmitted vector against \(K\) without translating the cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unpaired convention translation changes the feasible set.

notation.meaning: two-dimensional nonnegative ray on the first coordinate axis

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete feasibility failure from an untranslated coordinate convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[K=\{(t,0):t\ge 0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2,\qquad P(z_1,z_2)=(z_2,z_1).\] The vector \(z=(1,0)\) belongs to \(K\), but the transmitted vector \(Pz=(0,1)\) does not. Hence a receiver that interprets \(Pz\) using the original cone \(K\), rather than the translated cone \(PK\), rejects a feasible point. The same mechanism applies to any sign, ordering, or primal-dual translation that is not accompanied by its mathematically required cone transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Swapping coordinates while retaining a non-invariant cone can turn a feasible vector into an infeasible one. Unpaired sign or dual-cone translations fail by the same mechanism.
knowledge_statements.title: Convention Translation Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinate-swap example is correct, but no citation supports it, and the final sentence extends the example broadly to sign and primal-dual translations without stating their distinct transformations and hypotheses.

children.title: PSD Packed-Storage Consistency Boundary
children.top_down_role: Matrix reconstruction failures caused by incompatible packed-storage conventions.

children.title: Packed-Triangle Ordering
children.top_down_role: Upper-triangle or lower-triangle coordinate layouts used for symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal serialization convention for symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_n=\{(i,j):1\le j\le i\le n\}\) and \(q=n(n+1)/2\). A packed lower-triangle ordering is a bijection \(\pi:I_n\to\{1,\ldots,q\}\). For \(X\in\mathbb{S}^n\), the unscaled packed vector satisfies \[[p_\pi(X)]_{\pi(i,j)}=X_{ij}.\] Upper-triangle storage is analogous. Two interfaces agree only when they use the same triangle and bijection or explicitly convert between them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Packed symmetric storage is specified by a triangle and a bijection from its entries to vector positions.
knowledge_statements.title: Packed-Triangle Ordering

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact coordinate conversion between triangular serialization orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_{\pi_1}\) and \(p_{\pi_2}\) store the same triangular entries with identical scaling but different ordering bijections. There is a unique permutation matrix \(P\) such that \[p_{\pi_2}(X)=Pp_{\pi_1}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathbb{S}^n.\] The change is semantics-preserving only when all aligned primal vectors, dual vectors, coefficient vectors, and reconstruction maps are transformed by the corresponding permutation or inverse permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any two orderings of the same scaled triangular entries differ by a unique permutation, which must be applied consistently to all aligned data.
assumptions_latex: The packings store the same triangular index set.
The packings use identical coordinate scaling.

notation.meaning: permutation converting the first ordering to the second

knowledge_statements.title: Permutation Equivalence of Packed Orderings

children.title: Off-Diagonal Scaling Conventions
children.top_down_role: Normalization choices applied to packed off-diagonal matrix entries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isometric scaling convention for singly stored off-diagonal entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed triangular ordering, define \(\operatorname{svec}(X)\) by storing \(X_{ii}\) on diagonal coordinates and \(\sqrt2X_{ij}\) once for every \(i>j\). Then for all \(X,Y\in\mathbb{S}^n\), \[\operatorname{svec}(X)^{\mathsf T}\operatorname{svec}(Y)=\sum_iX_{ii}Y_{ii}+2\sum_{i>j}X_{ij}Y_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\langle X,Y\rangle_F.\] Without the \(\sqrt2\) factor, an ordinary Euclidean packed-vector product underweights every off-diagonal contribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying each singly stored off-diagonal entry by square root of two makes Euclidean packed-vector products equal Frobenius matrix products.
assumptions_latex: Each unordered off-diagonal entry is stored once.
knowledge_statements.title: Square-Root-of-Two Off-Diagonal Scaling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unscaled Packing with a Weighted Coordinate Metric
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent metric formulation of square-root-of-two coordinate scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{vech}(X)\) store diagonal entries and one copy of each off-diagonal entry without scaling. Let \(W\) be diagonal in the same order, with weight \(1\) on diagonal coordinates and \(2\) on off-diagonal coordinates. Then \[\langle X,Y\rangle_F=\operatorname{vech}(X)^{\mathsf T}W\operatorname{vech}(Y).\] Hence unscaled packing is geometrically equivalent to square-root-of-two packing when the packed space uses this weighted metric, equivalently after applying \(W^{1/2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unscaled triangular storage preserves Frobenius geometry under a coordinate metric that weights off-diagonal entries by two.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{vech}\text{ stores each unordered off-diagonal entry once}.

notation.meaning: packed metric with off-diagonal weight two

knowledge_statements.title: Unscaled Packing with a Weighted Coordinate Metric

assumptions_latex: Each unordered off-diagonal pair is stored once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scaling every stored off-diagonal entry by \(\sqrt2\) makes the Euclidean packed-vector product equal the Frobenius matrix product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isometric scaling convention for singly stored off-diagonal entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any fixed triangular ordering, define \(\operatorname{svec}(X)\) by storing \(X_{ii}\) on diagonal coordinates and \(\sqrt2 X_{ij}\) on coordinates corresponding to \(i>j\). Then \[\operatorname{svec}(X)^{\mathsf T}\operatorname{svec}(Y)=\sum_i X_{ii}Y_{ii}+2\sum_{i>j}X_{ij}Y_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\langle X,Y\rangle_F.\] If off-diagonal entries are stored without the factor \(\sqrt2\), the ordinary Euclidean vector product omits the second copy of each symmetric off-diagonal contribution and is not the Frobenius product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying singly stored off-diagonal entries by square root of two makes packed-vector dot products equal symmetric-matrix Frobenius products.
knowledge_statements.title: Off-Diagonal Scaling Conventions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The square-root-of-two scaling representation is mathematically correct and matches the leaf, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Matrix Reconstruction Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency of symmetric matrix recovery from packed solver coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact round-trip criterion for PSD packed-storage compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E:\mathbb{S}^n\to\mathbb{R}^{n(n+1)/2}\) be the sender's packing map and \(R:\mathbb{R}^{n(n+1)/2}\to\mathbb{S}^n\) the receiver's reconstruction map. They are reconstruction-consistent exactly when \[R(E(X))=X\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathbb{S}^n.\] This requires agreement on the stored triangle, coordinate ordering, and inverse scaling. The identity implies \(X\succeq0\iff R(E(X))\succeq0\) and preserves every matrix objective and constraint pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Packing and unpacking are consistent exactly when their composition recovers every symmetric matrix; triangle, ordering, and scaling must all agree.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Reconstruction Consistency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scaling-Mismatch Reconstruction Can Change PSD Membership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal witness that inconsistent off-diagonal reconstruction changes the represented cone point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[X=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\] If the sender stores the off-diagonal coordinate as \(\sqrt2X_{12}\) but the receiver treats that coordinate as the unscaled matrix entry, it reconstructs \[\widehat X=\begin{pmatrix}1&\sqrt2\\\sqrt2&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Its eigenvalues are \(1+\sqrt2\) and \(1-\sqrt2<0\), so \(\widehat X\) is indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-one two-by-two PSD matrix becomes indefinite when square-root-of-two packed scaling is decoded as unscaled storage.
assumptions_latex: The sender scales the stored off-diagonal coordinate by \(\sqrt2\).
The receiver does not undo that scaling.

notation.meaning: matrix reconstructed under the incompatible convention

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Mismatch Reconstruction Can Change PSD Membership

children.title: Inner-Product Preservation
children.top_down_role: Preservation of matrix-space geometry across vectorization conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint Conversion of Packed Linear Functionals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion between Euclidean packed coefficients and Frobenius-paired matrix coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the packing \(E_w\) above with nonzero weights, a packed vector \(a\) represents \(X\mapsto\langle C,X\rangle_F\) through \(a^{\mathsf T}E_w(X)\) if and only if \[C_{ii}=w_{ii}a_{ii},\qquad C_{ij}=C_{ji}=\frac{w_{ij}}{2}a_{ij}\quad(i>j).\] Thus coefficient decoding is governed by the adjoint of the packing map; it coincides with inverse coordinate conversion only when the packing is a Frobenius isometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Packed primal coordinates and packed functional coefficients use adjoint scaling; an off-diagonal matrix coefficient is half the corresponding weighted packed contribution.
assumptions_latex: E_w\text{ stores each unordered off-diagonal entry once}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a^{\mathsf T}E_w(X)=\langle C,X\rangle_F\ \forall X\iff C_{ii}=w_{ii}a_{ii},\ C_{ij}=w_{ij}a_{ij}/2.

notation.meaning: symmetric coefficient matrix under the Frobenius pairing

knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Conversion of Packed Linear Functionals

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Isometry Weights for Symmetric Packing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient weights for preservation of the Frobenius inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_w(X)\) store \(w_{ii}X_{ii}\) for each diagonal entry and \(w_{ij}X_{ij}\) once for each \(i>j\), in any fixed order. Then \[E_w(X)^{\mathsf T}E_w(Y)=\langle X,Y\rangle_F\quad\text{for all }X,Y\in\mathbb{S}^n\] if and only if \(w_{ii}^2=1\) for every \(i\) and \(w_{ij}^2=2\) for every \(i>j\). With positive weights, \(w_{ii}=1\) and \(w_{ij}=\sqrt2\). A common ordering permutation does not affect the identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-copy symmetric packing preserves Frobenius products exactly with unit-magnitude diagonal weights and square-root-of-two-magnitude off-diagonal weights.
assumptions_latex: Each diagonal entry and each unordered off-diagonal entry is stored once.
Packed coordinates use the ordinary Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E_w(X)^{\mathsf T}E_w(Y)=\langle X,Y\rangle_F\ \forall X,Y\in\mathbb{S}^n\iff w_{ii}^2=1,\ w_{ij}^2=2.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Isometry Weights for Symmetric Packing

assumptions_latex: A linear packing stores each diagonal entry once and each unordered off-diagonal entry once.
Packed coordinates use the ordinary Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Frobenius inner-product preservation holds exactly when diagonal weights have squared magnitude \(1\) and off-diagonal weights have squared magnitude \(2\).

notation.meaning: weight assigned to matrix entry i,j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact weight criterion for an isometric symmetric-matrix packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_w(X)\) store \(w_{ii}X_{ii}\) for each diagonal entry and \(w_{ij}X_{ij}\) once for each \(i>j\), in any fixed order. Then \[E_w(X)^{\mathsf T}E_w(Y)=\langle X,Y\rangle_F\quad\text{for all }X,YinfS^n\] if and only if \(w_{ii}^2=1\) for every \(i\) and \(w_{ij}^2=2\) for every \(i>j\). With positive weights this uniquely gives \(w_{ii}=1\) and \(w_{ij}=\sqrt2\). Ordering permutations do not affect the equality when applied consistently to both vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-copy triangular packing preserves Frobenius products precisely with unit diagonal weights and square-root-of-two off-diagonal weights, up to harmless signs and consistent permutations.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Product Preservation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated weight criterion is mathematically correct for one-copy triangular packing, but no source is supplied and statement_latex contains the malformed expression \(X,YinfS^n\), which should be \(X,Y\in\mathbb{S}^n\).

children.title: Cone-Block Descriptor Consistency Boundary
children.top_down_role: Invalid cone descriptors, block offsets, exponent parameters, or matrix side dimensions.

children.title: Cone-Block Dimension Consistency
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between declared cone-block sizes and associated data segments.

assumptions_latex: The cone descriptor is an ordered list \(D=(d_1,\ldots,d_q)\) of blocks.
Each block descriptor \(d_i\) determines a finite-dimensional cone \(K_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\).

notation.meaning: dimension implied by cone block i

review_flags: Exact solver-interface convention lacks a directly matching supplied source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to ordered product-cone descriptors in finite-dimensional solver interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the solver cone be the ordered product \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_q\), where the descriptor of block \(K_i\) implies dimension \(n_i\in\mathbb{N}\). A cone-domain vector \(s\in\mathbb{R}^N\) is dimension-consistent with the descriptor exactly when
\[
N=\sum_{i=1}^{q}n_i.
\]
Any declared total dimension differing from this sum, or any block whose declared dimension differs from the dimension determined by its cone type and parameters, violates cone-block dimension consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product-cone descriptor is consistent exactly when its block dimensions are valid and sum to the solver vector dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Block Dimension Consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but the block-dimension convention and cone-type parameter interpretation require an inspectable solver-interface source.

children.title: Block Offset Alignment
children.top_down_role: Alignment of cone-block boundaries within concatenated solver vectors.

review_flags: Offset conventions vary across solver APIs; a matching interface specification is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses zero-based half-open indexing; one-based interfaces require the corresponding index shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For ordered cone blocks of dimensions \(n_1,ldots,n_q\), let block \(i\) occupy the half-open coordinate slice \([o_i,o_{i+1})\). The offsets are aligned exactly when
\[
o_1=0,qquad o_{i+1}=o_i+n_i\quad(1le ile q),qquad o_{q+1}=N.
\]
Thus the slices are contiguous, pairwise disjoint, preserve descriptor order, cover every coordinate in \(\{0,ldots,N-1\}\), and contain exactly \(n_i\) coordinates each. A gap, overlap, permutation, or incorrect terminal offset is an alignment failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block offsets must define contiguous, nonoverlapping slices in descriptor order and cover exactly the entire cone-domain vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Block Offset Alignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-based alignment condition fits the leaf, but no interface specification supports this indexing convention. The statement also contains malformed commands such as `ldots`, `qquad`, and `le` without backslashes.

children.title: Cone Parameter Admissibility
children.top_down_role: Validity ranges for parameters attached to parameterized cone families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies only when the descriptor explicitly denotes the conventional nondegenerate three-dimensional power-cone family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\alpha<1\), define \[K_\alpha=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ |z|\le x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\}.\] Under the conventional nondegenerate power-cone descriptor, the exponent is admissible exactly when \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Endpoint or out-of-range values are not admissible descriptors for this declared family, irrespective of whether a separate interface defines limiting cones for them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conventional nondegenerate three-dimensional power-cone descriptor requires an exponent strictly between zero and one.
assumptions_latex: The selected family is the conventional nondegenerate three-dimensional power cone.
Coordinates use the displayed order and exponent convention.

notation.meaning: three-dimensional power cone with exponent alpha

review_flags: Endpoint handling, dual-cone flags, and coordinate ordering must be checked against the concrete interface.
knowledge_statements.title: Conventional Three-Dimensional Power-Cone Exponent Domain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the nondegenerate weight convention; interfaces that explicitly allow zero weights use a different admissibility domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(m\ge2\), \(k\ge1\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R^m\), define \[K_\alpha^{m,k}=\left\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^k:\|z\|_2\le\prod_{i=1}^m x_i^{\alpha_i}\right\}.\] Under the conventional nondegenerate descriptor, the weights are admissible exactly when \(\alpha_i>0\) for every \(i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1\). Zero weights describe reducible limiting cases and are admissible only if the selected interface expressly includes them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nondegenerate generalized power-cone weights lie in the relative interior of the probability simplex.
assumptions_latex: The descriptor denotes the displayed nondegenerate generalized power-cone family.
The interface does not expressly extend the family to zero-weight limiting cases.
review_flags: Some mathematical definitions or APIs admit zero weights; their declared parameter domain controls.
knowledge_statements.title: Conventional Generalized Power-Cone Weight Domain

assumptions_latex: Each cone family \(\tau\) has a specified parameter domain \(P_\tau\).
The descriptor supplies a cone type \(\tau\) and parameter tuple \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The descriptor is admissible if and only if \(p\in P_\tau\).

notation.meaning: parameter tuple supplied for the cone block
admissible parameter domain for the cone family

review_flags: Admissible parameter domains are solver- and cone-family-specific.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract interface condition; each supported cone family must separately specify its parameter domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone-block descriptor \((\tau,p)\) is parameter-admissible precisely when \(p\in P_\tau\), where \(P_\tau\) is the interface-specified domain for cone family \(\tau\). Membership must ensure that every encoded size is integral and positive where required, every real shape parameter lies in its permitted range, and the parameters determine a well-defined closed convex cone of the declared block dimension. If \(p\notin P_\tau\), the descriptor is invalid before numerical solution, even when its serialized fields are syntactically well formed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone descriptor is admissible only when all family-specific size and shape parameters lie in the cone type's declared domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone Parameter Admissibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract admissibility condition fits the leaf, but the substantive requirements encoded by each parameter domain are solver- and cone-family-specific and have no cited source.

children.title: Matrix-Side Dimension Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between matrix dimensions and cone descriptors derived from them.

assumptions_latex: The canonical constraint is \(Ax+s=b\) with \(s\in K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the slack-form minimization convention \(Ax+s=b\), \(s\in K\).

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the conic program
\[
\operatorname{minimize}_{x,s}\;c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax+s=b,\qquad s\in K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m},
\]
matrix-side dimensions are compatible exactly when \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(x,c\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), and \(b,s\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\). Moreover, the product-cone descriptor for \(K\) must have total dimension \(m\). These conditions make the objective scalar, the affine equation well typed, and cone membership defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rows of the constraint matrix must match the cone vector, while its columns must match the decision and objective vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Side Dimension Compatibility

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

children.title: Canonicalization-Recovery Semantic Integrity
children.top_down_role: Loss or corruption of source-model meaning across canonicalization and recovery.

children.title: Source-Semantics Preservation
children.top_down_role: Preservation of source-model meaning across interface canonicalization.

assumptions_latex: A source model has feasible set \(F\subseteq X\) and objective \(f:F\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\).
Canonicalization produces feasible set \(G\subseteq Z\) with objective \(g:G\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\).

notation.meaning: recovery map from canonical to source variables

review_flags: No supplied locator directly addresses modeling-system canonicalization semantics.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact semantic preservation, excluding numerical tolerances and approximate recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Canonicalization with recovery map \(R:G\to X\) preserves source semantics when
\[
R(G)=F\qquad\text{and}\qquad g(z)=f(R(z))\quad\text{for every }z\in G.
\]
Consequently, every canonical-feasible point recovers to a source-feasible point with the same objective value, and every source-feasible point has at least one canonical-feasible representative with that value. Hence the source and canonical optimal values agree, including the extended-real cases of infeasibility or unboundedness under the adopted conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonicalization preserves semantics when recovery maps canonical feasible points onto source feasible points without changing objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Source-Semantics Preservation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The surjective, objective-preserving recovery criterion is coherent and the property kind fits, but no source supports this particular definition of modeling-system semantic preservation.

children.title: Canonical Bridge Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Equivalence boundaries between source constructs and bridged cone representations.

assumptions_latex: The source and canonical models have feasible sets \(F\subseteq X\) and \(G\subseteq Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist maps \(E:F\to G\) and \(R:G\to F\) satisfying \(R\circ E=\operatorname{id}_F\) and \(g\circ E=f\).

notation.meaning: embedding into the canonical feasible set
recovery into the source feasible set
identity map on the source feasible set

review_flags: No supplied locator directly specifies bridge equivalence for canonicalization systems.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence permits multiple canonical representatives of one source point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A canonical bridge is equivalent to the source model when there exist maps \(E:F\to G\) and \(R:G\to F\) such that
\[
R\circ E=\operatorname{id}_F,qquad g(E(x))=f(x)quad(x\in F),qquad g(z)=f(R(z))quad(z\in G).
\]
The first equality makes every source-feasible point representable and recoverable; the objective equalities exclude distortion in either direction. The map \(E\circ R\) need not equal \(\operatorname{id}_G\), because auxiliary canonical variables may admit several equivalent representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bridge is equivalent when source points embed into canonical form, recover unchanged, and objective values agree in both directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Bridge Equivalence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the leaf, but the equivalence criterion lacks a source. The statement also contains malformed `qquad` and `quad` text where TeX commands were intended.

children.title: Primal Recovery Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss or corruption of source primal values during reverse mapping.

assumptions_latex: The canonical solver returns a point \(z\in G\).
The intended source recovery map is \(R:G\to X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal recovery fails when \(R(z)\notin F\), \(f(R(z))\ne g(z)\), or \(R(z)\) is undefined.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly characterizes recovery failures in solver interfaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic failure criterion for exact recovered primal points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a canonical primal point \(z\in G\), primal recovery succeeds only if \(R(z)\) is defined, \(R(z)\in F\), and \(f(R(z))=g(z)\). Therefore primal recovery failure occurs whenever
\[
R(z)\text{ is undefined},qquad R(z)notin F,qquad\text{or}qquad f(R(z))ne g(z).
\]
Failure may arise from an incomplete inverse transformation, inconsistent reconstruction of eliminated variables, or selection of auxiliary values that do not satisfy the source constraints, even though \(z\) satisfies the canonical constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal recovery fails when no source point is produced, the recovered point is infeasible, or its objective value is distorted.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Recovery Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, but the recovery criterion and listed mechanisms lack supporting evidence. The displayed formula also contains malformed `notin` and `ne` text without backslashes.

children.title: Dual Recovery Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss or corruption of source multipliers during reverse mapping.

assumptions_latex: A canonical dual certificate is \(y\in Y\).
The source model has a dual-certificate set \(D\) and recovery map \(R_d:Y\to D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual recovery fails when \(R_d(y)\) is undefined, is not in \(D\), or does not preserve the certified identity.
review_flags: Dual sign and certificate conventions depend on the canonical bridge and require a matching source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract criterion covering multipliers, dual slacks, and bridge-specific sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in Y\) satisfy the canonical dual feasibility and certificate equations. Dual recovery succeeds only when \(R_d(y)\) is defined, belongs to the valid source certificate set \(D\), and preserves the pairing or objective identity certified by \(y\). Dual recovery fails if any of these conditions is false. In particular, omitted bridge multipliers, incorrect adjoint transformations, or reversed constraint signs can yield a recovered object outside \(D\) or change the bound it certifies, despite canonical dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual recovery fails when transformed multipliers are missing, invalid, or certify a different bound because adjoints or signs were mishandled.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Recovery Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind fits, but the required pairing or objective identity is not explicitly defined, and its form depends on bridge-specific dual and sign conventions for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Auxiliary Variable Leakage
children.top_down_role: Exposure or misinterpretation of bridge-generated variables in source-level results.

assumptions_latex: Canonical variables decompose as \(z=(x,u)\), with source variables \(x\) and auxiliary variables \(u\).
The public recovery map should return an element of the source space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Auxiliary leakage occurs when the reported result is not invariant under changes of \(u\) that preserve the represented source point.
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses public-interface leakage of canonical auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concerns semantic output boundaries, not internal storage of auxiliaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose canonical points have the form \(z=(x,u)\), where \(u\) was introduced solely to represent the source model. A source-level result map \(Q\) is free of auxiliary leakage when there exists \(\widehat Q:X\to X\) such that
\[
Q(x,u)=\widehat Q(x)
\]
for every canonical-feasible \((x,u)\). Leakage occurs if the reported source solution contains coordinates of \(u\), requires users to interpret \(u\), or changes when \(u\) changes while the represented source point \(x\) remains fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary leakage occurs when internal canonicalization variables appear in, or improperly influence, the reported source-level solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary Variable Leakage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure phenomenon fits the leaf, but the domain and codomain of Q are not introduced, and the proposed public-interface invariance criterion has no supporting source.

children.title: Solution-Certificate Round-Trip Validation
children.top_down_role: Independent validation of reconstructed models, solutions, and reported certificates.

children.title: Model Round-Trip Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency between source models and representations recovered after solver-interface translation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A minimal semantic failure independent of serialization equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the source model have feasible set \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R:x\ge0\}\) and constant objective zero. If encoding followed by decoding produces \(\widehat F=\{x\in\mathbb R:x\le0\}\), then \(F\ne\widehat F\); thus the reconstructed model is not semantically equivalent to the source model regardless of names or constraint ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing a nonnegative scalar domain into a nonpositive domain is a round-trip failure because the feasible sets differ.
assumptions_latex: Source and reconstructed variables share the stated scalar interpretation.
review_flags: This example does not select a complete interface-specific equivalence contract.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Round-Trip Failure

assumptions_latex: Encoding maps a source model \(M\) to a canonical model \(C(M)\).
Decoding maps the canonical representation back to source semantics.
review_flags: The equivalence relation for interface round trips requires a modeling-system specification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic equivalence allows harmless reordering and renaming of internal objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A model interface is round-trip consistent when
\[
D(C(M))\equiv M,
\]
where \(\equiv\) means equality of the source feasible set, source objective on that set, optimization sense, and declared cone semantics. Equality of serialization bytes is unnecessary: constraint ordering, internal names, and equivalent auxiliary representations may differ. Round-trip consistency fails if encoding followed by decoding changes feasibility, objective values, optimization sense, variable domains, or the interpretation of any cone block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding and decoding must reproduce the same feasible set, objective, optimization sense, and cone meanings, up to harmless representation changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Model Round-Trip Consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is coherent and fits the round-trip leaf, but the selected components of semantic equivalence require a modeling-interface specification or other inspectable source.

children.title: Primal Solution Validation
children.top_down_role: Independent checks of recovered primal values against source-model semantics.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Solution Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based validation for the slack-form primal conic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal conic program
\[
\min_{x,s} c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax+s=b,\quad s\in K,
\]
a reported pair \((\widehat x,\widehat s)\) is validated as primal feasible at tolerances \((\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_K)\) only if
\[
\lVert A\widehat x+\widehat s-b\rVert\le\varepsilon_p,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(\widehat s,K)\le\varepsilon_K.
\]
The norm, distance, and scaling convention must be declared. This certificate establishes approximate primal feasibility; it establishes optimality only when paired with a valid dual point and an acceptable duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate a primal solution by checking its affine residual and distance to the declared cone under explicit tolerances.
assumptions_latex: The primal problem is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax+s=b,\ s\in K\}\).
A candidate pair \((\widehat x,\widehat s)\) and tolerances \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_K\ge0\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validation accepts only if \(\lVert A\widehat x+\widehat s-b\rVert\le\varepsilon_p\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(\widehat s,K)\le\varepsilon_K\).

notation.meaning: distance induced by the selected norm

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

review_flags: Tolerance scaling and norm choice remain interface-specific.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation dependence of unscaled absolute feasibility tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the same affine equality be represented as \(Ax+s=b\) or, for \(\alpha>0\), as \(\alpha(Ax+s-b)=0\). For residual \(r=A\widehat x+\widehat s-b\), fixed unscaled absolute tests require respectively \(\lVert r\rVert\le\varepsilon\) and \(\alpha\lVert r\rVert\le\varepsilon\). When \(\varepsilon>0\), these tests can disagree unless the tolerance is transformed with the representation. Exact zero-residual validation is invariant under every \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed absolute residual tolerance is not invariant under rescaling an equality, whereas exact zero-residual validation is invariant.
assumptions_latex: The two affine equations differ only by multiplication by \(\alpha\).
The same norm and fixed absolute tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\) are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert r\rVert\le\varepsilon\) and \(\alpha\lVert r\rVert\le\varepsilon\) need not be equivalent when \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Absolute-Residual Scaling Boundary

children.title: Dual Solution Validation
children.top_down_role: Independent checks of recovered multipliers against source dual conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Solution Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual validation under the slack-form minimization sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal convention
\[
\min_{x,s} c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax+s=b,\quad s\in K,
\]
the corresponding dual feasibility conditions are \(A^{\mathsf T}y+c=0\) and \(y\in K^*\). A reported \(\widehat y\) is validated at tolerances \((\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_{K^*})\) only if
\[
\lVert A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y+c\rVert\le\varepsilon_d,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(\widehat y,K^*)\le\varepsilon_{K^*}.
\]
This certifies approximate dual feasibility; an optimality claim additionally requires a compatible primal point and an acceptable primal-dual objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate a dual solution by checking the adjoint residual and membership in the dual cone under the interface's sign convention.
assumptions_latex: The primal convention is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax+s=b,\ s\in K\}\).
A candidate \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and tolerances \(\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_{K^*}\ge0\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validation accepts only if \(\lVert A^{\mathsf T}y+c\rVert\le\varepsilon_d\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K^*)\le\varepsilon_{K^*}\).

source_refs.source_title: Advances in Linear Matrix Inequality Methods in Control
source_refs.locator: 2.2 A primal-dual interior-point method p. 44

review_flags: Dual signs, norm scaling, and objective convention must match the implemented interface.

source_witnesses.source_title: Advances in Linear Matrix Inequality Methods in Control
source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 A primal-dual interior-point method p. 44

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Validated Dual Bound and Primal-Dual Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective consequence of exact dual validation under the leaf's sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min_{x,s}c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax+s=b,\ s\in K,\] let \(y\in K^*\) satisfy \(A^{\mathsf T}y+c=0\). Every primal-feasible \((x,s)\) then satisfies \[-b^{\mathsf T}y\le c^{\mathsf T}x,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y=\langle s,y\rangle\ge0.\] Thus \(-b^{\mathsf T}y\) is a certified lower bound; together with primal feasibility, zero pairing certifies optimality of both points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exactly validated dual point supplies the lower bound minus b dot y, and its gap with a primal-feasible point equals the nonnegative slack-dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: -b^{\mathsf T}y\le c^{\mathsf T}x,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y=\langle s,y\rangle\ge0.

notation.meaning: dual objective under the stated slack-form sign convention

knowledge_statements.title: Validated Dual Bound and Primal-Dual Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Dual Feasibility Need Not Certify a Global Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of residual-only dual validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_d=A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y+c\). For every primal-feasible \((x,s)\), \[c^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}\widehat y=\langle s,\widehat y\rangle+r_d^{\mathsf T}x.\] If \(z\in K^*\) and \(e=\widehat y-z\), then \[c^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\ge-\|s\|\,\|e\|_*-\|x\|\,\|r_d\|_*.\] Consequently, residual and cone-distance tolerances alone do not yield a rigorous global bound when feasible \(x\) or \(s\) are unbounded; exact feasibility or certified bounds controlling both error terms are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small stationarity and cone-distance residuals alone need not give a rigorous objective bound on an unbounded feasible region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\ge-\|s\|\|e\|_*-\|x\|\|r_d\|_*;\ \text{tolerances alone need not certify a global bound}.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Dual Feasibility Need Not Certify a Global Bound

children.title: Infeasibility Certificate Validation
children.top_down_role: Independent assessment of certificates supporting reported infeasibility.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone, with dual cone \(K^*=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle s,x\rangle\ge 0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
The decoded model feasibility system is \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), where \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(A^*:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is the adjoint of \(A\).
The solver certificate is mapped back to a vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) in the model's original coordinates.

notation.meaning: Dual cone of the primal cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validation of a decoded Farkas-type certificate sufficient to establish infeasibility of a conic equality system.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Infeasibility Certificates p. 106
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the conic feasibility system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), a decoded vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) passes a sufficient exact infeasibility-certificate validation when its dimensions and coordinate mapping are consistent and
\[
A^*y\in K^*,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0.
\]
Successful exact validation certifies \(\{x\in K:Ax=b\}=\varnothing\). Under the stated assumptions, these predicates are not asserted to be necessary for every infeasible conic system. Tolerance-based checks validate only the corresponding approximate predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate the decoded vector by checking coordinate consistency, dual-cone membership of the adjoint image, and a strictly negative pairing with the right-hand side. Passing these exact checks is sufficient to certify infeasibility, but the checks are not claimed to characterize every infeasible conic system.
knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Certificate Validation

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Infeasibility Certificates p. 106

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal system showing that certificate rejection does not imply feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb{S}_+^2\) and require \[X_{11}=0,\qquad X_{12}=1.\] This is infeasible because a PSD matrix with \(X_{11}=0\) must have \(X_{12}=0\). Nevertheless, \(\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\1&t\end{psmallmatrix}\) approaches \(K\) in distance as \(t\to\infty\), so the system is weakly infeasible. For \(A(X)=(X_{11},X_{12})\) and \(b=(0,1)\), the condition \(A^*y\succeq0\) forces \(y_2=0\), hence \(\langle b,y\rangle=0\); no strict seed-form certificate exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PSD conditions X11=0 and X12=1 are infeasible but arbitrarily close to feasibility, and no adjoint-PSD multiplier has a negative right-hand-side pairing.
knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Infeasible Two-by-Two PSD System

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Certificates and the Closed Attainable Image
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between strongly and weakly infeasible conic systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), let \(C=A(K)\). In finite dimension, a vector \(y\) satisfying \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\) exists if and only if \(b\notin\overline C\). Thus every strongly infeasible system admits a strict seed-form certificate, while a weakly infeasible system with \(b\in\overline C\setminus C\) is infeasible but admits no certificate passing that strict test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict Farkas certificate exists exactly when the right-hand side lies outside the closure of the attainable conic image; weakly infeasible systems have no such certificate.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is a nonempty closed convex cone in finite dimension}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Certificates and the Closed Attainable Image

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Rescaling and Normalization of Strict Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale invariance of an exact strict infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\), then every \(\alpha y\) with \(\alpha>0\) satisfies the same predicates. In particular, \[\widetilde y=\frac{y}{-\langle b,y\rangle}\] satisfies \(A^*\widetilde y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,\widetilde y\rangle=-1\). Normalization is valid only after independently verifying the strict negative pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict infeasibility certificate is invariant under positive scaling and can be normalized to right-hand-side pairing minus one.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Rescaling and Normalization of Strict Certificates

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
The decoded minimization model is \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), where \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear.
The solver output is decoded into \((x_0,d)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\) in the model's original coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validation of a decoded certificate of primal unboundedness for a conic minimization model.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the conic minimization problem \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), a decoded pair \((x_0,d)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\) is a valid primal-unboundedness certificate when its dimensions and coordinate mapping are consistent and
\[
x_0\in K,
\quad Ax_0=b,
\quad d\in K,
\quad Ad=0,
\quad \langle c,d\rangle<0.
\]
Successful exact validation certifies \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}=-\infty\). A direction satisfying only the recession and improvement conditions does not by itself certify primal unboundedness unless feasibility is also validated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate a feasible base point and a cone-feasible nullspace direction with strictly negative objective slope. Passing all exact checks certifies primal unboundedness; an improving recession direction alone is insufficient without validated feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness Certificate Validation

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary showing that a positive homogeneous-residual tolerance does not certify exact unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(K=\mathbb{R}_+\), and consider \[\inf\{-x:\varepsilon x=0,\ x\in K\}.\] Its feasible set is \(\{0\}\), so its optimal value is \(0\). Nevertheless, \(x_0=0\) is feasible and \(d=1\in K\) satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}d=-1<0\) and \(\lVert Ad\rVert=\varepsilon\). Thus a validator accepting \(\lVert Ad\rVert\le\varepsilon\) can accept an apparent improving direction for a bounded problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded one-variable conic problem can pass a positive-tolerance ray test, so exact unboundedness requires an exact nullspace condition or certified error bounds.
assumptions_latex: The validator accepts the homogeneous residual whenever \(\lVert Ad\rVert\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert Ad\rVert\le\varepsilon\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) do not imply primal unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Ray False Positive
